Q26.text: The academic system is failing doctoral students, who are some of the most vulnerable at universities. If there are serious problems between advisors and students, often students do not have the resources or power to ask for help. Q26.text: I am very lucky in that I found a program that has been a really great fit for me, but there’s a certain lack of transparency between the mentor faculty and students that is the main frustration I have with the academic system at my university. For example, our first year is spent rotating through different labs until we decide which to do our dissertation work in. Faculty aren’t always honest about whether they have the funding to support students beyond the rotation and often use it as an excuse to not keep students they were unhappy with, rather than explaining what they didn’t find satisfactory about their work. One PI said “I didn’t get any students for two years after I told a student I didn’t think my lab was a good fit and they told others I was mean so now I just tell them I won’t have the money to pay their stipend so they choose not to stay”. I understand it’s a hard conversation to have but it’s rather disheartening to know that we can’t count on honest feedback when we’re here to be trained.

Q26.text: Ate o momento, consigo  perceber que fazer um Doutorado em um pais com uma cultura extremamente diferente e que e automaticamente refletida na cultura educacional, e um desafio tremendo, que tem impacto direto na saude mental dos estudantes. Por exemplo, venho da cultura ocidental, onde hierarquias quase sao nulas (as relacoes sao bem horizontais); a autonomia, a proatividade e a liberdade no ambiente academica sao consideradas como qualidade e bem vistas pelos Professores; o equilibrio entre vida pessoal e profissional tambem sao bem vistos e devem co-existir. Entretanto, no Japao, a sociedade e extremamente hierarquizada e essa hierarquia e refletida fortemente no ambiente academico, onde os professores sao tomam uma posicao enorme de poder e respeito, colocando-os em uma posicao inacessivel ao estudante. E isso abre tambem precedentes gravissimos para a quase institucionalizacao do abuso moral e de poder (e, uma vez, que a hierarquia e sumariamente respeitada, esses episodios quase nao sao reportados por parte dos estudantes). Ainda, considerando esse posicionamento dos professores nessa hierarquia engessada, os estudantes nao sao bem vistos se questionam, apresentam personalidade e demandam discussao (a relacao e sempre muito de submissao e negacao de discussoes). E, por ultimo, o Japao e reconhecido como o lugar que as longas jornadas de trabalho 12-14 horas por dia sao bem vistas (nao import se isso leva a uma produtividade ou nao, se a pessoa esta sofrendo ou nao), o status valorizado aqui e quantas horas voce se mantem no ambiente de trabalho e anule a sua vida pessoal. Desse modo, a ciencia aqui, que demanda debate, discussao, opinioes e completamente negada pelo sistema hierarquico, bem como sao valorizados os estudantes que vao se degradando fisicamente ao longo do seu Doutorado. Adicionalmente, o Japao e um pais, extremamente xenofobico e, enquanto estudante internacional, esse preconceito e sentido em cada detalhe da vida academica, onde, nao importa o que voce faca, atinja ou demonstre: no final e cada esquina, voce sera sumariamente desacreditado, descredibilizado e desencorajado. E, toda essa situacao nao se aplica a mim, se estende a todos os outros estudantes internacionais que aqui convivo. E algo realmente muito grave e dificil de mudar.

Q26.text: First of all, in the Netherlands, bright people are leaving academia due to the lack of grants. It is very hard to pursue an academic career when you stay in the Netherlands. Therefore, I moved to the USA to follow working in academia as a postdoctoral researcher, and I hope that this experience will give me (some) advantage in grant applications when I move back to the Netherlands in 3-4 year.   Secondly, although i started working as a postdoctoral researcher here in the USA, I am still finishing my PhD program, due to the Dutch system. As molecular cell biologists, we need to have 2 published papers and a third submitted to a peer-reviewed journal, before you can finish your thesis and set a date for a defense. Since publishing has become harder over the years (more data needed, extensive peer-review cycles that are both very consuming when the manuscript is rejected after review and needs to be submitted elsewhere where the whole cycle will start again), I have not been able to finish my PhD in the time set to do so. I started as a PhD-student in August 2013 and was supposed to finish in 4 years. Then, I was extended with one year and I left for a postdoc in Augstus 2018. To date, June 2019, I'm still not finished since manuscript acceptance takes too long.   I was lucky that my new PI here in the USA was understanding that defense in the Netherlands depends on publications, but officially I am not working as a postdoc now, but as a research specialist on a postdoc project. I know of a lot of Dutch colleagues that had to let go of their dream of a postdoc in the USA, because of this problem.  I think it is unfavorable that PhD programs differ so much between countries. I think the Dutch system aims for a very high standard, which I like, but it diminishes opportunities to succeed later in your academic life.

Q26.text: Academia can be a great place to be - its a unique environment that can be relaxed and creative. Ultimately though, academia is geared towards giving power and a sense of entitlement to PIs, and has lost sight of its responsibilities regarding student wellbeing. Universities have given such power and status to PIs that they can't even control them anymore. PIs don't respect university/HR systems and standard work place etiquette.    A lovely example of academia failings: I collaborate with industry and have 1 university PI and 2 industrial PIs. I have had my industrial PI make inappropriate comments to me ranging from sexual harassment to being purely nasty. One example to give you a flavour: whats happened to your skin? how do you expect to be taken seriously when you look like a spotty teenager - you should really cover your spots up. Q26.text: The academic system is designed to train PhD students to become PIs. In the process of doing so, PhD students gain valuable experience and transferable skills that make them competent and resourceful individuals. However, the expectation is very much that you would continue on to a post-doc position. This, in my view, is not a good thing given the relatively few academic jobs available. PhD programmes should establish closer links to industry and and other non-research related science careers to ensure that PhD students gain the skills aligned with these careers after they graduate, and build networks to facilitate job opportunities. PhD programmes and institutions also do not articulate well enough the capabilities of PhD graduates to employers in the wider sector, and can improve on this.  PIs and funding bodies have a lot of incentive to employ PhD students and post-docs in the short term on temporary contracts, but the academic system should incentivise instead the hiring of permanent staff scientists for those who want to be in the lab full-time. For those that don't, greater exposure to other career paths (eg. talks, networking opportunities, work experience placements and internships) is needed for PhD students' career progression.  In many cases, poor supervision from the PI and a negative group environment can detract from the PhD experience - this is really hard to judge from a short interview.

My advisor quit her job as a professor and left me with no funding for my final semester of grad school, plus she has been a poor advisor overall because she is consistently underprepared, late, or distracted. The PhD has made me hate academia and question myself on every level, especially when it comes to the value of a PhD. Q26.text: The academic system needs a drastic overhaul. It has become a corrupt and abusive system. I would like to see major reforms at every single level. Most research is published for the sole reason of publishing a paper. Papers and impact factors have become the currency of academia; the desire to do Science for the sake of progress or humanity is largely non-existent. Most places and people care about the length of the CV, but no thought is spared towards the impact these studies may have had. Further, the Ph.D. student is left at the mercy of the supervisor and the academic system which tends to protect itself when questioned. Universities have become brands and they care too much about their brands. Harassment cases are quietly stamped out to protect the university's and the supervisor's reputation. This is true more so for international students who put their entire careers and lives on the line to work towards their Ph.D.s on a pittance. Lip service is paid to women empowerment, but women are consistently left out at every possible turn. A strong teaching effort is drummed up by universities, but everyone knows teaching takes away from one's ability to manufacture papers. It looks incredibly bleak for academia unless one is well-connected and comes with the right brand and backing. The way I see it, academia has stagnated and it does not look like things are changing for the better any time soon. Of course, one can write an entire article, and many have been written without much effect, about the publication system and the exorbitant cost of acquiring "knowledge" in today's world.

Q16.text: I find it absolutely baffling that academia, while propped up as the last bastion of ethical and moral purity, tolerates faculty and students with alarming behavioral issues. In my experience, I have seen faculty members get away with sexual harassment and abuse at multiple universities with supreme confidence. Further, the biggest lesson I have received during my Ph.D. is that academia rarely cares about merit or quality. There are, to the best of my knowledge, only two ways to get ahead: my advisor is well connected and/or I somehow manage to find my way onto a Nature or Science publication. Maybe this is to be expected given the shortage of jobs, but it makes academia an ideal breeding ground for abusive relationships. I also find that enough is not done to make incoming students understand how slim the chances of an academic career really are, post Ph.D. Maybe it is too much, and not even the point of a Ph.D., to train students for careers outside of academia. However, the system is nothing short of a scam if incoming students are, at the very least, not made aware of the reality of the job market. Precious few universities and departments actively expose their students to opportunities outside of academia by encouraging participation in workshops, conventions, presentations, alumni networks, etc. And no, it is not the sole responsibility of the incoming student to know how the job market is. It is similar to arguing that sweatshops employing immigrants in the Middle Eastern countries carry none of the blame and arguing instead that the blame must rest on the people working there "voluntarily".  And make no mistake, academia today is eerily similar to a sweatshop.

Q60.text: Yes! I entered my dissertation program focusing on research that bridges two different fields. In the beginning of my program, I was revered for that smart, forward-thinking twist to my research, and I was told repeatedly this is where the field needs to go (inter-disciplinary). Now, I am struggling to finish my dissertation, because every topic I suggest for my dissertation has been rejected by everyone in the department, since it is not traditionally within my field. And I never wanted this to happen to me, I had three options (I knew they were feasible, because another graduate student I worked with previously swiped one of those topics and graduated early and with praise) for dissertation topics as I entered the PhD program, because I knew I didn't want to be like other students I saw in my department that just appeared to take funding opportunities away from everyone while not progressing to graduation. Now I am that student. I even had a NSF DDIG proposal ready to submit (edits from the department lasted over 5 months, and it was ready!), and I was told they day of submission to our Office of Research, I should not submit, because no one in the department could supervise the project. I have since seen students AND professors independently come across those topics I have been steered away from, and those topics have been funded by major federal institutions, and the research yielded multiple publications in noteworthy journals. I am doing a dissertation project now that was not my idea, I have been handed the data, and it is my job just to analyze data that no one has used since the 1980's, just so I can graduate in 6 years. I know I sound like a complainer who is blaming everyone else for my problems. Maybe that is the case. I am saddened, because with those rejected topics have also gone my rose-colored glasses about the ability of research in academia to allow you to pursue passion projects. And even though my department publicly touts inter-disciplinary projects, there is no support for that in my department. It clearly took me too long for that to sink in.   Overall, I wish I had a mentor explain those hard facts to me; I wish I was smart enough to read between the lines to see inter-disciplinary research is not what my department produces; and I wish it did not have to be that way. Now, I just hope to graduate (later than I intended and with a project I am not sure contributes to modern society in any way), find an academic job (seemingly a one-in-a-million chance), and work to support inter-disciplinary research every day of my life.

This was a huge disappointment for me, because I thought I would have a strong and deep mentorship on research practice in the university setting.  The publish-or \-perish mentality is also a waste of the little time professors and postdocs have. This mentality makes people push for half-backed research results  (or hyped buzzwords) in order to increase publication count (or be present at a conference). The result (in my field at least) is a flood of low quality papers that are 90% written by students. This low quality takes enormous time from reviewers and makes conferences boring as participants barely ask questions or discuss the topics. Q60.text: When the survey questions uses the term "programme", it makes me assume that there should be a structure in the PhD graduate studies. I don't believe there is a structure, and I am not sure that it is possible or desirable to have one. Graduate school is not like the undergraduate school. While the undergrad school looks like a production of line of professionals, the graduate school experience is more of a one-to-one coaching. Therefore, "programme" could be a misleading term. I would not like to be in a strict standardized PhD program. I would rather have access to senior researchers who would actively advise me in various topics.   Now, we face the worst of the two worlds. US PhD programs are littered with artificial barriers, e.g., required lectures, required exams, required publications, required teaching assistant practice, etc). Meanwhile, these programs do not provide access to senior researchers (only to busy professors who don't practice research themselves because they are overloaded with lectures and administrative duties).   I think the survey should have also explored the topic of conferences and workshops. Conferences and workshops are sometimes advocated as events for students to get feedback. However, they are overcrowded, professors are busy meeting other professors, and people barely ask questions after the talks. The exception was the Doctoral Symposiums, where PhD Students get feedback on their research from a panel o professors. This was a great experience that I have in more than one conference.  The survey could have addressed bullying more deeply. As a graduate student, I saw the bullying of colleagues as the most serious issue in the university that I attended (UC Irvine). I would like to see more awareness and discussion about that. Is bullying cultural? Or is it a consequence of excessive competition in the US academic system?

In my case, I can't complain as much given that apart from working long hours and some things not going as you expected, I have been lucky with my supervisors which have always looked for a way to pay me a salary and fund the projects for my PhD thesis. Regarding my University, I only have contact with it when I have to pay the enrollment fees each year and visit the evaluation board that follows what I have been doing during that year (a 5-minute meeting). I do not receive any specific training but they do offer some seminars that you can attend to if you have the time (which is never).   As I said, although my experience has been good, I do consider that overall doing a PhD is not well valued nor recognized as one of the highest degrees, if not the highest. We are well trained and educated people with careers, masters and lots of experience. Although we are overqualified, we are normally underpaid and work extra hours, not only at the lab/office but also at home. This includes weekends. Therefore, the "underpayment" increases while your life balance decreases. Moreover, none of this assures you a stable, successful or any kind of future which is very unsettling and makes you kind of want to be a PhD student the rest of your life. Not sure this is an academic system issue alone but it is clear that the number of PhD student keeps increasing, and the present and future working conditions do not increase with it.

Q26.text: I find the academic system flawed and the concept of the positions outdated. In my mind, you should not be catagorized on each degree or position you complete, but evaluated by seniority and experience like on the job market. Citing a paper from the researcher who also wrote something similar but published later than us: just because the editor told the PI to do this and this editor happens to be an immediate colleague and dept. chair, a short-term researcher created problem for me by circulating the fact that I am imposing more work, but that was not true as it's for the PI to decide in this person's case and I asked this person to inform the PI about her problem-well this person never did so, infact later put the blame on me again-and this time my PI started giving me explanations! What I write here is just a short compact incidents which needs more expansion for a proper explanation. There have been few more instances. So it's for the PIs: that if a topic is not their expertise then they should rely on the expertise of their students who are doing the actual work, treat your student's proposal as your own which means if you don't send your own full proposal to someone you have never met-do the same for the students, just because a person is european and is talkative doesn't necessarily mean that the other  non-european student is stupid!

Q26.text: The academic system that we follow was set up with the right ethos. But in the execution we have all collectively faltered. It was one field of work which accommodated heterogeneity and diversity in all forms especially ideas and way of life but increasingly the system is trying to homogenize people making them loose their individuality. In older studies, journals reviewed and argued the science behind what the authors did, but now they review and make authors add more experiments which they want to see not necessarily needed for proving what the authors did. If big data is the current trend every research group is expected to have omics in their paper.  There is also this wave of applied research which as a standalone field is very good but inadvertently penetrates into basic research. All research cannot be applied immediately. Lots of drugs that are there in the market exist because their mechanism of action was a phenomenon some graduate student/post doc uncovered which could eventually get targeted. The original study may not even have proposed it. This also encourages researchers to portray hypothetical forced biomedical applications of their research findings and mislead people  when actually there may be none.  I also feel the system inherently assumes that people in academia don't have a life beyond work. They reinforce this assumption in their expectations from students and PIs. In fact its almost considered unusual if you are single and want to leave for home at decent hours after work. Family is the qualifier you need to enjoy time after work. This notion is largely in India. There are other inherent assumptions too like people doing science should look shabby and unkempt. This portrayal of scientists has become like a norm and if you don't fit into their mold you are not considered a serious scientist. Q26.text: The academic system is quite flawed in my opinion. Most of the classes I had to take in my first year were useless and interfered with time I could have better spent in the lab. Important skills that would have benefited most students in my graduate studies (e.g. statistical knowledge) were never even touched on.  I had a very bad relationship with my first PI and my department had no way of knowing until I brought it to their attention. As I had never been a graduate student, I thought the situation was normal until I started discussing it with other students. By the time I realized what a toxic situation it was, I had already spent 3 years on the project. Furthermore, after running into some former students by chance, I learned that I wasn't the first student to be treated this way. This suggests that there are PIs out there who have a history of treating students unfairly but basically it is either swept under the rug by the department or never even brought to the attention of the department. I was definitely scared to speak out as my PI hinted that her recommendation would be the most important thing in my future. As far as I know, she is still a PI in the department and still accepting students. Even though I did interview with the lab and spoke to the grad students alone, they did not tell me any of the problems in the lab. But looking back I probably wouldn't either because it might get back to the PI.  As well, almost all PIs are academic. This means that many have no advice or connections to help students who would like to pursue non-academic career paths. I definitely feel like I am on my own once I graduate.

Q16.text: I started my PhD in a different lab then the one I am in now. I had a very bad relationship with my previous PI and moved lab after 3 years. I had to completely change projects and as a result I am in the 6th year of my PhD and won't finish till at least my 7th or 8th year. With the low pay and high cost of living, I have many things 'on hold' until I graduate and can get a better paying job. The low pay and high stress and workload of an academic job is one reason I am not even considering continuing in academia. One large concern I have going into my future career is that I want to have children fairly soon after I graduate as I am already 30. It's hard to think about finishing a PhD, finding a job, and also having children before I am too old.  At present I can't even say for certain that I will find a good job or one I am interested in...all I know is lab-based research.

Q55.text: I wish I'd known that I could change departments when going from undergrad to grad studies. I thought since I did an undergraduate in biochemistry and I couldn't pursue a different graduate program. This limited the pool of PIs and projects I was looking into. I think this is probably common knowledge for many students but as my parents did no attend university, they had weren't able to guide me and prospective universities don't really advertise this.  I also wish I had known to look at the number of publications per year that my prospective PI was publishing. If there are very few, it could point to problems in the lab unless they are pursing lengthy studies (e.g. animal aging). Also are their postdocs in the lab? I now work in a lab with postdocs and having that extra mentoring is amazingly useful. I would now look for labs where the project I am placed on is ongoing and one-on-one mentoring/teaching is available - either from a postdoc or ideally, another graduate student who is passing the project on as they are about to graduate. My first project was leftover (and unpublished) from about 6 years before and hadn't been investigated since. This is a big problem because not only do you have no one to talk to but other labs could be close to publishing results that may make the previous work obsolete.

Q26.text: Garbage. While I've been lucky to have an excellent mentor and dedicated committee, the department and school I'm in offer at best little support for graduate students, and at worst, active attempts to sabotage those students. The default assumption is that a funded graduate student will teach all five years of their funding package, and the burden of responsibility of those teaching assignments has steadily increased over the five years of my PhD. For example, introductory lab teaching responsibilities have increased from 2 courses/week per TA to 3 courses/week per TA. This adds another 30 students' worth of grading to grading responsibilities, and another 5 hours per week between actual lab run time (3 hours), setup and cleanup (1 hour) and office hours (1 hour per lab session). This makes it impossible to confine teaching responsibilities to the 20 hours/week we're paid for (if you're spending 15 hours a week teaching, that leaves 5 hours a week to grade 90 lab reports. You try grading 90 lab reports in 5 hours. It doesn't happen--and that's not counting troubleshooting via email or addressing student concerns over email). Additionally, the number of trainings for teaching responsibilities we are expected to complete rises steadily every year, creating an unpredictable time commitment that varies from semester to semester. The end result is a burdensome, difficult to navigate system that means for most of the time you're working, you're doing teaching-related activities. Late in the programme, as I am, this can be deadly--you're faced with a choice of whether to assume debt for your last year or years or quit the programme due to simply not having time for research due to teaching responsibilities.  This wouldn't be so bad if those assignments were predictable and reliable, but they aren't. Colleagues haven't received their contract or their funding until well after the semester's actually started; I've been badgered for weeks by the financial services offices on campus because my tuition remission hasn't gone through in a timely manner. The actual wages do not reflect the cost of living. I am lucky because I receive a degree of financial support from my family, but medical and other kinds of debt among graduate students at my institution is common. I've been cycled through five separate teaching assignments before the semester started, with the administrators responsible indicating that I might not have one, even if my funding package guarantees it. Overall, it means there's a great deal of insecurity in funding even well into the programme and with a funding package.   There is no ability to unionize or organize for better working conditions. This university is in a right-to-work state, and the graduate student government, while claiming to be lobbying for better wages, is in effect toothless and has had no success in improving working conditions. With the expected ruling that graduate student workers are students first and workers second, there is little likelihood that this will change.

Q26.text: There's something genuinely freeing about it at first -- you get to follow your curiosity, read whatever you want, pursue questions that actually feel important to you. but the longer I'm in it the more I see how much of the work is shaped by things that have nothing to do with the ideas themselves: funding cycles, publication metrics, the constant pressure to build a CV that might get you hired somewhere one day. It's like the system was designed to reward a very specific kind of ambition, and I'm not sure I have it, or honestly whether I want it. I love research, I think I always will, but i have a lot of doubt about whether the academic path is where that love survives.

Q16.text: The isolation, honestly -- I didn't expect that. even when you're surrounded by other PhD students everyone is kind of locked in their own project, their own anxieties, and there's not a lot of space to just talk about whether any of this is worth it without it feeling like weakness or complaining. And I worry sometimes about what this is doing to me long-term, like whether years of living with this much ambient uncertainty hardens you in ways you don't notice until later. I also think about money more than I thought I would -- not just the stipend being what it is, but watching friends from undergrad settle into lives that look stable and comfortable while I'm still in this in-between state where the payoff might never come. that's not a reason to quit, and I know that, but it sits with me.

Q55.text: That the work itself -- the actual thinking and reading and writing -- is only maybe half of what the PhD ends up being about. The other half is navigating a system: understanding what your supervisor actually needs from you (which is sometimes different from what they say they need), learning to publish strategically rather than just when the work feels ready, building visibility in your field before you have much to show for it. I wish someone had been honest with me about that early on, because I came in thinking it was mostly an intellectual project and I spent a long time being confused and a bit resentful about everything else that kept getting in the way. it doesn't make me regret starting, but i would have approached it differently.

Q41.text: Ideally still academia -- I want to teach, I want to run my own research program, and I think I'd find it hard to give that up entirely. But I'm more honest with myself now than I was when I started about how unlikely the path actually is, and so I've started thinking more seriously about research-adjacent roles outside universities. policy, maybe, or something in the NGO or think-tank world where the work still feels meaningful but the career isn't just a waiting game for a tenure-track position that might not exist by the time I'm ready for it. I haven't fully made peace with that as a plan B, it still feels a bit like settling, but i'm trying to hold it as a real option rather than just a fallback I don't look at too closely.

Q60.text: Just that I found this more useful than I expected -- not the survey itself necessarily, but the act of trying to articulate things I usually just carry around without examining too closely. I hope something comes of the research. The PhD experience feels like it's gotten harder to navigate over the last decade and i'm not sure the institutions involved have fully reckoned with that yet.

Q17.text: The freedom to just sit with a problem for a long time -- that's the thing I keep coming back to. No one's telling me what to think about or when to think about it, and even on the days when that feels more like being lost than being free, i still value it. And the conversations, when they happen -- with my supervisor when things are going well, or with other students who are genuinely excited about what they're doing. those moments remind me why I started.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I would say that I love the opportunity to work on problems I like. However, I have to see it many times as an artistic and entrepreneurial endeavor. The funding is limited. If I want to work on things I like, I have to learn to get funding and publish a lot, and maybe make sacrifices. The publishing metric seems unfair at times and I hope that good work will ultimately be the reason I get a job, but i have a lot of doubt. The payoff for going the academic route seems more uncertain each day. I want to go down it because I want to solve my own problems and teach, but I don't want to break my heart or lose my soul in the process. It seems that the work-life balance is a real struggle for not just grad students, but pretty much anyone in contact with the academic system. In the end, I wonder if I just have to accept being chained up to this system, and I have to sacrifice both financial and emotional opportunities as I pursue postdocs. On the other side, I care a lot less about money and I want to enjoy what I do. It's just uncertainty about the payoff. Could I be happy doing something else?

Q26.text: The academic system is simultaneously the place where I've grown most intellectually and the place that has asked the most of me personally. It rewards a particular kind of person -- usually male, usually unburdened by the expectation of domestic labor or the quiet tax of being perpetually underestimated -- and honestly, that design isn't incidental. And yet I stay, because the work itself is genuinely meaningful to me. The creativity, the rigor, the possibility of contributing something that matters. I just think the system extracts disproportionate costs from those of us who don't fit the default mold, and we're expected to be grateful for the access.

Q16.text: The personal cost to my relationships has been something I didn't anticipate fully. There's this unspoken assumption that a woman who is serious about a career like this must have either resolved the partnership question or quietly sacrificed it, and I find myself navigating that in ways my male colleagues simply don't. Also, honestly, the mental health piece -- I've had stretches where I wasn't okay, and the culture around that is still pretty poor.

Q55.text: That your confidence will be attacked from so many directions -- imposter syndrome, yes, but also the more insidious kind that comes from being in rooms where people look through you -- and the work itself won't automatically fix that. I wish someone had told me that fighting for your place in those rooms isn't a distraction from the research, it's part of the job, and that learning to advocate for yourself early matters as much as any methodological skill.

Q41.text: Academic research and teaching, ideally within a university setting. I'm committed to that path even knowing what it asks of you -- I want to keep doing research that matters and to be the kind of mentor I didn't always have.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this research is actually used for something. Surveys like this can feel extractive in their own way -- you ask people to excavate difficult experiences and then... what? I'd like to think the data goes somewhere that makes the structures a little less hostile for the next cohort. For women especially, and for anyone who comes in carrying more than the institution was designed to accommodate. I don't want to sound cynical, because I'm not, not entirely. I'm still here and I still believe in what I'm doing. But I think the gap between what universities say about wellbeing and inclusion and what they actually do is pretty wide, and I hope whoever reads these responses sits with that discomfort rather than smoothing it into a nice report.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly. Being paid -- however inadequately -- to think hard about something that genuinely interests me, to read widely and argue and be wrong and revise, that part I find pretty sustaining. My immediate lab environment has been good too, which I know isn't guaranteed. And there's something about the creative dimension of research I didn't fully anticipate -- the fact that I get to make something, contribute something that didn't exist before. That matters to me, even on the days when everything else feels heavy.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I feel very at home in academia. I think it creates a more free, creative and flexible environment than non-academic careers, a space where I can apply my mind and pursue whatever I want. In general, I can see how the system has the potential to exploit PhD students, but I have been very lucky with my marvellous supervisor and labmates. However, it is a competitive system and I have had to deal with jealousy and bullying from peers and even senior faculty members other than my supervisor. My institution is welcoming of women and other minorities and celebrates individualism. However, I think the system in general is rigged to accommodate those who can put aside many aspects of their personal lives, making it inherently harder for women, or other primary caregivers, to flourish. I have felt a lot of pressure to devote all my time and energy to my PhD, with bad consequences for my personal relationships and mental health.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: That I may not get a life partner due to traditional gender expectations in my culture and due to the fact that I am prioritising my studies, anxiety which is exacerbated by the fact that most of my female role models in academia are single.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Overall, self-confidence is the key to success. I am building my own brand and I have to promote myself, even if it makes me feel uncomfortable, or if it's not normal for women in my culture. If I do not believe in myself, who will? And I can say NO.

Q17.text: Honestly the intellectual freedom is hard to beat -- I get to spend most of my time on problems I actually find interesting, which I dont take for granted. the autonomy is real, even if it comes with its own pressures.

Q26.text: Personally, I think my experience is overall positive compared to some of my colleagues. I think one of the major struggles I see in our academic experience as PhD students is the variance in the quality students have with their advisors. Some being narcissistic, overly competitive and overbearing, while others are completely absent. I consider myself lucky in having found a supervisor who is somewhere in-between hands-on and hands-off. However, I would prefer more guidance in terms of  getting papers published, research project ideas, my thesis etc. I think the fact that our supervisors careers (tenure) depend on us (the student) publishing papers puts unnecessary pressure to preform and leads to situations where the supervisor does not put the student first and/or consider them in their decisions.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's a system that produces genuinely important knowledge while running on a kind of quiet exploitation — and I think those two things are related, not coincidental. The assumption seems to be that passion is compensation enough, that marinating on your work at 11pm is just what you do when you care. And maybe I get that, but I also notice (being the first in my family to do this) how much of academic success is scaffolded by things the institution never quite names: financial buffers, connections, the psychological ease of feeling like you already belong in these rooms. The science itself still excites me, it really does. But I'd be lying if I said the structure around it didn't wear on me sometimes

Q16.text:
The financial stuff, honestly — and I know funding comes up in a lot of these conversations, but I mean it in a specific way. Stipends are designed to be "livable" by some abstract measure, but they don't account for the fact that every unexpected expense (a car repair, a medical bill, a conference you're expected to attend) hits differently when you don't have parents who can absorb the overflow. I've watched labmates book flights on a whim or take unpaid internships over the summer to "explore options," and I just... can't do that. And I think that gap quietly shapes who ends up building certain kinds of careers.

The other thing is a kind of ambient loneliness that I wasn't prepared for — not social loneliness exactly, but the feeling of navigating an institution that wasn't really designed with someone like me in mind. There's a lot of unwritten knowledge here, a lot of doors that open because someone knows someone, and figuring that out as you go, without a roadmap, takes a real toll. I'm managing, and I still believe in what I'm doing, but those are the things that keep me up more than the science does

Q55.text: That it's okay — genuinely okay — to treat the PhD as a job with hours, rather than a calling that colonizes your entire life. I came in thinking that the students who seemed most devoted, most willing to blur every line between work and the rest of themselves, were the ones who were doing it right. It took me longer than it should have to realize that a lot of that performance is just that — performance, or in some cases a kind of coping that gets mistaken for dedication. Setting limits on my time doesn't make me less serious about the science; if anything, it's made me more focused during the hours I am working. I wish someone had said that plainly to me on day one instead of letting me absorb the opposite lesson from the ambient culture of the lab

Q41.text: Research scientist or physician-scientist role where the work stays connected to patients and actual clinical outcomes — I'm not interested in climbing an academic ladder for its own sake, and I've been pretty honest with myself about that. Industry isn't a backup plan to me; it's genuinely where a lot of the translational work happens, and I'd rather be somewhere my research has a clear line to impact than spend my career chasing grants in an underfunded lab. Academia isn't off the table if the environment is right, but "the environment is right" is doing a lot of work in that sentence

Q60.text: Just that I hope these surveys actually get read by people with the power to change something, because I think a lot of PhD students answer honestly and then wonder whether it goes anywhere. The things I've described aren't unique to me — I've had enough late-night conversations with other first-gen students, other people quietly stretched thin, to know that. The system isn't broken in dramatic ways; it's broken in these slow, structural ways that are easy to dismiss as individual struggles when they're really not. I'm still glad I'm here and still believe the work matters, but I'd feel more hopeful about the future of research if I saw the institutions actually respond to what students are telling them, rather than just collecting it

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly — the fact that my specific questions matter and I get to be the person who follows them. There's something that hasn't gotten old about designing an experiment, getting a result that surprises you, and sitting with it. And I genuinely love the people in my lab, the kind of conversations that spill past the bench into bigger questions about what the work is actually for. Those parts still feel like the reason I came, even on the days when the rest of it doesn't

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: We need more emphasis on work-life balance and that it's ok, or even encouraged, to have a life outside of the PhD. I've been told by my adviser, whom I love dearly, that it's essentially a grad student's job to get burnt out. I don't think that's healthy. Also, the pay is low enough that there's always some level of financial stress even as I make ends meet, since I don't have a financial fallback family member that I could reach out to in case of emergency/hardship. Most of my peers come from affluent/otherwise advantaged families whereas I don't, and most of them acknowledge that without their families' help they could not make ends meet. It reinforces the classism and discrimination inherent in academia/PhD programs.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: It's a marathon, not a sprint. It is ok to stick up for your own work-life balance and schedule. As long as you get your work done productively and intellectually robustly, you do not have to constantly be marinating on work. You're a whole person, not just a grad student. Don't let anyone pressure you otherwise/feel guilty for having a life.

Q55.text: That mentorship at research universities is much more transactional than I expected. I wish someone had told me that advisors are balancing grants, their own research, and departmental politics -- their relationship with you is shaped by all of that, not just your work. Coming from a small liberal arts college I had a pretty idealized picture of what that relationship would look like.

Q41.text: Teaching-focused faculty, ideally at a liberal arts college. I'd also be genuinely interested in science communication or public-facing research roles if the academic job market doesn't cooperate -- which, honestly, feels like a real possibility these days.

Q60.text: Just that I think surveys like this matter — it's easy for institutional problems to stay invisible when students don't have a venue to name them. I hope the data actually reaches people with the power to act on it, because the issues around mentorship and faculty culture aren't edge cases, they're pretty widespread from what I can tell. I'm early enough in my PhD that I'm still figuring out what I think, but I'm glad this kind of research exists.

Q17.text: The intellectual community, honestly. Getting to talk about ideas with people who are genuinely invested in them -- that part has been better than I expected. And there's something kind of freeing about having real time to dig into a question, even when the research itself is frustrating.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I went to a liberal arts college for undergrad, which heavily influenced my expectations of academia, and working in a PhD program at a university is not the same as being at a liberal arts college. The faculty treat students worse, which has been a big adjustment. I do love the research and other grad students, though.

Q26.text: The academic system has real intellectual richness, but it's structurally ill-equipped to protect people in vulnerable positions -- particularly students navigating the delicate power structure of supervisor relationships. the support infrastructure lags badly behind mental health demands placed on PhD candidates.

Q16.text: The precarity of academic careers weighs on me more than I anticipated -- the odds of securing stable position feel genuinely discouraging at times, and it's hard to invest so fully in a path that may not be sustainable.

Q55.text: How much the PhD experience is shaped by the advisor relationship -- not just intellectually, but structurally and emotionally. I didn't appreciate how asymmetric that power dynamic actually was, or how little formal recourse exists when it goes wrong.

Q41.text: Academic research or science communication -- ideally both, though I'm increasingly aware of how few stable research positions actually exist.

Q60.text: The systemic issues I've described aren't edge cases -- they represent structural failures that institutions consistently underestimate. mental health support needs to be proactive rather than reactive, and the power imbalance in supervisor relationships needs formal accountability mechanisms, not just informal advice to "choose your advisor carefully." Researchers doing important work are being lost to an environment that prioritises output over wellbeing.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- being able to pursue questions that genuinely matter to me. That part hasn't lost its pull, even when everything else feels pretty heavy.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system is failing doctoral students, who are some of the most vulnerable at universities. If there are serious problems between advisors and students, often students do not have the resources or power to ask for help. Additionally, work-life balance is supported in theory but not practice. The  graduate programs state that this is of importance, however at the level of the individual labs this is not reinforced. Academia can do better to support its students who are the life-blood of research and teaching at universities. Providing mental health support, resources for coping with advisor-advisee conflicts, protecting students' intellectual property from the fallout of soured advisor-advisee relationships, and promoting healthier work-life balance would make the academic system  more positive and inclusive.

Q26.text: Honestly, the system has a lot going for it intellectually — the community, the conversations, the sense that what you're doing actually matters — but I think there's a real culture of, not dishonesty exactly, but of people not saying what they mean, particularly in the faculty-student dynamic. I came into this after a genuinely rough burnout during my master's and I'm probably more attuned to that kind of thing now, more aware of when someone's giving you reassurance versus actual feedback. The best supervisors I've encountered are honest in a way that's almost jarring by comparison, and the worst leave you with vague encouragement that you have to decode for weeks. So I'd say the system rewards people who are already fluent in reading between lines -- and it doesn't do a great job of being transparent about that requirement upfront.

Q16.text: The thing that comes up more than I expected is career uncertainty — not in the sense of "I don't know what I want" but more like, the information available to you about what an academic career actually looks like is surprisingly thin until you're deep enough in to see it. I've been actively trying to seek out honest accounts from people a few years ahead of me, and even then it's hard to get a straight answer about what the job market actually looks like, or what a postdoc involves day-to-day beyond the official description. That opacity, combined with the fact that I burned out once already and am very protective of not repeating that, makes the career planning side of things feel higher-stakes than I'd like. I keep industry options open partly because of that — not as a fallback exactly, but as a genuine hedge against a system that doesn't always give you the information you'd need to make a fully informed choice.

Q55.text: That it's okay — genuinely okay, not just performatively okay — to say no. I came in with this sense that saying yes to everything was how you demonstrated commitment, and I think that cost me a lot during my master's, honestly. The phrase I keep coming back to is "protect your own time," which sounds obvious in retrospect but nobody actually says it to you at the start -- they say "be enthusiastic" and "take every opportunity," and those two things are in real tension that I had to learn the hard way. I wish someone had been upfront about that tradeoff earlier rather than leaving me to figure it out through exhaustion.

Q41.text: Leaning towards an academic postdoc as a first step, though I'm genuinely keeping industry open as well — not as a backup but as a real option. I think the honest answer is that I don't have enough information yet to commit fully, which is part of why I've been trying to talk to people who've made both choices. The burnout history makes me want to be careful about what kind of environment I end up in, and academia isn't automatically the safer bet on that front.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually feeds back into how departments think about support structures, because I think a lot of what PhD students struggle with is structural rather than individual — and it's easy for institutions to treat it as the latter. The transparency issue I keep coming back to isn't really about bad actors, it's more that the whole system has evolved in a way that disincentivises honest communication, and I dont think most people even notice they're doing it. So if there's anything useful in what I've written here, I guess I'd want it to point in that direction rather than just documenting individual experiences in isolation.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual community is the thing I'd point to first — the conversations you can have here, the sense that the people around you are genuinely invested in ideas rather than just performing investment. There's something I find pretty rare about being in an environment where it's completely normal to care deeply about a fairly obscure problem and have people around who get why that matters. I also genuinely enjoy the autonomy over my time, which I think I appreciate more than I otherwise would, having come through a burnout — you notice absence of that quickly when you've lost it once, and having it back is not something I take for granted.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I am very lucky in that I found a program that has been a really great fit for me, but there’s a certain lack of transparency between the mentor faculty and students that is the main frustration I have with the academic system at my university. For example, our first year is spent rotating through different labs until we decide which to do our dissertation work in. Faculty aren’t always honest about whether they have the funding to support students beyond the rotation and often use it as an excuse to not keep students they were unhappy with, rather than explaining what they didn’t find satisfactory about their work. One PI said “I didn’t get any students for two years after I told a student I didn’t think my lab was a good fit and they told others I was mean so now I just tell them I won’t have the money to pay their stipend so they choose not to stay”. I understand it’s a hard conversation to have but it’s rather disheartening to know that we can’t count on honest feedback when we’re here to be trained.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Don’t always say ‘yes’/ don’t set unrealistic deadlines for yourself. The times when I’ve been the most overwhelmed is when I took on too much for too short of a timeframe. Realizing I could say no to extra side projects or saying yes I can help but I can’t get to it for a few days and being able to talk through what my PI actually sees as my priorities has made things a lot better. During my masters, I had a period of a few months where I worked 7 days a week with no time off and I was getting burnt out and not being as productive of a lab member as I could have been because I was trying to do too much. Forcing myself to maintain a more normal work life balance and not seeing every single weekend as an opportunity to fit more into my workload has done wonders for my mental health and I do a lot better in the time I am in lab.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least as I have experienced it here in Germany, operates on carefully maintained hierarchy where those at the top hold DISPROPORTIONATE power over everyone below -- and for international students whose visas are tied to work contracts, this power is not merely structural but deeply personal, almost suffocating at times. The mentorship the system promises is often absent in practice, replaced by an expectation of output without any reciprocal investment in one's actual development as a researcher. And honestly, it's been kind of exhausting to realize how much of what I believed about the integrity of academic inquiry was, at best, an idealized notion I brought with me from outside -- the reality is that a skewed vision of facts and results is tolerated, even rewarded, so long as it serves the group's publication targets.

Q16.text: What concerns me perhaps more than anything else I've described is the ISOLATION of it all -- there is no institutional channel through which one can safely raise these grievances without risking the very contract that keeps your visa valid, and that particular trap is something the system seems almost designed to preserve rather than dismantle. I've watched colleagues quietly leave, or worse, quietly comply, and the absence of any real whistleblower protection for people in my position makes it feel less like an oversight and more like a feature. and tbh, the mental health support that is nominally available is so detached from the structural realities of our situation that going to a counsellor feels almost absurd -- they can offer coping strategies but they cannot renegotiate the power your supervisor holds over your entire legal right to remain in the country.

Q55.text: That the relationship with your supervisor is not merely an academic arrangement but a near-total dependency -- and that no amount of research passion insulates you from the consequences of being assigned to someone who treats that dependency as a management tool rather than a responsibility. I wish someone had told me to investigate my prospective supervisor's group dynamics and former students' experiences with the same rigor I applied to evaluating the research topic itself. The science, honestly, I could always figure out -- it's the human architecture around it that I was completely unprepared for.

Q41.text: Research career -- a postdoc, most likely, though I hold that plan with considerably less enthusiasm than I would have expected when I first arrived. The research itself still rallies me up in a way nothing else quite does, but I am under no illusions now about the structural conditions I am walking into -- and I suppose knowing that is, in its own grim way, a kind of preparation.

Q60.text: Only that I hope the data collected here is taken seriously rather than filed away as another set of statistics that institutional inertia will conveniently absorb without consequence -- because the experiences I've described are not exceptional, they are ORDINARY, and that is precisely what makes them so difficult to address. The structures that produce these conditions are not accidental, they are maintained, and surveys like this one are only valuable if someone upstream actually has the will (and the institutional standing) to act on what they find. I genuinely hope that is the case here.

Q17.text: The research itself -- the actual intellectual work of it, when I am left alone long enough to do it properly. There are moments, not as frequent as I had hoped, where a problem opens up in a way that makes everything else recede, and in those moments I remember precisely why I came here. It's the only part of this that still feels genuinely mine.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: In the growing times of global scientific collaborations and diversification of the scientific talent pool, I am very shocked by the academic system. Having pursued both my Master's and PhD at reputed institutes and research groups in Germany, I have witnessed how there is nothing 'International' about the graduate programmes except for the students.  The lack of a proper support system for International students is a major let-down. Case in point, most PIs recruit international students knowing well about how visa extensions and working contracts go hand-in-hand. They then use this to exploit students, even threatening them to work without a work-life balance. Vacations are only sanctioned if  results as expected by the PI are available. More horrific, is the fact that Science is being carried out to please the PI's ego or a skewed vision of facts lending to publications of either cherry-picked data not entirely reflecting the complete scenario or simply 're-inventing the wheel'. And, to think of the tax-payers' money going down the drain for this rallies me up! Also, the utter lack of mentoring or interest in the graduate student's academic career or PhD experience (forget about future career prospects) has left me questioning my choices of an academic career.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: Lack of proper mentoring and the hierarchical mentality of several PIs.  Visa issues (work contract and visa extensions go hand-in-hand). This is also exploited by PIs by threatening or demanding extreme working hours and no vacation days.

Q55.text: The general attitude of the PI and his research group and university that I am currently working at. This would have discouraged from pursuing my PhD here.

Q60.text: Six years of data and the conclusion is pretty clear: the incentive structure is broken and nobody in a position to fix it has any reason to. The exploitation is load-bearing. I don't say that to be dramatic -- I say it because it's the most parsimonious explanation for why "we need reform" has been the consensus for 30 years and nothing changes. Anyway. Q17.text: The actual research, when I get to do it. Which is less often than you'd think given how much of a PhD is administrative nonsense, grant-chasing, and managing up. But when you're deep in a problem that nobody has solved and you're the one who might -- that part is genuinely good. it's not worth the pay, it's not worth the opportunity cost, but it's real. I also like the flexibility, in theory. In practice my PI treats "flexible hours" as "available at all hours," so that one's complicated.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: 6 years in a PhD program. It is very varied and really depends on every individual PI and student. We can set the bar really low and say "yes the student graduated and also published a paper" but that is not good. Not all PhDs are also created equal. Some PhD students can graduate without publishing (field dependent), whereas some are expected to publish at least two first-author papers. But no worries, if the PhD students remain in the academic system, they can do 1 to 3 more postdocs in their 30s and earn an OK income that is on average lower than their counterparts who did not do a PhD. You could raise a small family on that income in some places that are not expensive. Don't worry about them not having retirement funds like a 401K. In my opinion, no one should do a PhD unless they don't have a better option in life. In the majority of cases, it is not a good experience and I don't recommend it to anyone.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's a system that rewards a pretty specific kind of person — someone who's comfortable with slow, incremental progress, who finds meaning in the grant-writing treadmill, and who doesn't mind that the incentives are almost entirely misaligned with actually solving problems. I think there's genuine intellectual richness buried in it, and I've had moments where the work felt genuinely meaningful, but the structural stuff -- the way funding shapes what questions are even askable, the publish-or-perish logic that punishes risk-taking -- makes it hard to stay enthusiastic long-term. It's not broken in an obvious way, it's more like it's optimized for its own perpetuation rather than for the people in it or the science it's supposedly advancing.

Q16.text: The opportunity cost thing weighs on me more than I expected it to, honestly — like, every month I spend in a wet lab running assays that may or may not pan out is a month I'm not building something, not iterating fast, not doing the kind of work that actually maps onto what I want my life to look like. I don't think I fully understood that going in, or maybe I thought the skills transfer would be cleaner than it is. There's also a quieter concern around identity, I guess — most of my cohort seems to have fully bought into the academic track, and there's a social cost to being the person who's mentally already halfway out the door. It's not that anyone's hostile about it, it's more that the whole culture assumes you want what they want, and after a while that assumption starts to feel kind of isolating.

Q55.text: That the culture isn't just context -- it's the product. I came in thinking I'd do good science and the institutional stuff would mostly be noise I could tune out, but the incentive structure doesn't stay in the background, it actively shapes what questions get asked, what methodologies become standard, who gets mentorship, what counts as a good result. If I'd understood that the system isn't a container for doing research but is itself the thing you're constantly navigating and being reshaped by, I think I would've been a lot more deliberate about where I applied and what kind of lab I picked -- or whether I started at all, honestly. The skills I've built are real, but I didn't account for how much cognitive bandwidth would go toward surviving the structure rather than doing the work I actually came here to do

Q41.text: Starting a company, most likely — or at minimum getting into an early-stage venture where I'm close enough to the problem that I can actually move fast on it. The research skills are real and I don't want to throw them away, but the academic career path feels like it would just reproduce the same constraints I've been bumping up against here. Industry R&D is a fallback maybe, but even that feels too slow and too political in most places. Honestly, the thing I keep coming back to is that I want to be in a position where the feedback loop between an idea and its impact isn't mediated by grant cycles or review timelines -- and the only context where that's actually true, as far as I can tell, is building something yourself.

Q60.text: I appreciate that this survey exists, genuinely — not in a polite way, but because I think the experience of PhD students who are reorienting mid-program is pretty underrepresented in how institutions think about retention and outcomes. Most of the formal data captures whether you finished, not whether finishing was the right call or whether the program served what you actually came to do. I'd be curious whether any of this feeds back into how departments think about recruiting people with non-traditional goals, because I suspect the mismatch I've experienced isn't that unusual, it's just that most people don't say it out loud until they're already gone. The advisor relationship has genuinely been a bright spot for me -- I want to be clear about that, because I've said a lot of critical things and I don't want the picture to read as uniformly bleak. There are real people doing real work in good faith inside this system. I just think the system itself needs more honest accounting of who it's actually serving and whether that matches its stated purpose.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly, even if it's more constrained than I expected going in — there's still something genuinely irreplaceable about being paid, however modestly, to spend your days thinking hard about a problem that actually interests you, and having the access to people and resources that makes that thinking sharper than it would be on your own. My advisor specifically has been a real asset in that regard, someone who pushes back in ways that are actually useful rather than just territorial. And there's a kind of depth you get to bring to a question when you're not context-switching every hour -- I do value that, even when I'm frustrated with everything orbiting around it. I think what I'd miss most, if I left tomorrow, is the density of smart people willing to have a genuinely weird conversation about something they care about. that part doesn't scale the same way outside academia, at least not yet.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I'm not really worried about funding right now, but I have grown to dislike the way projects get funded in general/the way publishing works/the general culture of my field (neuroscience). I get the impression that many labs are unable to try out of the box projects and aren't even able to share some of their work (especially at the times they would like to). Most PhD students in my program spend like 50 hours a week just executing wet lab work, which is often menial and leaves little time for serious thought, reading papers, etc. if the student still wants to have a life. I think we need more diversity in the way labs operate if we want to solve the various issues facing the field- reproducibility crisis, stagnation of practical progress in clinical applications, poor advisor relationships, and so on.

Q26.text: The academic system, as I have experienced it, has genuine intellectual richness but is organised around incentive structures that I think distorts what research is actually for. The pressure to publish -- to produce output that is measurable and rankable -- creates a kind of anxiety that is not really about the work itself but about its visibility. Honestly, my experience with supervision has made this particularly clear, decisions seem driven more by what looks productive than what is actually good for the science.

Q16.text: One thing that sits alongside everything else is the sense of intellectual isolation -- I had not quite anticipated how solitary the work would feel even within a university environment. There is something disorienting about spending extended period developing expertise that almost no one around you shares or fully understands. It makes the supervisory relationship carry an outsized weight, and when that relationship is not functioning well, its effects spreads into almost every part of the experience, honestly more than I expected.

Q55.text: I wish I had understood earlier how much the supervisory relationship would define the texture of the entire experience -- not just practically but psychologically. I had assumed there was more diffuse support structure, that the institution itself would provide some counterbalance, but the reality is that so much depends on a single person's choices and priorities, and there is very little recourse if that relationship becomes dysfunctional. honestly it shapes everything, more than anyone tells you at the start.

Q41.text: Academic research is still where my interests genuinely lie, though I find it increasingly difficult to separate that interest from the question of whether the institutional conditions actually makes it sustainable. I'm honestly not sure I want a career where so much depends on publication metrics that seem only loosely connected to the quality of the actual work. There are alternatives -- policy roles, research-adjacent positions -- that I think about more seriously than I expected when I started

Q60.text: I suppose I would say that surveys like this one feel valuable, but also somewhat insufficient -- the issues that weigh most heavily on PhD students are structural and would require institutional will to actually address, not just data collection. The supervisory model in particular seems to me long overdue for serious rethinking, and I hope whatever comes from this research reaches people with the capacity to act on it rather than just being filed somewhere. its been useful, at least, to articulate some of this.

Q17.text: The intellectual environment itself -- the access to ideas, to people who take questions seriously, to a kind of sustained thinking that most contexts don't really permit -- is something I genuinely value, and I don't want to lose sight of that even when other parts of the experience are difficult. There is something that still feels like a privilege about spending time on problems that matter to you, even if the structures around that work can distort it in ways I find troubling. honestly the university as a place, as an atmosphere, remains something I appreciate more than I sometimes let myself acknowledge.

Q26.text: The academic system has genuine strengths -- the intellectual environment, the freedom to go really deep on a problem -- but it's weirdly obsessed with publication counts as proxy for scientific value. Q16.text: The federal funding situation, honestly. Cuts to agencies like USGS and EPA make me genuinely uncertain whether the career I'm training toward will actually be there in a stable form. it's not catastrophizing -- it's just hard to invest five years in applied government science when the political landscape keeps shifting under you.

Q55.text: That failure is information, not judgment. Q41.text: Applied government science -- USGS, National Park Service, that kind of thing. I want to do work that's directly connected to public land management and policy, where the science actually feeds into decisions. Academia's not really where I see myself, tbh.

Q60.text: The funding instability thing really does keep coming back to me -- not just personally, but as a structural problem for applied science broadly. Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual depth. Q26.text: highly competitive and probably not designed with wellbeing in mind. From first year it's pretty clear that success depends more on networking and institutional backing than actual research quality -- at least thats what I've observed. The training itself is valuable, I wont deny that, but culture around it is kind of unsustainable. Everyone chasing same metrics: publications, grant money, citations, without much questioning whether it advances anything meaningful. I'm treating PhD as chance to build skills and keep options open rather than as entry point to academic career. The system rewards people willing to sacrifice lot for uncertain payoff, and honestly I'm not sure that tradeoff makes sense for me long-term

Q16.text: mental health aspect is probably bigger concern than I anticipated. not just personal stress but watching peers struggle -- some quite severely -- and culture around it is just to push through. There's not lot of genuine support, more like lip service. Also the financial side, stipend barely covers living costs rn, which adds background stress thats hard to ignore. I guess I also underestimated how much progress depends on who you know internally, not just quality of your work. Supervisors vary enormously and luck of assignment matters probably more than it should. These arent unique concerns, I know that, but experiencing them firsthand is different from reading about it

Q55.text: how much supervisor selection actually determines your experience -- I spent most of my pre-PhD research evaluating the topic, almost none on evaluating the person. That imbalance was real mistake. Beyond that, I wish I'd understood earlier that academic path is genuinely narrow in ways that aren't obvious from outside. I arrived kind of assuming PhD was clear entry into research career, and recalibrating that took probably six months of unnecessary anxiety. Having industry alternatives in mind from day one isn't defeatist, it's just rational given the odds. Knowing that earlier would have changed how I approached whole first year

Q41.text: Research-oriented industry roles probably, or something science-adjacent where I can still do analytical work without the academic pressure. Biotech, policy, data science -- honestly keeping options open is the whole point. I came in thinking tenure-track was the goal but rn I'm fairly certain that tradeoff isn't worth it for me. Industry research gives more stability and probably more tangible impact, which matters more to me than prestige at this point

Q60.text: just that I hope data from surveys like this actually gets used to change something rather than just documenting that problem exists. the concerns I raised aren't new -- mental health, financial strain, luck-based supervision -- and they've been raised before. what's lacking is structural response. I'm not pessimistic exactly, more realistic. Individual resilience only goes so far when system itself creates these pressures. If research community is serious about sustainability it needs to address incentive structures, not just offer more counselling sessions. anyway, appreciate the chance to reflect, it was useful exercise even if slightly bleak

Q17.text: probably the skill acquisition, if I'm being honest. learning to design experiments, analyze data properly, actually understand literature critically -- those are transferable and I can see direct value regardless of where I end up. Also the flexibility of schedule is something I didn't expect to appreciate as much as I do, it suits how I work. and there's something satisfying about being surrounded by people who care deeply about specific problems, even if the culture around it is dysfunctional. the intellectual environment itself is genuinely stimulating, I just wish it came without the pressure and scarcity mindset. so -- skills, autonomy, and the people, mostly. the research itself is interesting enough but I wouldn't say it drives me the way it seems to drive others
