Q26.text: Honestly, the system is quite dysfunctional -- peer review feels like lottery, hiring depends more on connections than on quality of work, and the meritocracy that supposedly defines academia is largely fiction. And yet the intellectual side of it is genuinely stimulating. I stay because of the research itself, not because of the structures around it, which are pretty exhausting to navigate.

Q16.text: The mental toll of overwork is something I didn't quite anticipate. I spend far more hours than any contract specifies, and expectation that this is normal -- even virtuous -- is honestly pretty troubling. And the job market uncertainty weighs on you constantly, no matter how much you try to focus on the work itself.

Q55.text: Choosing the right supervisor matters more than the prestige of the institution or the funding. I picked my lab partly for the topic and partly because the position was available, and I only understood later how much the PI's management style -- and their willingness to actually advocate for you -- shapes everything. No metter how strong your research idea is, a difficult supervisor can make it nearly impossible to do good work.

Q41.text: Research in industry -- ideally at a lab where I can do work that actually matters without the dysfunction of academic structures. I'm not ruling out a postdoc entirely, but more as a bridge than a goal. academia as a long-term career feels increasingly unlikely to me, and I'm kind of okay with that.

Q60.text: I hope this kind of research actually leads to something concrete -- there's a lot of surveys circulating in academia and not much visible change. The structural problems I described are well-known to anyone inside the system; the question is whether institutions have any real incentive to fix them, and I'm honestly not sure they do.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- the ability to go deep into a problem that genuinely interests me, without someone dictating exactly how to solve it. There are days where everything else fades and it's just you and the research question, and those days make a lot of the frustration worth it. I also value the people, the conversations with colleagues who care about ideas. That part of academic life is hard to replicate elsewhere.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It is a system with multiple pitfalls. The process of peer review is, on my opinion, the most important of them, because of its lack of objectivity and because the blind revision can protect bad scientist that do not do a fair job reviewing articles. Secondly, the actual academic system too often tends to select PIs that sacrifice their social life for their career and that are not capable of having normal relationships with PhD students and other people in the lab. Managing skills should also be taught to PIs.

Q16.text: The lack of meritocracy; no metter how good you are, you will always get your PhD. The differences in length of a PhD in different countries. The fact that during a PhD the chances to get one or more publications are depending almost exclusively to the PI.

Q26.text: My research institute is located outside the town where the affiliated university is (approximately 40 minutes with public transport to the faculty). Q26.text: The academic system is intellectually rich but structurally precarious, I think. There is genuine beauty in freedom to pursue ideas and contribute to knowledge -- but the financial disadvantages researchers face, especially early-career, and the competitive culture that quietly erodes mental health make it difficult to sustain that passion long term. I believe deeply in the value of research, though the system itself could be far more humane and honest about what it actually asks of people

Q16.text: One thing that has concerned me -- maybe more than I expected going in -- is the sense of isolation that can quietly settle in during a PhD, even in environments that look collegial from the outside. The pressure to always appear competent and certain feels genuinely at odds with what research actually is, which is fundamentally uncertain. and I worry too about the long-term psychological cost of spending years in a system that measures your worth almost entirely through publications and external validation

Q55.text: That the emotional difficulty of a PhD is not a sign of failure or inadequacy -- it is, honestly, almost a structural feature of the process itself. I wish someone had told me at the beginning that feeling lost or overwhelmed does not mean you chose the wrong path, it just means you are doing something genuinely hard. I spent too long in the early stages interpreting my own uncertainty as evidence I did not belong here, when in fact that uncertainty is inseparable from research. knowing that earlier would have saved me a lot of quiet suffering.

Q41.text: Research and teaching within the university environment is honestly where I feel most at home. I am drawn to an academic career -- the kind that allows you to keep generating knowledge and passing it on -- though I'm also realistic, maybe even cautious, about the tenure-track path and what it actually demands of people. the financial precarity and the psychological weight of that system give me pause, but I don't think I'm ready to abandon the aspiration entirely.

Q60.text: Just that I think surveys like this one matter -- there is something valuable in creating space for PhD students to reflect honestly on their experience, and I hope the responses here are useful in some way. The mental health dimension of doctoral training is still, I think, under-acknowledged in most institutional conversations, and the financial dimension even more so. I don't have a neat conclusion, only the hope that those designing and administering these programs read responses like mine with some genuine curiosity about what might change

Q17.text: What I enjoy most is the intellectual freedom -- the sense that the questions I am pursuing are genuinely mine, and that the work I do each day is in service of something I actually care about. There is a particular pleasure in reading widely, following an idea across disciplines, sitting with a problem long enough that it slowly begins to yield. I also love the university environment itself, honestly -- the conversations with colleagues, the seminars, the feeling of being surrounded by people who take ideas seriously. It is not always comfortable, and the pressures are real, but the core of the experience -- the research itself -- is something I find genuinely sustaining, maybe more than I expected when I started.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Me siento cómodo con el sistema de grados académicos a seguir. Vale decir, tener una maestra, luego un doctorado y finalmente una habilitación a dirigir la investigación se ve justificado visto el grado de complejidad del conocimiento. Por otro lado, y no menos importante, se debe buscar la manera de hacer que la sociedad logre valorar el trabajo investigativo para así justificar mejores salarios. Es inadmisible la desventaja económica de profesionales preparados en el mundo académico.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Haría exactamente lo mismo salvo que hubiera dejado un espacio de tiempo (1 o 2 años) entre mis estudios de pregrado y el doctorado, principalmente con el fin de haber comenzado el doctorado con mayor madurez emocional

Q41.label: What type of career are you interested in pursuing after your graduate degree?
Q41.text: Me gustaría seguir una carrera en donde pueda dedicar la mayor parte del tiempo a las actividades de investigación cientifica así como las actividades de docencia universitaria. Formalmente, parece ser que la carrera "tenure track" satisface estas expectativas, pero sin embargo en mi nacen dudas respecto a este camino a causa del nivel de presión y competividad existente, que muchas veces no tiene ningun sentido.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: La experiencia de hacer un PhD es maravillosa. Las personas que llegamos a esto tenemos un alto grado de pasión por el conocimiento y en particular ganas de participar del aparato científico. Muchos de nosotros conservamos la curiosidad y las ganas engendradas en la infancia. Todo esto hace que aceptemos condiciones financieras y de vida generalmente peores que aquellas que tendríamos trabajando en el sector industrial. La colonización del capital en el mundo científico a traído beneficios, como el crecimiento exponencial del numero de personas dedicadas al trabajo investigativo. Por otro lado, las consecuencias de esta colonización en la salud mental de los científicos es un tema mayor que debe ser abordado. Se agradece entonces el esfuerzo que se hace al darle importancia a este tema a través de esta encuesta.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?

Rife with favour-trading that undermines true peer review, and powerful figures heading groups that encourage the kind of desperate corner-cutting and data tampering within the 'publish or perish' model that falls on the shoulders of vulnerable students and early career researchers struggling to stay afloat under increasing pressure to perform and decreasing funding available to do responsible, vigorous research. Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It looks to me that the system continues to use practices that were used 40 or 50 years ago, specially in the advisor-advisee relationship. This doesn't make much sense to me since graduate studies have changed a lot specially now that there so many people pursuing PhDs. When a PI has to oversee more than 3 students at the time and has to take part in many activities to stay competitive, the result is very bad overall. Most of the students are left very untrained and ''at their own'', so your research becomes less insightful and relevant. You are not holding discussions, because there is no time! The PI is spread up onto many many things. So in this context, I think a solution is to either, put less pressure on PI's so they can advocate better to their research and to their advisees, or to have more intermediate scientists that can overtake some of the research and advising duties from the PI.

Q26.text: The academic system here is quite hierarchical and, honestly, slow-moving. There is genuine intellectual culture but it often gets buried under administrative procedures and the need of deferring to seniors even when you have better ideas. It rewards patience more than innovation, I think. What frustrates me most is that fundamental research rarely connects to anything tangible, and the system does little to bridge that gap.

Q16.text: One thing that concerns me is the limited exposure to applied problems -- working in a fundamental research setting means you rarely interact with people who are actually solving real-world problem. And the publication culture here, honestly, sometimes prioritize quantity over quality rather than actual contribution. I dont know if the skills I am developing will really be relevant outside of academia

Q55.text: I wish I had known how rigid the research environment would be before committing. Not just the hierarchy, but the way your work gets siloed -- no one really push you to think about applications or impact. honestly I would have chosen a problem with more direct relevance, or at least done internship in applied setting first.

Q41.text: Academic research position, probably a lecturer or research scientist role at a university. Honestly I sometimes wish I had gone a more applied route -- industry or policy work -- but at this point my profile is shaped for academia so that is the realistic path.

Q60.text: Just that I hope research like this actually reach the people who design doctoral programs, because a lot of what I shared is not unique to me -- many of my peers feel the same way but don't have a space to say it. The system needs more flexibility and, honestly, more willingness to connect fundamental research to real problems. I appreciate the opportunity to reflect on this.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- the ability to go deep into a problem and actually think, without someone pushing you toward short-term deliverables. I also genuinely enjoy the discussions with my mentor, who is quite open to ideas even if the broader system is not. That kind of engagement is hard to find elsewhere.

Q26.text: Honestly, its a system that kind of rewards you intellectually but punishes you financially and personally for choosing it. I've learned so much and found real meaning in teaching and working with other researchers -- those parts have been genuinely good. But the stipend is ridiculously small for the amount of work expected, and there's this unspoken assumption that passion is supposed to compensate for that. I guess it does, up to a point, and then it doesn't. The career pipeline is also pretty brutal -- you invest years of your life and there still might not be a position at the end of it. I still believe in what academia is trying to do, I just wish the system was more honest about what it asks people to sacrifice

Q16.text: The mental health side of it, honestly. I don't think I was prepared for how isolating the later stages would feel -- you're technically surrounded by people but everyone is in their own head, dealing with their own deadlines. and I've had some pretty low periods that I didn't really know how to talk about or who to talk to about them. The other thing that weighs on me is the feeling of being behind in life in ways that are hard to articulate -- friends from undergrad have mortgages, kids, stable salaries, and I'm still on a stipend that barely covers rent. I don't regret the PhD, but I do sometimes feel like I've traded a version of adulthood for this, and I'm not always sure the trade was worth it

Q55.text: That the emotional and financial toll would be cumulative -- it doesnt hit you all at once, it just quietly compounds over years until one day you realise you're exhausted in a way that a holiday wont fix. I think if I'd known that going in I would have been more intentional about protecting my time and my mental health early on, rather than assuming I'd figure it out as I went. Honestly I also wish I'd known how uncertain the academic job market actually is, not in a vague sense but concretely -- like, the numbers. Nobody really tells you that clearly at the start.

Q41.text: Industry, tbh -- not really by choice but I've kind of made peace with it. The academic job market is just too uncertain and I cant keep deferring the financial stability thing indefinitely. I'm looking at research or policy-adjacent roles where I can still use what I've built, but I wont pretend it's the path I would have chosen if the system worked differently.

Q60.text: Honestly, just that I hope this kind of research actually leads to something -- it's easy to feel like surveys disappear into a void. The PhD experience has its good and bad sides and I've tried to be candid about both here. I guess the thing I'd want people to take away is that the financial and mental health pressures aren't just background noise, they're central to how the whole thing feels, and I don't think the system treats them that way. Anyway, I appreciate that someone is looking into this.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- there's something genuinely special about spending your days thinking hard about something that actually matters to you, and that's not nothing. And the people. I've met researchers who are just incredibly passionate and generous with their ideas, and those relationships have been one of the best parts of this whole thing. Teaching has also been unexpectedly rewarding -- seeing students actually engage with material I care about is kind of the best feeling. I guess what I enjoy most is that it still feels meaningful, even on the hard days. That's not something I think I'd easily find in a regular job, which is honestly part of why the pivot to industry is complicated for me.

Q41.text: honestly, I don't know. I have a job waiting for me in the Industry sector, where I've been interning last year, but it isn't really my dream job or what I would love to do in long-term. I would love to stay at the University and teach, I really enjoyed doing that during my PhD, but there isn't much funding and available jobs right now, and after I spent 5 years being very poor, because of ridiculously small stipendium and just a very little support from grants, I feel like I need to go to the Industry now.

But it also took a lot from my mental health, it was enormous financial burden and I feel like I am very behind other people at my age, who now have careers, families and houses. I guess it has its good and bad sites.

Q26.text: The Japanese academic system -- at least as I have experienced it -- is built on hierarchy so rigid that it actively suppresses the kind of intellectual exchange I had come to expect from academia. In Brazil, my undergraduate advisors treated debate as the engine of knowledge; here, I find that disagreement is interpreted as insubordination, and junior researchers are expected to produce without receiving meaningful guidance in return. The absence of mentorship is not incidental -- it is structural, almost deliberate, a consequence of system that values conformity and output over the formation of independent scholars. And for international students, it's been especially isolating -- you are visible enough to be othered, but invisible enough that no one notices when you're struggling.

Q16.text: The most persistent concern is one I struggle to articulate without feeling exposed -- the erosion of confidence that comes not from any single failure, but from the cumulative weight of being made to feel peripheral. I entered this program with clear sense of intellectual direction; what I did not anticipate was how systematically that clarity would be undermined, not through overt hostility, but through indifference, through the absence of the academic dialogue that makes rigorous thinking possible. There is also the mental health dimension, which I think is largely invisible to the institution -- it is not considered a structural problem to be addressed, just a personal weakness to be managed privately. And honestly, I worry about the long-term effect this environment will have on my capacity for research -- whether, by the time I reach a postdoc in Europe, I will have enough of myself left to rebuild

Q55.text: The centrality of the advisor relationship -- not merely as academic guidance, but as the entire structure of support that either sustains or destroys you in this process. I came here trusting that institution itself would provide some scaffolding, that there were systems in place to catch students who fall through the cracks. There are not. What I know now is that if your advisor is absent -- emotionally, intellectually, structurally absent -- then you are alone in ways that no orientation handbook prepares you for, and for an international student, that aloneness is compounded by a cultural distance that can feel, on the worst days, completely insurmountable

Q41.text: A postdoc in Europe -- that has been the plan since before I arrived here, though its meaning has shifted considerably. It began as an ambition; it has become something more like a lifeline. I want to work in an environment where intellectual exchange is valued, where I can rebuild the kind of scholarly identity that has been, honestly, worn down considerably by this experience. A research institute position afterwards, somewhere I can do serious work without the politics that seem to define Japanese academic culture. I'm still committed to research -- that much hasn't changed -- but I need a different context to do it in

Q60.text: I would only add that I hope the data collected here is used to prompt genuine structural change, not simply to produce paper that catalogues what PhD students already know -- that many of us are surviving rather than thriving, and that the word "thriving" has started to feel almost ironic in context of international doctoral study. The survey asked useful questions, but there are absences: there is no question about xenophobia, about the specific isolation of being a non-Japanese student in a system that does not formally exclude you but culturally does so in ways that are hard to name and harder still to report. I am grateful for the opportunity to reflect, though reflection is its own ambivalence -- it makes the situation clearer without making it more bearable. I hope someone reads this carefully.

Q17.text: The research itself — the actual intellectual work, when I manage to access it without the noise of the institutional environment closing in. There are moments, usually late at night when the lab is empty, when I am deep enough in a problem that the rest of it recedes, and I remember why I wanted to do this in the first place. That kind of absorption is, I think, the closest thing to genuine enjoyment I've experienced here. But honestly, even that is complicated -- it's hard to separate love of the work from anxiety about whether the work is good enough, whether I am producing enough, whether my advisor has even noticed what I'm doing. The enjoyment exists, but it's been increasingly difficult to find it beneath everything else.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Ate o momento, consigo  perceber que fazer um Doutorado em um pais com uma cultura extremamente diferente e que e automaticamente refletida na cultura educacional, e um desafio tremendo, que tem impacto direto na saude mental dos estudantes. Por exemplo, venho da cultura ocidental, onde hierarquias quase sao nulas (as relacoes sao bem horizontais); a autonomia, a proatividade e a liberdade no ambiente academica sao consideradas como qualidade e bem vistas pelos Professores; o equilibrio entre vida pessoal e profissional tambem sao bem vistos e devem co-existir. Entretanto, no Japao, a sociedade e extremamente hierarquizada e essa hierarquia e refletida fortemente no ambiente academico, onde os professores sao tomam uma posicao enorme de poder e respeito, colocando-os em uma posicao inacessivel ao estudante. E isso abre tambem precedentes gravissimos para a quase institucionalizacao do abuso moral e de poder (e, uma vez, que a hierarquia e sumariamente respeitada, esses episodios quase nao sao reportados por parte dos estudantes). Ainda, considerando esse posicionamento dos professores nessa hierarquia engessada, os estudantes nao sao bem vistos se questionam, apresentam personalidade e demandam discussao (a relacao e sempre muito de submissao e negacao de discussoes). E, por ultimo, o Japao e reconhecido como o lugar que as longas jornadas de trabalho 12-14 horas por dia sao bem vistas (nao import se isso leva a uma produtividade ou nao, se a pessoa esta sofrendo ou nao), o status valorizado aqui e quantas horas voce se mantem no ambiente de trabalho e anule a sua vida pessoal. Desse modo, a ciencia aqui, que demanda debate, discussao, opinioes e completamente negada pelo sistema hierarquico, bem como sao valorizados os estudantes que vao se degradando fisicamente ao longo do seu Doutorado. Adicionalmente, o Japao e um pais, extremamente xenofobico e, enquanto estudante internacional, esse preconceito e sentido em cada detalhe da vida academica, onde, nao importa o que voce faca, atinja ou demonstre: no final e cada esquina, voce sera sumariamente desacreditado, descredibilizado e desencorajado. E, toda essa situacao nao se aplica a mim, se estende a todos os outros estudantes internacionais que aqui convivo. E algo realmente muito grave e dificil de mudar.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: A potencialidade da minha pesquisa ser muito menos explorada e ser fadada a menores alcances (achievements) ao considerar todo o abandono, a falta de interesse e o desapoio do meu Orientador de Doutorado (das coisas mais tristes e angustiantes que tenho enfrentado nesse Doutorado). No Brasil, sempre trabalhei com infra-estrutura e recursos escassos, mas eu tive grandes Professores, que me orientavam, eram modelos de inspiracao como seres humanos e profissionais para mim (foram eles,  sem duvida alguma, o maior fator de eu ter escolhido a carreira academica). Desse modo, mesmo com recursos fisicos escassos, eu tive a chance de atingir grandes resultados, porque tinha grandes professores por tras de mim. Entretanto, apos ter convivido com 4 grandes professores-orientadores que muito me ensinaram, durante o meu Bacheralado e Mestrado, desde que iniciei meu Doutorado no Japao, tenho sofrido claramente o completo abandono, desinteresse, falta de motivacao/liberdade e, aparentemente, falta de conhecimento solidos para dar suporte a minha pesquisa por parte do meu Orientador. Por consequencia, cai em um circulo vicioso: a falta de orientacao e suporte do meu Orientador, ja me levaram a series crises de Sindrome do Impostor (como cheguei ate aqui se eu era uma farsa?) e, por conseguinte, dia apos dia, reconheco que o unico desafio daqui para frente nao e so terminar o meu Doutorado, mas sim, manter a minha saude mental ate o final (o que e ainda agravado pelo fato de ta morando fora e em uma cultura completamente diferente do Brasil).

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Sem duvida, nao teria escolhido vim para o Japao. Poderia ter esperado mais, uma outra oportunidade de fazer meu PhD fora em um pais da Europa ou dos EUA. E, considerando toda a situacao inimaginavel que tenho vivido ate aqui, posso dizer sem sombra alguma de duvida, que nao ha fator nenhum mais critico que a escolha do Orientador/Supervisor de Doutorado. Essa relacao e mais seria que casamento e pode comprometer seriamente a carreira futura, a saude mental e a potencialidade profissional do futuro cientista de forma notoriamente drastica. Mas o pior, e saber que quando eu fui convidada para esse PhD aqui, eu nunca conseguiria prever/perceber a situacao real daqui (entao so vivendo mesmo para saber, nao teria como adivinhar ou voltar atras).

Q41.label: What type of career are you interested in pursuing after your graduate degree?
Q41.text: Inicialmente gostaria de entrar em um pos-doutorado academico em alguma outra instituicao ao redor do mundo - principalmente na Europa - para retomar a minha confianca pessoal e profissional de que eu sou capaz, de que eu possa sim contribuir para a formacao de novos Mestres e Doutores em um futuro proximo. Eu preciso dessa transicao oferecida pela possibilidade do Pos-doc para entao, encontrar uma oportunidade como Pesquisador em um Instituto de Pesquisa.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: Peco desculpas por toda a falta de acentuacao do meu Portugues. Considerando que estou escrevendo em um teclado Japones, nao tenho como acentuar as palavras. Caso necessitem de mais informacoes adicionais, estou apta a responder mais questoes e detalhar a dificuldade do PhD em outra cultura.

Q26.text: The academic system, from my experience so far, is one that rewards intellectual contribution genuinely, but at which the structural hierarchy creates a dependency between students and their supervisors that is quite difficult to navigate. For international students this dependency feels more acutely, because the recourse mechanisms available are either informal or poorly understood by us. Honestly there is real intellectual value in the community around me, but the distribution of power is rarely acknowledged in open.

Q16.text: One concern that occupies me quite a lot is the career uncertainty beyond the PhD itself -- the academic job market seems increasingly difficult to access for someone who does not have strong and early established networks, and for international student, building this from the beginning of program is considerably harder than I had anticipated. I guess I came here with more optimism about that side of things than the reality supports.

Q55.text: That the relationship with your supervisor is, more than any other single factor, determinative of how the entire experience will unfold — and that choosing carefully at the beginning, before the dependency has already formed, is something you have very limited ability to correct for afterward. I wish someone had been honest with me about what questions to ask before I committed to this particular arrangement.

Q41.text: Postdoctoral research is the most immediate path I am thinking toward, with the longer-term hope of moving into industry research -- probably in a role where the work is applied but still intellectually substantive. I am honestly uncertain about academic positions in the traditional sense, the job market rn makes that seem like a difficult thing to plan around, and for someone without the kind of institutional connections that come more naturally if you have studied in one place for a long time, it feels like a gamble I am not sure I can afford to make.

Q60.text: Only that I hope the findings from research like this actually reach the people who design doctoral programs, because there is a significant gap between what universities say they offer in terms of support for international students and what is practically accessible when you are in a situation of dependency with your supervisor and uncertain about the consequences of raising concerns formally. The intellectual experience has been genuinely valuable to me, and I don't want that to be lost in what I have said -- but the structural conditions around that experience are harder than they needed to be, and I think that is something the institution could do more to address if it chose to.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom to pursue questions that genuinely interest me, and the access to community of people for whom ideas are taken seriously -- that is honestly what I value most, despite everything else. There is something about working at the boundary of what is known that feels meaningful in way that is difficult to replicate, even when the conditions around that work are far from what they could be.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: One of the biggest advantages being in academia can be the biggest disadvantage for students and somewhat to an advisor. However, the impact is, personally way bigger to students. Despite the presence of committee members, Ph.D. life is a pure one-on-one relationship with your own advisor. Unless both sides are willing to collaborate together, this relationship can be easily jeopardized and there is always a power imbalance. Especially for students who have earlier on careered advisors, the expectation gets very higher with unexpected amounts of expectation and pressure. Furthermore, in the department, many of conflicts from senior and junior faculty members directly influenced to students as well. However, it is not easy to report any problems to the outside of the department because graduate students are in a very low rank in the entire university system. For students, conducnting research should be only concerns along with their futures. Yet, this relationship in the department or with an advisor makes them challenge their journey to be a Ph.D.

Q26.text: Honestly it can feel pretty arbitrary -- the Dutch system ties your defense to publications, so you're at the mercy of reviewer timelines long after the science itself is done. and you have essentially no control over that part. I still love the intellectual challenge of it, but the structural side is kind of exhausting

Q16.text: The employment situation is something I didn't fully anticipate -- being classified as a research specialist rather than a postdoc because my PhD isn't finished yet has real consequences for benefits and how colleagues perceive you. the system doesn't account for that kind of limbo very well, I think.

Q55.text: That the publication requirements in the Netherlands would turn into such a bottleneck -- I think I would have been much more strategic about journal choice and co-author dynamics early on if I'd understood how directly those decisions would affect when I could actually finish.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually informs some policy changes -- the cross-national inconsistencies in PhD systems create real hardship for people and I think it's underappreciated how much the structural stuff (publication requirements, defense timelines, employment classification) affects both wellbeing and scientific output. it would be good to see that taken seriously.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- being able to dig into questions that genuinely interest me and follow where the data leads. molecular cell biology has this kind of puzzle-like quality that I find really satisfying, even on the hard days.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: First of all, in the Netherlands, bright people are leaving academia due to the lack of grants. It is very hard to pursue an academic career when you stay in the Netherlands. Therefore, I moved to the USA to follow working in academia as a postdoctoral researcher, and I hope that this experience will give me (some) advantage in grant applications when I move back to the Netherlands in 3-4 year.   Secondly, although i started working as a postdoctoral researcher here in the USA, I am still finishing my PhD program, due to the Dutch system. As molecular cell biologists, we need to have 2 published papers and a third submitted to a peer-reviewed journal, before you can finish your thesis and set a date for a defense. Since publishing has become harder over the years (more data needed, extensive peer-review cycles that are both very consuming when the manuscript is rejected after review and needs to be submitted elsewhere where the whole cycle will start again), I have not been able to finish my PhD in the time set to do so. I started as a PhD-student in August 2013 and was supposed to finish in 4 years. Then, I was extended with one year and I left for a postdoc in Augstus 2018. To date, June 2019, I'm still not finished since manuscript acceptance takes too long.   I was lucky that my new PI here in the USA was understanding that defense in the Netherlands depends on publications, but officially I am not working as a postdoc now, but as a research specialist on a postdoc project. I know of a lot of Dutch colleagues that had to let go of their dream of a postdoc in the USA, because of this problem.  I think it is unfavorable that PhD programs differ so much between countries. I think the Dutch system aims for a very high standard, which I like, but it diminishes opportunities to succeed later in your academic life.

Q26.text: The system is structurally broken in ways that are hard to ignore — inadequate training pipelines, an absurd ratio of PhD graduates to permanent positions, and culture that tolerates toxic lab dynamics because of funding dependencies. Complaints go nowhere because the power asymmetry is baked into the hierarchy. And honestly, the mental health support available through the university feels pretty performative -- counselling waitlists that stretch weeks, wellness webinars. it doesnt really address the conditions that cause the distress in the first place.

Q55.text: The ratio of PhD graduates to permanent positions -- I knew the numbers going in, but I didn't really internalize what they meant for how supervisors treat students when students are essentially replaceable. I wish I'd known to scrutinize lab dynamics as carefully as research fit. the intellectual work can be great and still be happening inside a deeply dysfunctional environment.

Q60.text: The structural issues I've described aren't unique to my situation -- they're systemic, and I think that's worth emphasizing. Individual supervisors behaving badly, inadequate pastoral support, the mismatch between PhD training and available careers... these are policy failures, not just bad luck. I'd genuinely welcome research that influences how universities structure supervision accountability and how funding bodies think about graduate-to-position ratios. this survey feels like a step in that direction, and I hope the findings reach people with actual decision-making power.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual engagement is still real for me — the actual biology, the moments when an experiment clarifies something genuinely puzzling. that part hasn't been diminished by everything else. I also appreciate the relative autonomy to pursue questions I find meaningful, even if the structural conditions around that work are pretty frustrating.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system is clearly antiquated and has not changed sufficiently to meet current needs of PhD students, postdocs, technicians or other employees. The system needs to be updated such that PhD students receive and, more importantly, have time to receive training for non-academic positions. In addition, more permanent research positions should be added for those that are brilliant in their field, but do not want to become a PI. Q26.text: Honestly, it's a system built on power imbalances and the assumption that you'll just absorb whatever's done to you because you care too much about the work to walk away. the checks on supervisors are basically non-existent, and when things go wrong -- and they do -- institutions protect themselves first. I came in wanting to contribute to something meaningful. I'm leaving with a very different picture of what academia actually values.

Q16.text: The isolation, honestly. There's this unspoken rule that you don't talk about what's happening to you because it reflects badly on you, not the person causing the harm. I watched other students go through similar things and say nothing, and I said nothing for way too long too. That culture of silence is its own kind of damage -- it makes you doubt yourself constantly, wonder if you're being too sensitive or too demanding. And then there's the financial piece, which nobody prepares you for properly. The stipend sounds fine on paper until you're actually living on it while also trying to hold yourself together mentally. it adds this low-grade financial stress on top of everything else that just grinds you down over time.

Q55.text: That the power imbalance isn't just uncomfortable -- it's structural and deliberate, and the institution will not save you from it. I wish someone had sat me down and said: your supervisor has almost total control over your career trajectory, there are very few real checks on their behaviour, and if something goes wrong you will be the one expected to manage it quietly. Knowing that going in wouldn't have made it okay, but I might have been quicker to document things, quicker to find external support, less willing to give the benefit of the doubt for so long. I spent a lot of time thinking I must be misreading the situation. I wasn't.

Q41.text: Something outside academia -- that much I know for certain. I'm drawn to roles where I can actually use the skills I've built without the power dynamics and the precarity. Project management, policy work, maybe something in the nonprofit or public sector space where the work still feels like it matters but I'm not sacrificing my mental health to do it. I want a job where I can leave at the end of the day and not carry it home with me. That sounds like a low bar but honestly, after this, it feels like everything.

Q60.text:
Just that I hope this data actually goes somewhere useful. Surveys like this feel important and then disappear, and the people who most need to hear what's in them -- university leadership, funding bodies, the people who design supervision frameworks -- often don't, or do and don't act. I've been candid here because I think the honest picture matters, not the sanitised one. If even one structural thing changes because enough people said the same thing loudly enough, that would mean something.

And for anyone reading individual responses: please take the mental health stuff seriously. It's not a side issue. For a lot of us it was the central issue, and the academic system treats it like a personal failing rather than a predictable outcome of how it's set up. that needs to change.

Q17.text: Genuinely? It's gotten hard to answer that. There was a time when I'd have said the research itself -- the feeling of sitting with a problem long enough that something clicks. I still think that's real, I just can't access it the way I used to. The damage kind of sits on top of it. If I'm being honest, what I've valued most has been the other students -- the ones who got it, who you could be real with about how hard it is without having to perform okay. That community, such as it was, kept me going more than the work did by the end.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Academia can be a great place to be - its a unique environment that can be relaxed and creative. Ultimately though, academia is geared towards giving power and a sense of entitlement to PIs, and has lost sight of its responsibilities regarding student wellbeing. Universities have given such power and status to PIs that they can't even control them anymore. PIs don't respect university/HR systems and standard work place etiquette.    A lovely example of academia failings: I collaborate with industry and have 1 university PI and 2 industrial PIs. I have had my industrial PI make inappropriate comments to me ranging from sexual harassment to being purely nasty. One example to give you a flavour: whats happened to your skin? how do you expect to be taken seriously when you look like a spotty teenager - you should really cover your spots up. I raised this with my uni PI and described other events that had made me uncomfortable and it was shrugged off as typical behaviour from this industrial PI. the take home message was basically that we gain funding and resource from the collaboration so leave it. At this point I had had a diagnosed breakdown after a very rough first year, so was in no position to argue. As a PhD student you sometimes forget that you're a person who is entitled to opinions and feelings.  Academia needs a huge shake up (a big old slap really!), from the top down.

I  believe that this is down to my PIs - and the thought of someone ever having to feel how I have done breaks my heart. I am so pleased to see that nature is surveying people to try and act on issues around student well being. Next step: create guidelines and expectations for PIs. We need to being about a cultural change.

Q26.text: The academic system here is quite different from what I was used to back in India, where the focus is more on absorbing knowledge than producing it independently. Honestly it took me some time to adjust with that expectation, but I think the PhD environment -- especially when you have a good supervisor who actually guides you -- pushes you to grow in ways you wouldn't otherwise. Its demanding, sure, but I find that challenge meaningful rather than discouraging

Q16.text: One thing that has been on my mind is the pressure around publishing -- its something nobody really prepares you for, and coming from a background where research was more about coursework, I wasn't expecting how much your worth as a researcher gets tied to output. Also the feeling of isolation sometimes, especially when you are far from family and the work is slow. But honestly these are things I think most PhD students go through and I've learnt to see it as part of the process rather than a sign something is wrong with me specifically.

Q55.text: That research is not linear -- I spent a lot of time in my first year feeling like I was failing because things weren't progressing the way I expected, but actually that uncertainty and the dead ends are just part of the process. I wish someone had told me that early on, it would have saved me a lot of unnecessary anxiety honestly.

Q41.text: Academic research, ideally -- I would love to stay in a university setting, either as a researcher or doing some part-time lecturing. Teaching and research together feels like the right fit for me, I genuinely enjoy both and I think contributing to the next generation of scholars while still doing my own work is something I find really motivating.

Q60.text: Honestly just that I think surveys like this are actually valuable -- its easy to feel like the PhD experience is a very individual and isolated thing, but knowing that someone is trying to understand it and maybe improve things is reassuring in a way. I hope the responses are useful and that the findings eventually feed back into how universities support students, especially those coming from very different educational backgrounds like myself.

Q17.text: The freedom to actually dig into a problem that I find genuinely interesting -- that is something I didn't really have before. And honestly the intellectual conversations, with my supervisor and with other researchers, those moments where ideas start to click together are what make the difficult parts feel worth it.

Q26.text: The academic system is, at its best, a genuine community of inquiry — but the incentive structures that govern it seem almost designed to undermine that ideal. Publication pressure and grant competition push researchers toward safe, incremental work rather than genuinely rigorous exploration, which honestly makes the whole enterprise feel like a performance of productivity rather than pursuit of knowledge. My own experience has been more insulated from the worst of this than I expected, mostly because my advisor values depth over output, but I'd be naive to think that insulation persists beyond the PhD.

Q16.text: Honestly, what concerns me more than I expected is the gap between academic knowledge production and its uptake in policy — research that most directly bears on real decisions often seems to circulate only within discipline that produced it. I'm not sure the system has any structural incentive to change this, which makes my own career aspirations feel somewhat quixotic.

Q55.text: That the metrics by which you'll be assessed — publications, conference appearances, grant applications — have almost no correlation with the intellectual work you'll find most valuable, and that learning to pursue the latter while satisfying the former is a skill nobody explicitly teaches you but everyone implicitly expects you to have already.

Q41.text: Policy-oriented research, ideally in a government or public-sector context where there's at least a plausible mechanism for evidence to influence decisions — though I'm under no illusion that the pathway from research to policy is direct or reliable.

Q60.text: Only that I think surveys like this one serve a genuinely useful function, even if the findings rarely make it back to the people who completed them — which is, I suppose, another small instance of the same research-to-practice gap I mentioned earlier. I hope the data is useful to someone making actual decisions about doctoral programs, rather than just circulating within the field that studies them.

Q17.text: The intellectual intimacy of it, honestly — the conversations you can have with people who are genuinely invested in ideas for their own sake, which is rarer than it should be even within academia. My advisor and I have had exchanges that changed the way I think about problems, and whatever frustrations attend the broader system, that kind of engagement feels like the actual point of the enterprise.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Sometimes it seems that people (grad students, faculty, institutions) are more concerned with producing science that will get them publicity or name recognition, not science that actually moves a field forward and contributes meaningfully to a discipline. It feels as though sound, rigorous work is sometimes neglected in favor of vapid, flashy press releases. Thankfully I don't get this from my advisor, but the academic climate sometimes feels superficially self-promoting. Science is a difficult, prolonged endeavor, but every other press release coming out of a big university makes it seem like someone just found the silver bullet to solve one of the grand challenges facing society. Science just doesn't work like that, but it seems that people fabricate this façade to impress peers/funding agencies/tenure committees etc. I don't think this is a helpful environment to create.

Q26.text: Broken, and designed to stay that way -- the incentives protect the institution, NEVER the student. I spent years being gaslit by someone with total power over my career, and every time I tried to escalate, the department basically shrugged. you're just... disposable. That's the honest answer. There are good people in it, sure, but the system as a whole selects for a kind of compliance that I think is genuinely damaging -- to your work, your sense of self, everything. I left. Best decision I made in years, and I only wish I'd done it sooner.

Q16.text: The financial piece -- I haven't even touched that. Living on a stipend that barely covered rent while my advisor kept dangling "just one more year" like a carrot... the precarity is its own form of control, honestly. And the isolation. Nobody warns you how alone you'll feel, even surrounded by other PhD students, because you can't really talk about what's happening without risking it getting back to the wrong person. I think the mental health fallout is something I'm still processing -- like, I didn't realise how much of my identity I'd handed over until it was basically gone. financial dependence + social isolation + one person holding absolute authority over your future is a combination that should ring alarm bells for anyone designing these programs, but it doesn't, because it's always been this way. It took me a long time to stop seeing leaving as failure. The system failed. Not me.

Q55.text: That your advisor's opinion of you is not an objective measure of your ability -- full stop. I genuinely believed, for years, that the constant criticism meant something true about me. It didn't. It meant something true about him, and about a power structure that lets one person's dysfunction become your entire reality. If I'd known that going in -- really known it, not just abstractly -- I think I would have found my footing faster, or gotten out sooner. do your due diligence on your advisor like your career depends on it, because it literally does. Talk to their former students. Ask the uncomfortable questions before you sign anything.

Q41.text: Industry, no question. I left academia and I'm not going back -- not for a post-doc, not for anything. I have an industry job now and honestly the difference in how I'm treated as a professional is... striking. I'd actively discourage anyone with the choice from going the academic route without first building real-world experience, because you need that foundation to know when you're being treated badly. Academia will convince you the dysfunction is normal. Industry reminded me it isn't.

Q60.text:
Just... thank you for actually asking. I don't know what comes of these surveys but I hope someone reads them and does something with it -- not just files it away. If even one person designing these programs sees this and thinks harder about the power structures they're building, that matters.

I want to be clear: I don't regret the intellectual work. I loved the ideas, the reading, the thinking -- that part of me is intact. What I resent is that the system used that love as leverage. You care about the work, so you tolerate things you NEVER should have tolerated. That's the mechanism and people need to name it.

If any prospective PhD students ever see research like this -- please, do your homework before you commit. The program matters less than the advisor. The advisor matters less than whether they have a documented history of treating students like people. and if the department can't give you names of students to talk to... that's your answer right there.

I'm okay now. took a while, but I'm okay. I just don't want other people to lose five years finding out what I did.

Q17.text:
The intellectual freedom -- or what felt like it, at least at the start. The reading, the thinking, the sense that you're sitting with genuinely hard questions and nobody's telling you to wrap it up. I loved that. I still do, honestly, it's just... not something I needed a PhD to have, it turns out. I can read and think in industry just fine, without the rest of it.

But I want to be honest: even that got contaminated eventually. When your advisor controls whether your ideas are "good enough," the joy of thinking starts to feel conditional. You stop trusting your own intellectual instincts because someone's spent years telling you they're wrong. so even the thing I loved most -- I had to reclaim it after I left. and I have. But it took time.

The ideas were real. The love of the work was real. The system that was supposed to support it was NOT.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I would NEVER recommend anyone get a Ph.D. until they are 40--get a real job first then if you want continue education.  I have slight ptsd and depression due to my Ph.D. experience.  I am still a paying student now but am considering withdrawing from current university and enrolling in a different university where I know I will finish.  The academic system is a system is well developed and well hidden abuse [of students and staff].  The poor leadership of department has allowed this abuse to continue.  I have 'fought' but I have no 'cards' as my advisor has to sign my degree.  Thus, I left after 5 years of a 4 year program to get a job; I have an awesome job now, but still not Ph.D. from current university.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: In hindsight, I would have never joined my current advisors lab.  So I would consider talking with previous students to see the 'true colors' of the advisor you are considering.  Previous students are students NOT associated with advisor.  Unfortunately current and former students may lie [which is what happened to me; all related to the trauma of abuse.]  So..I think if you are interested in a Ph.D. get a job for a year or two before you join--you need to develop what the 'real' world is not a world of a professor is--this will develop a backbone so your advisor cannot run over you.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: Glad you are doing this survey.  Only thing not covered is advisor playing favorites within the lab group, but that could be under discrimination.  Also the university and department was not covered here...meaning does your department support you when a student reports advisor bullying (in my case no my department sees no problem with a student taking 7 years to complete a 4 year Ph.D. when the last 2 chapters sit on advisors desk for 5 years).  Not covered also is did you leave before finishing? and are you currently working on finishing?  Are you going to another university because you can't finish etc.  In summary, my Ph.D. program taught me the I am a terrible writer, terrible presenter, terrible scientist etc.  I learned how to handle toxic and hostile working environments.  It has taken about 3 years post-advisor to acknowledge that I am not a terrible writer, terrible presenter or a terrible scientist.  I am in fact awesome.

Q26.text: The academic system has real intellectual freedom -- you get to pursue questions that genuinely matter, which I dont take for granted. The community around me is honestly what makes it work. The structural logic of it all, though, feels somewhat indifferent to actual people.

Q16.text: The pressure to perform certainty about your future, I think — it's something that doesn't get named very often. Everyone around you seems to have a clear narrative about where they're headed, and if you don't, there's this low-level anxiety that maybe you're doing something wrong. I'm genuinely open to different paths, but the system doesn't really create space for that kind of openness. It reads it as lack of ambition, which isn't quite the same thing.

Q55.text: That it's okay — actually healthy — to not have a fixed endpoint in mind. I spent a lot of energy early on trying to construct a clear five-year trajectory, partly because that's what the culture seemed to reward. It took me a while to realize that staying genuinely curious matters more than performing certainty, and that the people you work alongside will shape your experience far more than the institution itself.

Q41.text: Honestly, I'm open to both academic and non-academic paths -- what matters more to me is that the work involves research or teaching in some meaningful way, and that it leaves room for a life outside of it. I dont feel the pull toward a tenure-track position at all costs, which I think used to worry me more than it does now.

Q60.text: Something I'd add -- and I'm not sure where else to put this -- is that surveys like this one feel genuinely useful, maybe because it's rare to be asked to reflect on the experience rather than just perform it. I hope the responses are actually read. The thing about PhD culture is that the feedback loops are so slow and indirect, so its hard to know if naming these things changes anything. But I think it matters to try.

Q17.text: The people, honestly -- that's the clearest answer I have. Q26.text: The academic system incentivizes quantity over quality in ways that actively undermine reproducibility and honest science -- it's kind of exhausting to watch, honestly. The publish-or-perish structure rewards flashy results over rigorous methodology, and institutions have shown little appetite to reform this. That said, the intellectual community itself is where I find meaning. the structure is broken, not the vocation.

Q16.text: Career precarity is something I didn't fully get into above. The postdoc pipeline is brutal, and the lack of stable positions means most of us are making contingency plans that pull focus from the research itself. I find myself thinking about science policy roles more than faculty positions -- not because I want to leave, but because the math just doesnt work out.

Q55.text: That the incentive structure is the problem, not individual researchers failing to work hard enough. I spent the first year trying to optimize within a broken system before realizing thats just not how it works. Knowing it earlier would have redirected energy toward advocacy and reform much sooner, rather than internalizing the dysfunction as a personal failure.

Q41.text: Science policy or research integrity advocacy, probably. I'm interested in roles where you can actually push on the structural problems rather than just survive within them -- so organizations working on open science, reproducibility initiatives, or academic reform. Faculty positions aren't off the table entirely but the math makes it hard to bet on that path rn.

Q60.text: The reproducibility crisis isn't going away on its own, and I think surveys like this are actually part of how change happens -- aggregating the lived experience of people inside the system matters. My main hope is that the data gets used not just to describe the problem but to push for concrete reforms: better incentive alignment, more stable funding structures, actual consequences for p-hacking and selective reporting. I'm probably more optimistic about change than my earlier answers suggest, but its conditional on people being willing to act on what they find.

Q17.text: The intellectual community, genuinely. Being around people who care deeply about hard problems -- that part doesnt get old. And there's something meaningful about doing work that, at least in theory, expands what we know. the day-to-day research itself is rewarding even when the system surrounding it isn't.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: There is enormous pressure to publish in glam journals to secure the next in your career. The ultra competitive job market (for long-term academic career options) does not even want to try the best candidates but is rather looking for the scientific output in glam journals. This hurts reliable, robust and reproducible research since researcher tend to oversell their data to write a "sexy" breakthrough story. People need to play the game to have a reasonable perspective to stay in the system. Critical research, scientific outreach and questioning the system is either not rewarded or can be detrimental to career options. Scandals are likely hushed up and whistle blowers punished.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's more hierarchical and self-interested than I expected going in — I think I came in believing collaboration was the norm, but in practice people are pretty protective of their work and their opportunities. That said, there's still something genuinely stimulating about being around people who care deeply about ideas, even if the system itself rewards positioning over merit (or at least that's how it feels rn).

Q16.text: The job market, honestly — it's something I try not to think about too much, but it's always there in the background. I came in knowing it was competitive, but I don't think I fully grasped how much of it comes down to who you know and which institution you're affiliated with rather than the actual quality of your research. And the funding situation for postdocs is just... it's precarious in a way that makes long-term planning feel kind of pointless sometimes. I still want to stay in research (ideally in a center or agency setting rather than a traditional faculty role), but I'm more realistic now about what that path actually looks like, and its not always encouraging.

Q55.text: That collaboration in academia is a lot more transactional than it looks from the outside — I think I assumed people shared ideas freely and helped each other out of genuine intellectual generosity, but a lot of it is actually strategic (which isn't always bad, but it was a bit of a shock). If I'd understood that earlier I probably would have been more deliberate about building my own network rather than waiting for it to happen organically.

Q41.text: Research-focused roles, ideally in a research center or institutional agency setting — I'm less drawn to the traditional faculty track than I used to be, partly because of what I've observed about how those positions actually work in practice. Something where I can focus on the research itself without quite so much of the positioning and politics.

Q60.text: Just that I think surveys like this are genuinely useful -- it's rare to feel like someone in the system is actually trying to understand what the experience is like from the inside. I hope the data gets used in a way that leads to some concrete changes, though I'll admit I'm a bit skeptical about how much institutional appetite there is for that. But I appreciate the opportunity to reflect on it, and honestly some of these questions made me think about things I'd kind of pushed to the back of my mind.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- having the time and actual mandate to dig into a problem without someone needing it wrapped up by end of quarter. I genuinely enjoy that part. And being around people who are serious about ideas, even if the culture around it is more complicated than I expected (the positioning, the politics -- it gets old), the work itself is still something I find pretty absorbing.

Q26.text: A feudal structure dressed in the language of meritocracy, honestly. In the military you have hierarchy too but there is also accountability — someone can be court-martialed for abuse of power. Here, a supervisor can damage a student's entire career trajectory with zero recourse. The intellectual challenge I genuinely love, but the power dynamic is... something else entirely. I've seen things in this environment that would not be tolerated in any other professional context, and everyone just shrugs like its normal.

Q16.text: The isolation from clinical work has been harder than I expected — as a doctor you are used to immediate feedback, patients get better or they dont, but in academia you can spend months on something and have no idea if it matters to anyone. and the mental health support structures here are, lets say, not built for people who came from high-pressure professional backgrounds.

Q55.text: That the relationship with your supervisor is not just important — it is *everything*, and unlike clinical work there is almost no formal mechanism to change it if it goes wrong. Choose them like you're choosing a commanding officer who has no CO above them.

Q41.text: Return to clinical medicine — I still hold my MD registration and residency is where I'm heading. Academia has been... educational, lets say, but not in the way I anticipated.

Q60.text: The systemic problem is that universities have outsourced accountability entirely to the market — students cant leave without losing years of their life, so the usual consumer protection logic doesnt apply. I've watched colleagues spiral into genuine psychiatric crises because there was no one to report to who wasn't also beholden to the same supervisor. In medicine we have ethics boards, licensing bodies, mortality and morbidity reviews — structures that assume humans in power will sometimes abuse it. Academia just has... vibes, honestly. I hope this data is useful to someone.

Q17.text: The intellectual depth you can reach when the work is going well — there's genuinely nothing like it. In clinical medicine everything is urgent and practical, which I love, but here you get to *actually think* for months about one problem. that part I wouldn't trade.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The word that probably describes it best is medieval.... I guess a PhD can be a great experience if you have somewhat nice supervisors and professors and a decent project... However, it can be horrific if you land for 3-4 years in a bad place with no support and an overrated prof.  Why is it that at universities, the origin of science, knowledge and enlighment, we still have the most medieval system still in place in the western world? Why are professors elected for lifetime and have nearly unlimited power, being able to decide on peoples careers, advancements, paper positions (although they often did not contribute that much)? There is a reason we elect political leaders regulary and they can just be elected twice: to prevent an abuse, an unhealthy accummulation of power. Similarly, economic leaders must defend their action at least yearly to stackholders and are swiftly fired if having performed badly. However, all those rules seem to be out of order in academics, where profs govern until retirement and are normally not being hold responsible for their mistakes and bad decisions. Universities harbour the most hierarchical, authoritorian system still in place today which predisposes to power abuse... and belive me, i do not in general have problems with hierarchical systems, i stent 3 years in the army.

Q26.text: The academic system, as structured, optimizes for outputs that are measurable and attributable to senior researchers while diffusing accountability for conditions that impede junior researchers. Q16.text: The absence of a formal grievance pathway that operates independently of the department is a structural gap I didn't anticipate. Q55.text: The formal authority of a supervisor to approve work and the informal authority to undermine it are not mutually exclusive -- they can coexist in the same person, within the same institution, without triggering any corrective mechanism. Q41.text: Academic research remains the context in which the work I find meaningful is most readily pursued, but the institutional structures that house it have proven less reliable than I initially assumed. Q17.text: The problems themselves -- the actual intellectual work of formulating questions that resist easy resolution and building arguments that hold under scrutiny. Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: In Sweden, the typical student is a salaried employee on exactly one project tied to exactly one of the advisor's grants. The focus is on engineering papers, which make minimal publishable contributions in write-only journals, rather than scientific problems. Students also strive to write minimal papers that address the interests of senior professors, rather than solve real problems.

Q26.text: Structurally broken in ways that are pretty predictable once you see them. The system does reasonable job of training researchers but almost no job of preparing people for careers -- academic or otherwise -- and that gap is getting harder to ignore. Supervision quality is wildly inconsistent and there's basically no accountability mechanism for it. Honestly, what I've found most valuable is the intellectual community, not the formal training, which says something about where the system's actual priorities lie.

Q60.text: The main thing I'd add is that this kind of survey is genuinely useful, but only if institutions are actually willing to act on the patterns it surfaces. I've seen too many reports sit in a drawer. The structural issues I've described -- supervision accountability, career development, the mental health culture -- are not surprising to anyone who's been through the system. What's missing isn't data, it's institutional will. Tbh I hope this one gets read by someone with actual decision-making power.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system is designed to train PhD students to become PIs. In the process of doing so, PhD students gain valuable experience and transferable skills that make them competent and resourceful individuals. However, the expectation is very much that you would continue on to a post-doc position. This, in my view, is not a good thing given the relatively few academic jobs available. PhD programmes should establish closer links to industry and and other non-research related science careers to ensure that PhD students gain the skills aligned with these careers after they graduate, and build networks to facilitate job opportunities. PhD programmes and institutions also do not articulate well enough the capabilities of PhD graduates to employers in the wider sector, and can improve on this.  PIs and funding bodies have a lot of incentive to employ PhD students and post-docs in the short term on temporary contracts, but the academic system should incentivise instead the hiring of permanent staff scientists for those who want to be in the lab full-time. For those that don't, greater exposure to other career paths (eg. talks, networking opportunities, work experience placements and internships) is needed for PhD students' career progression.  In many cases, poor supervision from the PI and a negative group environment can detract from the PhD experience - this is really hard to judge from a short interview.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Have a good think about career paths and thoroughly explore opportunities before starting. Pick a PhD in a field with clear connections to industry and hireable skills, that also interests you. Spend more time in the first 1/2 of the PhD deciding on career path, to plan an exit strategy about ~2y before graduation.

Q26.text: The academic system is built for people who already belong to it. My supervisor was stretched too thin to actually supervise anyone, and the department head had his own ideological agenda that made genuine intellectual work harder. International students are an afterthought -- the system tolerates us as long as we dont demand too much. That's been my experience, pretty consistently.

Q16.text: The isolation, honestly. Nobody prepares you for how alone you feel when youre far from home and the institution treats your presence as a transaction. There's no real support structure for international students dealing with mental health or financial strain -- you're expected to just manage. And the career path feels increasingly pointless. I've watched colleagues burn out chasing postdocs that lead nowhere, and I dont want that.

Q55.text: That the quality of your PhD depends almost entirely on your supervisor, not your institution or your project. I wish someone had told me to treat the supervisor selection like the most important decision of my whole academic career -- because it is. Everything else you can adapt to. A bad supervisor, you mostly cannot.

Q41.text: Science policy -- working in public institutions or research-funding bodies where I can actually influence how research gets done and who it benefits. I'm done with the traditional academic track. The system I've experienced doesn't reward good work, it rewards endurance, and I'm not interested in that game anymore.

Q60.text: The main thing I'd add is that surveys like this matter, but only if someone actually reads them and acts on the findings. I've seen too many "we value your feedback" exercises that produce a report nobody reads. If this data is used to push for real structural changes -- better supervision frameworks, actual support for international students, something -- then it was worth filling out. If not, it's just more data collection that makes the institution feel like it's doing something. I hope it's the former.

Q17.text: The research itself, when I actually get to do it. There's something real about spending time on a problem that hasn't been solved yet -- that part I dont take for granted. It's just that the system piles so much administrative noise and institutional dysfunction on top of it that the actual intellectual work gets crowded out more often than it should.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Completely broken. The director of the institute, an economist, openly mocked whoever even slightly challenged growth/neoliberal economics. My supervisor, and that of many others in my department, had way too many BA/MA/PhD students to supervise, applications to write, and articles to publish. It took my supervisor four to six months to read my manuscripts, and the comments on them would be limited to nothing but one-liners. Just terrible.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The complete disregard for the effort that foreigners make to leave their country and study abroad. Throughout the PhD all people, regardless of background, were treated the same. This may sound ideal at first, but given the cultural and educational differences between the foreigners -who came from all corners of the world- and the locals who had spent either their whole lives in the same country/culture or even the same university, treating everyone the same way shows who little they care about the diversity and how it impacts expectations on both sides.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: That PhDs are at a disadvantage in the job market due to general ignorance regarding that a PhD is. That most employers prefer to hire people with a Master's, especially in Europe, because 'they're good enough' and because they don't have to pay them as much.

Q26.text: Structurally flawed in ways that seem almost designed to concentrate power in individual supervisors while leaving students very little recourse. There's genuine intellectual community out there, but the institutional scaffolding -- opaque expectations, geographic dispersal of peers, the rosier picture painted at recruitment -- makes it harder to access than it should be. Honestly, I find that pretty dispiriting, even as I can see what the system is trying to do.

Q16.text: The uncertainty about what comes next has been a persistent low-grade concern — not just where I'll end up, but whether the skills I'm building here actually transfer to the paths I'm considering. Exploring academia, government, and industry simultaneously is honestly kind of energising, but it also signals how little confidence I have that any one of them is actually open to me.

Q55.text: How dependent everything is on a single relationship — the supervisor. I wish I'd known to treat that choice as the most consequential decision of the entire program, not an afterthought once the department said yes. I wish I'd asked harder questions at recruitment rather than taking the institutional presentation at face value. The department sells you a vision of community and support that, in practice, sits almost entirely with one person.

Q41.text: Multiple paths, honestly — I'm actively looking at academic positions, government policy or research roles, and industry, without having closed off any of them. The PhD was supposed to clarify this and it kinda hasn't, though I'm treating that as information rather than paralysis.

Q60.text: Just that I hope the data from this kind of survey actually reaches the people who can do something with it. The structural issues I've described aren't novel -- I suspect they're pretty widespread -- and it's kind of disheartening to think that these problems are well-documented and yet persist. If nothing else, I hope whoever reads these responses genuinely reckons with the gap between how PhD programs are marketed and what they actually deliver day to day.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual freedom — the ability to follow a question as far as it goes without someone pulling me back toward something more immediately useful. That part has genuinely delivered, even when a lot else hasn't.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?

Although the university as a whole has made many changes to meet altered expectations, the faculty and management and department heads have not adjusted their system to the new situations in academia.
