Q26.text: The academic system is intellectually rich but structurally exploitative -- the knowledge produced and mentorship available are genuinely valuable, but the pipeline itself seems designed to funnel enormous numbers of highly trained people toward vanishingly few tenure positions, while paying them appalling wages during the training period. I've gained tremendously in scientific terms, but honestly I find it difficult to recommend the path to others without significant caveats about financial reality and career prospects

Q16.text: The mental health crisis among graduate students is something I think about a lot -- there's almost no institutional acknowledgment of the psychological toll that years of underpaid, high-stakes work takes, and the stigma around seeking help remains appalling. the lack of transparency around funding decisions has also been source of real anxiety throughout.

Q55.text: How genuinely poor the academic job market is -- not in the abstract way people mention it when you're applying, but in concrete statistical terms. I wish someone had shown me the actual placement data for my field before I committed years of underpaid work to pipeline that leads, for most people, nowhere near tenure track.

Q41.text: Government or non-profit research, honestly -- the work-life balance and mission-driven focus are increasingly appealing compared to academic track that has such slim odds of leading anywhere stable. I'm still interested in doing science, just not in system that seems designed to exploit the people doing it.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually reaches people with power to change things -- the problems I've described aren't individual failures, they're structural, and they require structural responses. Stipend levels, transparency in funding, honest career placement data shared with prospective students before enrollment. I appreciate the survey existing, but honestly the cynical part of me wonders whether findings like these ever translate into meaningful policy. I hope I'm wrong about that.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom is genuinely something I value -- being able to spend years deeply engaged with a specific set of questions, building real expertise, and occasionally producing results that feel like they matter. the conversations with colleagues and mentors have been the best part, honestly, even when everything else about the structure feels broken.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: What I have learnt, in terms of research tools, methods, statistical analyses and all technical and intellectual knowledge, has been quite what I expected and what I wanted to learn. Very satisfying. The financial part, how graduate students are commonly used as cheap easy labor to get papers out of the door for supervisors, and poor recognition of the financial burden that graduate school represents is disappointing. And the struggle for obtaining a research position, the prospect of a minimum of 5 years of post-doctoral positions before potentially obtaining the sought after tenure positions in north America, is appalling

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: Not getting even a small financial recognition of the extra work and education involved with doing a PhD compared to a Master (all graduate student in my lab, Masters and PhDs, are paid a similar rate)

Q26.text: Structurally dysfunctional, tbh. The incentives are misaligned at almost every level -- funding priorities, publication norms, how supervisors are selected and evaluated (spoiler: they're largely not). There's genuine intellectual richness in the work itself, but the institution seems almost designed to resist efficiency. The people who thrive are either politically savvy or just lucky enough to land in a functional lab.

Q16.text: The training gap in quantitative methods has honestly been a bigger issue than I expected — neuroscience is increasingly computational, and my program just hasn't kept up. I've had to self-teach a lot of what I actually need, which takes time away from the research itself. and the general opacity of departmental decision-making is its own kind of exhausting.

Q55.text: How much the lab environment determines basically everything. Not the university, not the department -- the specific lab. I would've been a lot more rigorous about evaluating potential supervisors before committing; the selection process felt like a formality at the time and it really isn't.

Q41.text: Academic neuroscience is the primary goal, but I'm keeping biomedical data science genuinely open -- not as a fallback but as a real alternative if the academic job market stays as brutal as it is rn. The computational skills I've had to build on my own are actually more marketable in industry than I expected, which changes the calculus a bit.

Q60.text: The lack of coordination between PhD programs and the actual skill demands of the field feels like a systemic failure no one wants to own. And the emotional cost of navigating institutional dysfunction on top of doing actual research is rarely acknowledged. I hope this data is useful to someone.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly. Getting to spend most of my time on problems I actually find fascinating -- that part is real, and I don't want to undersell it. Neuroscience is genuinely interesting work, even when the institutional context around it makes everything harder than it needs to be.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: HORRIBLE. I love science but the highly politicized, brutally inefficient, and poorly organized academic institutions I've encountered so far are driving me out of it.  I am frequently disappointed by the lack of coordination between research groups (even different individuals within my own lab). I feel I may be an outlier but I crave a more hierarchical structure in which higher levels can coordinate research so we stop wasting huge amounts of time and resources.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: My current biggest pet peeve is that my biomedical program (and I believe many others) is not preparing me well for either the kinds of academic or non-academic jobs I'd like, specifically there is a striking lack of resources or support for learning critical quantitative skills including statistics and programming.

Q26.text: The academic system here -- at least from what I've experienced in China -- is kind of built on optics and performance metrics more than genuine research culture. There is real intellectual challenge and I value that, I do. But there's also pressure that don't always feel academically motivated (or maybe I'm just not seeing the full picture yet). Foreign students especially, we're sometimes more like a statistic for internationalization than actual researcher in the community. So... mixed, honestly.

Q16.text: The imposter syndrome is a real concern, honestly -- I look at my labmates and they seem to carry ten years of instinct that I just don't have yet, and it's hard to know if that gap closes with time or not. The publication pressure also something I didn't expect to feel this strongly, there's an expectation to produce on a timeline that doesn't always fit how research actually works. I'm young (I know that about myself) so maybe things improve. but right now it feels like carrying a lot at once

Q55.text: That imposter syndrome is not a proof you're in wrong place -- it's just how this feels at the beginning, I think. I assumed that becoming capable would announce itself more clearly from inside. It doesn't. And honestly nobody warns you that the hardest part is learning to trust your own judgment when the system around you gives almost no feedback on whether you're actually growing

Q41.text: Academic research -- ideally a postdoc first and then a faculty position somewhere that actually values the work over the metrics. I know that's not easy to land but its what I'm aiming for rn.

Q60.text: Just that I appreciate the survey existing -- these questions made me think more carefully about my situation than I usually let myself. I hope the data is useful for something concrete. And I guess if there's one thing I'd want researchers or administrators to take from responses like mine: the experience of foreign PhD students is not monolithic, and being international doesn't mean you're fine just because you got the visa and the enrollment. Some of us are doing okay (I think I am, mostly). But the structural stuff -- the way we're counted rather than mentored -- that's worth looking at more directly.

Q17.text: The intellectual part -- genuinely. When a problem resists you and then suddenly it doesn't, that feeling is hard to replicate anywhere else. I also enjoy that there's no ceiling on how deep you can go into something, nobody tells you to stop thinking. The autonomy is real, even when everything else feels constrained.

Q26.text: The academic system, as I have experienced it, functions less like an institution of knowledge and more like a feudal hierarchy dressed in the language of intellectual merit. Resources flow upward — toward established professors, toward high-impact journals, toward grant-winning labs — while the labour that sustains the entire edifice is extracted from graduate students who are told, repeatedly, that their suffering is a rite of passage. The publish-or-perish culture doesn't merely incentivize productivity; it actively punishes integrity, rewarding those who generate volume over those who do careful, honest work. And the international students — people who have uprooted their lives and crossed continents for this — face a compounded vulnerability, dependent on visa sponsorship and supervisor goodwill in ways that make dissent nearly impossible. And make no mistake: the dysfunction is not incidental. It is structural. The system was not designed to cultivate researchers so much as to produce cheap, replaceable academic labour while concentrating prestige among a small, self-reproducing elite. Honestly, the only thing that might change any of this is transparent, comparative data — and institutions actually willing to be held accountable by it, which is a much harder ask than it sounds.

Q16.text:
The mental health crisis among PhD students is something I find genuinely alarming, and it remains — somehow — still treated as a private failing rather than a systemic outcome. When the majority of your cohort is experiencing anxiety or depression at rates that would trigger mandatory intervention in any other workplace, that is not a personal resilience problem. That is an institutional design problem. and the silence around it compounds everything: you are expected to perform gratitude for an opportunity that is quietly destroying you.

I'm also concerned by how completely unprepared most of us are for careers outside academia — not because we lack ambition or skills, but because the entire PhD structure is oriented toward reproducing more academics, most of whom will never find stable academic positions. No one sits you down in year one and says, honestly, the odds are not in your favour, here are transferable skills you should be developing. Instead you are encouraged to publish, to present, to perform academic citizenship — activities that have near-zero value outside the university and consume years of your life in the process. When I look at peers who left early, they are, without exception, doing better: financially, psychologically, professionally. That tells you something. It tells you something the institution has no incentive to say out loud.

Q55.text: The base rate for permanent academic positions. Not the vague reassurance that "if you work hard it will work out," but the actual numbers: how many PhDs graduate in your field each year, how many tenure-track positions open, what the conversion rate actually looks like across a decade. Had someone handed me those figures in week one, I would have made entirely different decisions -- about which skills to develop, about which relationships to invest in, about whether the whole enterprise was worth the cost it demands. Honestly, that information exists. It is not hidden exactly, just never volunteered, because sharing it openly would hollow out the recruitment pipeline and nobody at the top of the hierarchy has any incentive to do that.

Q41.text: Outside academia entirely. I've been clear-eyed about this for a while now -- the numbers don't lie, and tbh I stopped wanting to be part of a system I fundamentally don't respect. I'm orienting toward roles where merit and output are actually legible: data analysis, policy research, maybe the public sector or an NGO with genuine accountability structures. Somewhere that the work I do has a traceable impact and isn't mediated by whether the right senior person decided to champion me this particular year.

Q60.text:
The survey itself is a small act of courage on the part of whoever commissioned it, and I mean that without irony. Gathering this data is exactly the kind of transparency I described as necessary -- and the fact that someone is actually doing it, rather than gesturing at it in mission statements, matters. I hope the findings are published prominently and not quietly shelved when they become inconvenient for institutional PR.

What I'd add, for whoever reads these responses: please resist the urge to aggregate the pain into statistics that make it manageable and distant. Behind every elevated anxiety score is a person who restructured their entire life around a promise that was never going to be kept. The exploitation isn't dramatic or sudden -- it's slow, cumulative, and delivered with the vocabulary of mentorship and opportunity. That's what makes it so hard to name, and so easy for institutions to deny.

And honestly, if this data ends up being used to nudge a few policy levers while leaving the fundamental incentive structure intact, that's not nothing, but it's not enough either. The publish-or-perish machinery, the visa dependency of international students, the fiction of meritocracy -- those are load-bearing walls, not cosmetic features. I don't expect a survey to demolish them. But I do hope this is one more piece of evidence that makes the demolition harder to defer.

Q17.text:
If I'm being honest, the intellectual work itself — when you can actually get to it, which is rarer than advertised. There are moments when a research question opens into something genuinely surprising, when the data contradicts what you expected and you have to sit with that discomfort and rethink. Those moments are real. I don't want to pretend they aren't.

But I'd be lying if I said the enjoyment is uncomplicated, because the institution has a remarkable talent for colonising even that. The curiosity that brought me here hasn't died, but it's been made into a performance -- packaged into abstracts, instrumentalised for grant applications, evaluated by metrics that have almost nothing to do with whether the work is actually true or important. So what I enjoy most is probably the version of this that exists in spite of the system: a good conversation with a peer, an unexpected finding, an hour of reading where nobody is asking what it will produce. Honestly, those things keep me going. but they're scraps, not a diet.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system needs a drastic overhaul. It has become a corrupt and abusive system. I would like to see major reforms at every single level. Most research is published for the sole reason of publishing a paper. Papers and impact factors have become the currency of academia; the desire to do Science for the sake of progress or humanity is largely non-existent. Most places and people care about the length of the CV, but no thought is spared towards the impact these studies may have had. Further, the Ph.D. student is left at the mercy of the supervisor and the academic system which tends to protect itself when questioned. Universities have become brands and they care too much about their brands. Harassment cases are quietly stamped out to protect the university's and the supervisor's reputation. This is true more so for international students who put their entire careers and lives on the line to work towards their Ph.D.s on a pittance. Lip service is paid to women empowerment, but women are consistently left out at every possible turn. A strong teaching effort is drummed up by universities, but everyone knows teaching takes away from one's ability to manufacture papers. It looks incredibly bleak for academia unless one is well-connected and comes with the right brand and backing. The way I see it, academia has stagnated and it does not look like things are changing for the better any time soon. Of course, one can write an entire article, and many have been written without much effect, about the publication system and the exorbitant cost of acquiring "knowledge" in today's world.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: I find it absolutely baffling that academia, while propped up as the last bastion of ethical and moral purity, tolerates faculty and students with alarming behavioral issues. In my experience, I have seen faculty members get away with sexual harassment and abuse at multiple universities with supreme confidence. Further, the biggest lesson I have received during my Ph.D. is that academia rarely cares about merit or quality. There are, to the best of my knowledge, only two ways to get ahead: my advisor is well connected and/or I somehow manage to find my way onto a Nature or Science publication. Maybe this is to be expected given the shortage of jobs, but it makes academia an ideal breeding ground for abusive relationships. I also find that enough is not done to make incoming students understand how slim the chances of an academic career really are, post Ph.D. Maybe it is too much, and not even the point of a Ph.D., to train students for careers outside of academia. However, the system is nothing short of a scam if incoming students are, at the very least, not made aware of the reality of the job market. Precious few universities and departments actively expose their students to opportunities outside of academia by encouraging participation in workshops, conventions, presentations, alumni networks, etc. And no, it is not the sole responsibility of the incoming student to know how the job market is. It is similar to arguing that sweatshops employing immigrants in the Middle Eastern countries carry none of the blame and arguing instead that the blame must rest on the people working there "voluntarily".  And make no mistake, academia today is eerily similar to a sweatshop.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: How important it is to mentally prepare for a non-academic job early. I waited too long before I realized how bleak academia really was.

Q26.text: The academic system -- at least as I've experienced it -- is structured in ways that serve institutions far more than the people moving through them; there's a kind of learned helplessness that gets enforced at every stage, from the dependency relationship with supervisors to the cheerful fiction that completing PhD translates into viable career prospects. Honestly, it protects itself remarkably well while leaving students to absorb all the risk.

Q16.text: The opportunity cost, honestly -- years of reduced income, professional stagnation, a CV that looks worse to non-academic employers than it did before I enrolled -- is something I didn't fully reckon with at the outset. and I'm not sure the research environment itself has done much to offset that; there's a persistent sense that the work I'm doing matters to almost no one outside a very narrow circle, which is kind of exhausting to sit with long-term.

Q55.text: How rarely supervisors are held to account for anything -- not outcomes, not conduct, not basic professional obligations that would be non-negotiable in any other employment context. I understood intellectually that the relationship was important; I didn't understand how completely your progress, your wellbeing, and your eventual employability could be at the mercy of one person's indifference or ego, with essentially no institutional recourse if things go wrong.

Q41.text: Research or teaching -- ideally both -- though I'm increasingly aware that wanting those things and having a realistic path to them are quite different propositions, given where I am in my career, what my field looks like, and the supervisory situation I've been navigating.

Q60.text: Only that surveys like this one -- assuming the data goes somewhere useful -- feel like one of the few moments where the experience is actually being witnessed rather than managed. I hope something comes of it, though I'll admit I'm not particularly optimistic that institutional incentives will shift in any meaningful way for the people still in the middle of it.

Q17.text: The intellectual work itself, when I can get to it -- the reading, the thinking, the occasional moment where an argument actually coheres -- is genuinely still something I value, even if it's increasingly hard to access beneath everything else the degree demands. I came in caring about ideas and I still do, which is maybe the one thing the experience hasn't managed to erode entirely.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The firm hierarchy certainly has advantages but in my experience, they are outweighed by the disadvantages—the infantilization of students, the lack of role models for communicating in this environment, the institutional comfort with lack of mentorship and guidance on careers, the overconfidence in using research techniques for the first time without support, the expectation that students should suffer and what that entails. All of this is compounded for an older student who was mid-career.

Q26.text: Genuinely brilliant in its ideals and genuinely dysfunctional in its execution — which I know sounds like a cop-out but I think it's the most honest framing I can offer. The system was designed, or at least evolved, around a model of disciplinary depth that doesn't really accommodate people whose work sits at the intersections, and there's this enormous gap between how institutions market themselves (collaborative! interdisciplinary! innovative!) and the actual structures of hiring, funding, and departmental politics that reward the same conventional outputs they've always rewarded. I came in believing the rhetoric. I don't entirely regret that -- it meant I pushed for something genuinely interesting -- but I've had to grieve some of what that idealism cost me in terms of time, support, and redirected research. the intellectual rewards are real. The institutional support, tbh, a lot less so.

Q16.text: The job market anxiety is something I haven't fully named yet, and honestly it sits underneath almost everything else — not just the generic "will I get a job" fear, but the more specific, grinding worry that because my work is genuinely interdisciplinary, I'm going to fall through the cracks of every hiring committee that needs to slot me into a recognizable box. I've watched colleagues with tidier, more conventional projects get traction in ways that feel unavailable to me, and I can't always tell how much of that is real versus catastrophizing. And then there's the networking piece, which I find kind of mortifying to admit concerns me as much as it does — I know the field runs on relationships and visibility and conference presence, and I feel like I came in late to understanding that, like someone handed me the rulebook halfway through the game. The dissertation itself has also quietly shifted in how I experience it; it started as the thing I was most excited about and has become, somewhere along the way, more of an obstacle to clear than a contribution I'm proud of making -- and that transition happened so gradually I barely noticed it until it was the dominant feeling. I don't think that's irreversible, but it concerns me that I let it happen.

Q55.text: That the informal political infrastructure of a department — who actually holds influence, what the real priorities are beneath the stated ones, which faculty genuinely support interdisciplinary work versus which ones merely tolerate it as a branding exercise — matters as much as, probably more than, the formal structures you evaluate before you enroll. I came in assessing the institution on its stated values and published research, which is what you're supposed to do, and I completely underestimated how much the day-to-day reality of being here would be shaped by dynamics that are entirely opaque until you're already inside them. I didn't know the right questions to ask, honestly, and I'm not sure I would have known even if someone had told me they existed. If I had known how to probe those things before I committed — or even that probing them was necessary — I might have made the same choice, but I'd have made it with clearer eyes and probably would have negotiated differently for the kind of structural support my work actually needed from the start.

Q41.text: Academic research, genuinely — I want the thing where you get to keep asking questions and have enough autonomy to pursue them without constantly justifying their disciplinary home to a committee that doesn't quite know what to do with you. Ideally something that combines serious research with public-facing work or science communication, because I care about the work reaching people outside the academy and I think I'd find a purely internal-facing career kind of suffocating. the honest version of that is a tenure-track position at an institution that actually means it when they say they value interdisciplinary work, which I'm aware is a narrow target. I'm also trying to stay open to research roles outside traditional universities — think tanks, policy-adjacent research centers, maybe well-funded nonprofits — not because I've given up on the academic path but because I've gotten more realistic about the fact that the job market is going to require flexibility, and I'd rather have a genuine second option than a fallback I secretly resent. What I'm most resistant to, tbh, is ending up somewhere that asks me to sand down the edges of my work to fit a narrower institutional identity. That feels like the real loss I'm trying to avoid.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research gets taken seriously at an institutional level and doesn't end up as another piece of evidence that gets cited in a report and then filed somewhere. The experience of doing a PhD — particularly one that doesn't fit cleanly into a single disciplinary home — is genuinely hard to capture in a survey format, and I'm aware that my answers probably skew toward the frustrations in ways that don't fully represent the intellectual rewards, which are real and which I don't want to lose sight of entirely. I think I came into this survey more willing to name things than I expected to be, which maybe says something about where I am right now. I'd be curious what the broader patterns look like across respondents, whether the institutional-support gap I've experienced is idiosyncratic or whether it's structural and consistent -- I suspect the latter, but it would be useful to know. Thanks for doing this.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, even in its constrained form — the fact that I get to spend my days genuinely thinking about something I find important, and that there's still a version of my work week that involves reading something unexpected and having it rearrange how I understand the problem I'm trying to solve. That hasn't gone away, even when everything around it has gotten harder. I also genuinely value the people — not the departmental politics, but the lateral relationships with other grad students, the conversations that happen at the edges of seminars, the occasional collaborator who actually gets what you're trying to do and engages with it on its own terms rather than through the lens of how it maps onto their own project. and there's something about being in an environment where the default assumption is that ideas matter, even when the institution undercuts that assumption in practice, that I don't want to take for granted. I'm aware I'm describing something I partly have to reconstruct from what it used to feel like, rather than what it feels like right now on a given Tuesday, but I think the underlying thing is still real. The work itself — not the dissertation as obstacle, but the actual questions underneath it — is still the reason I'd do this again, probably.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system is in a very special place to communicate our science but also to make sure the public is aware of inherent error (as a good thing) in our work. We need to work hard everyday to communicate our science effectively, or the academic system will become less and less trustworthy and then cease to have any impact. Further, I have noticed some people run their academic lives like a business, and it's hard to see their passion anymore, but these are some very successful people. I am worried to be successful in an academic system, I have to think of a job I get (and have worked my whole life for) as just a boring job to be successful or to work with passion everyday and not be successful.  Also, it is very clear to me some people just need to retire so we can move the field in a newer direction, more consistent with the technological developments that are rapidly occurring.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: You do not have to spend your entire career on your dissertation topic. MOST professionals in my field are successful at doing something entirely different than their dissertation. Just use the dissertation to demonstrate a flexible skill  (like statistical analysis) and finish it so you can get out of the program! Your dissertation is not your life's work, you must finish your dissertation before you can start your life's work.

Q41.label: What type of career are you interested in pursuing after your graduate degree?
Q41.text: I am interested in a traditional academic job with a strong research focus, then emphasis on teaching, and last an emphasis on service. I hope to not have a traditional lab but some lab space for a variety of research projects I can focus on and just collaborate with professionals in other departments who have the instrumentation I need. I hope to teach undergraduate students, graduate students, and create specialized "short courses" for more outreach professional training. I hope to focus my service in collaboration with local and regional law enforcement as a consultant for forensic cases.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: Yes! I entered my dissertation program focusing on research that bridges two different fields. In the beginning of my program, I was revered for that smart, forward-thinking twist to my research, and I was told repeatedly this is where the field needs to go (inter-disciplinary). Now, I am struggling to finish my dissertation, because every topic I suggest for my dissertation has been rejected by everyone in the department, since it is not traditionally within my field. And I never wanted this to happen to me, I had three options (I knew they were feasible, because another graduate student I worked with previously swiped one of those topics and graduated early and with praise) for dissertation topics as I entered the PhD program, because I knew I didn't want to be like other students I saw in my department that just appeared to take funding opportunities away from everyone while not progressing to graduation. Now I am that student. I even had a NSF DDIG proposal ready to submit (edits from the department lasted over 5 months, and it was ready!), and I was told they day of submission to our Office of Research, I should not submit, because no one in the department could supervise the project. I have since seen students AND professors independently come across those topics I have been steered away from, and those topics have been funded by major federal institutions, and the research yielded multiple publications in noteworthy journals. I am doing a dissertation project now that was not my idea, I have been handed the data, and it is my job just to analyze data that no one has used since the 1980's, just so I can graduate in 6 years. I know I sound like a complainer who is blaming everyone else for my problems. Maybe that is the case. I am saddened, because with those rejected topics have also gone my rose-colored glasses about the ability of research in academia to allow you to pursue passion projects. And even though my department publicly touts inter-disciplinary projects, there is no support for that in my department. It clearly took me too long for that to sink in.   Overall, I wish I had a mentor explain those hard facts to me; I wish I was smart enough to read between the lines to see inter-disciplinary research is not what my department produces; and I wish it did not have to be that way. Now, I just hope to graduate (later than I intended and with a project I am not sure contributes to modern society in any way), find an academic job (seemingly a one-in-a-million chance), and work to support inter-disciplinary research every day of my life.

Q26.text: The academic system here is structured and well-organized in many ways, which I do appreciate — there are clear milestones and the expectations are quite transparent. But honestly it can feel very closed off if you are international student, especially when many informal things just assume you speak German or already have local network. I'm still figuring out where I fit, and I think the system rewards those who already know how to play it

Q16.text: One thing that has been on my mind is the loneliness that comes with being far from home and not having a strong community here outside of the lab — and honestly the lab itself is not always the warmest place for socializing. I also worry sometimes that the skills I am building are quite specialized for academia and I'm not always sure how translatable they will be if I go into industry research, which is where I'm leaning. its something I think about more than I expected when I started.

Q55.text: I wish I had known how important it is to build connections outside your immediate lab from the very beginning — not just with other researchers but also with people in industry, because you don't realize until later how much those networks matter for where you actually wanna go. Q26.text: Opaque, honestly. There's so much nobody tells you -- about how competitive it actually is, how common it is to have experiments that just won't replicate. I thought I was the only one struggling. and the system kind of relies on that, I think -- on people not knowing how widespread it is.

Q16.text: The isolation, mainly. I didn't expect to feel this -- cut off. Other students seem to know things I don't, have results, have a plan. I don't know if that's real or just how it looks from outside. But it's hard not to internalize it. and honestly the thought that this might not lead anywhere -- career-wise -- that concerns me more than I want to admit.

Q55.text: That reproducibility is genuinely hard -- not just for me. I spent months thinking my experimental failures were a me problem, some gap in my skills or my thinking. and it took way too long to figure out that this is just... how it is a lot of the time. I wish someone had said that at the start.

Q41.text: Honestly, I'm not sure anymore. I came in thinking academia, but -- I don't know if I have the stomach for it. the uncertainty, the constant proving yourself. rn I'd take anything stable. Industry maybe, something in biomedical research or data, but I'm not picky. I just want to feel like the work leads somewhere.

Q60.text: Just -- thank you for asking, I guess. It's not something I say often but it actually helps to write this down. I don't talk about most of this with anyone in my department. there's this pressure to seem like you're managing, like struggle is something to hide. I hope whatever this data is used for, it goes somewhere. that someone reads it and thinks about how isolating the early PhD experience can be, especially when your results aren't coming. I'm not sure what I expected from a survey but I think I needed to say some of this out loud.

Q17.text: The questions themselves, I think. when an experiment fails for the fifth time I still find myself genuinely curious about why. That part -- the problem itself -- hasn't gone away. It's almost the only thing that hasn't. Everything else feels uncertain or exhausting, but the actual science still pulls me in. I don't know what to do with that, given everything else, but it's real.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Confusing -you don't know what is expected to be achieved by you and how well you are doing as a PhD student. Cruel - you are still judged by the number of papers and overworking is considered normal. People don't speak about a need for more free time and emotional support in fear they will be presumed weak and "discarded"

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: I expected to get more data, but I struggle to establish a working model which would give me data (biomed research). When I get data, I struggle with reproducibility of data. After 40 weeks of my PhD, I can show you maybe 10 graphs with my data, and only 1-2 of them can be statistically analysed. The rest of them - are pilot experiments which were discontinued for some reasons. I take this all close to my heart and feel I am a failure. I cannot compare myself to others - I hear stories about someone's success so frequently, and papers mostly show positive results - as if it's only me who is not gifted, knowledgeable or lucky enough to have some good results.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Be ready for anything. Embrace yourself for a possibility of having no positive results or published papers during your PhD.

Q26.text: The system rewards independence but doesn't invest equally in developing it. Q26.text: Honestly, it relies too much on luck -- the luck of having a good supervisor, project that actually cooperates, good timing. The science itself can be genuinely interesting, but the structure around it is pretty arbitrary. I've seen talented people struggle while others advance mostly because their experiments happened to work (or they had right connections). It's not very meritocratic, though I guess that's true for most competitive fields

Q16.text: Mental health is probably the biggest one. Wet-lab work has this particular demoralizing cycle -- weeks of preparation, experiment fails, repeat. I didn't anticipate how much low-grade anxiety would accumulate over time, and honestly the department is pretty quiet on that topic. Like it's just expected you'll manage somehow

Q55.text: That experiments failing is not a sign you're doing it wrong -- it's just the baseline. I spent the first year assuming I was the problem, taking every failed protocol personally. Turns out most of it is just biology being uncooperative, and your supervisor probably knows this but doesn't really say it upfront.

Q41.text: R&D, but more on the development side honestly -- I'm less drawn to pure academic research than I thought I'd be when I started. Something applied, ideally in industry, where experiments failing doesn't mean your funding disappears

Q60.text: Just that I hope the data from this is actually used to improve things, not just filed away. The PhD system has structural problems that individual supervisors or departments can't really fix on their own -- and a lot of people are quietly struggling in ways that don't show up in completion rates or publications. It would be good if someone was genuinely listening.

Q17.text: The intellectual side, when it's working -- there's something genuinely satisfying about being the person trying to figure out a problem no one has solved yet. And honestly the lab community, the people around you who understand what youre going through without needing it explained. Those parts are real, even when everything else is kind of a mess.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: PhD candidate is there to get opportunity, to get some freedom and ind of restrictions regarding budget - and hopefully also trust (even though not blind one). Such a person is then supposed to spend all the time, energy and invention on working towards publication. And then another one. At least two over 4 years, preferentially more and write a thesis by the way. Of course there is teaching, attendance of various courses and conferences, but lets call it "the fun after the hard work".

Q26.text: The US academic system, at least in my experience, is optimized for publication output rather than actual scientific progress. Professors are so burdened with grant writing and administrative work that they rarely have time to do real research themselves -- and students get very little mentorship as a result. it's kind of exhausting to watch, honestly. Compared to European models, the structure here feels transactional, more concerned with producing papers than producing scientists.

Q16.text: Honestly, the culture of exploitation is probably what concerns me most -- PhD students here are treated as cheap labor, expected to produce papers under conditions that would be unacceptable in industry. There's also very little recourse when advisors behave badly; the power imbalance is significant and institution rarely intervenes. it's kind of a structural problem, not an individual one

Q55.text: I wish I'd known how little structured mentorship actually exists here. The assumption going in was that an advisor would actively guide your research; in reality you're largely left on your own while they chase the next grant. looking at European PhD models beforehand would have at least calibrated my expectations, even if it probably wouldn't have changed my choice.

Q41.text: Research scientist in industry or government -- somewhere I can actually focus on doing science without teaching loads or endless committee work. Academia in the US at least doesn't seem like a place where that's really possible anymore.

Q60.text: I think the survey captures many of the right dimensions, but I'd add that the problems I've described aren't really about individual bad actors -- they're baked into the incentive structure of US academia. Funding mechanisms, publication metrics, and the oversupply of PhD students all combine to create conditions where exploitation is almost rational from an institutional standpoint. it's hard to fix that with better advisor training or complaint hotlines. I'd be curious whether the researchers here are looking at comparative data across systems, because I suspect the contrast with European programs would be illuminating. The issues aren't inherent to doing a PhD -- they're specific to how this country has structured it.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom is probably the one thing I'd point to -- when you do get time to actually think about a problem without grant deadlines or teaching prep crowding in, there's something genuinely valuable about that. and the research itself, when it's going well, is still interesting to me. it's just that those moments feel rarer than they should be, given that research is ostensibly the whole point of being here.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Academic system is very bureaucratic and professors spend too much time in teaching and administrative duties. Since I like doing research, this discouraged me to pursue a professorship. There is a lack of full-time/tenured researchers who can provide solid advice on research methods and practice. Professors mostly don't do research themselves, besides quickly reviewing papers or thesis. This was a huge disappointment for me, because I thought I would have a strong and deep mentorship on research practice in the university setting.  The publish-or \-perish mentality is also a waste of the little time professors and postdocs have. This mentality makes people push for half-backed research results  (or hyped buzzwords) in order to increase publication count (or be present at a conference). The result (in my field at least) is a flood of low quality papers that are 90% written by students. This low quality takes enormous time from reviewers and makes conferences boring as participants barely ask questions or discuss the topics. Instead, I feel that most people are mostly interested in seeing and being seen.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: I would have started my PhD in Germany and not in the US. PhD in US is too bureaucratic, too expensive, and PhD students waste almost two years taking useless lectures and preparing for nonsense exams. On top of that, PhD students are also shamelessly exploited as cheap teaching-assistance labor. Conversely, PhD in Europe is 100% focused on research, which leads to better quality papers and good work-life balance.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: When the survey questions uses the term "programme", it makes me assume that there should be a structure in the PhD graduate studies. I don't believe there is a structure, and I am not sure that it is possible or desirable to have one. Graduate school is not like the undergraduate school. While the undergrad school looks like a production of line of professionals, the graduate school experience is more of a one-to-one coaching. Therefore, "programme" could be a misleading term. I would not like to be in a strict standardized PhD program. I would rather have access to senior researchers who would actively advise me in various topics.   Now, we face the worst of the two worlds. US PhD programs are littered with artificial barriers, e.g., required lectures, required exams, required publications, required teaching assistant practice, etc). Meanwhile, these programs do not provide access to senior researchers (only to busy professors who don't practice research themselves because they are overloaded with lectures and administrative duties).   I think the survey should have also explored the topic of conferences and workshops. Conferences and workshops are sometimes advocated as events for students to get feedback. However, they are overcrowded, professors are busy meeting other professors, and people barely ask questions after the talks. The exception was the Doctoral Symposiums, where PhD Students get feedback on their research from a panel o professors. This was a great experience that I have in more than one conference.  The survey could have addressed bullying more deeply. As a graduate student, I saw the bullying of colleagues as the most serious issue in the university that I attended (UC Irvine). I would like to see more awareness and discussion about that. Is bullying cultural? Or is it a consequence of excessive competition in the US academic system?

Q26.text: The academic system, at least as I've experienced it, feels like it's designed for people who already belong -- who have the right connections, the right background, the right passport. International students are kinda expected to navigate everything on their own, and support structures that exist on paper rarely translate to actual help. There are good people, good research happening, but the structural inequalities are hard to ignore when you're on receiving end of them. honestly it's been more isolating than I expected, and that wears on you over time

Q16.text: Mental health has been a real concern -- anxiety and at times depression that I don't think I adequately prepared for, and accessing support through the university has felt more bureaucratic than helpful. and honestly my partner's employment situation has added a lot of stress that bleeds into everything else. it's hard to focus on research when there's so much uncertainty at home, and I don't think supervisors really factor that in

Q55.text: How little the institution actually does for you beyond the paperwork -- I came in assuming there'd be more community, more scaffolding, but it's largely on you to build that. And if you're not embedded in the right lab culture or social network from day one, you can find yourself pretty isolated without really understanding why. I wish someone had told me that upfront, honestly

Q41.text: International public sector work -- ideally something like FAO or another UN body, or government-level policy work with an international focus. I came into this degree with that direction in mind and I still want to pursue it, though I'll admit the PhD experience has made me think more carefully about what kind of institution I actually want to work in. not every organization that does good work has a healthy internal culture, and I've learned that matters to me

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually feeds into something -- policy changes, better support structures, something tangible. International PhD students carry a disproportionate amount of invisible weight, and I think institutions are often aware of it but comfortable looking away because we're less likely to escalate or cause disruption. Mental health support needs to be proactive, not something you have to fight to access when you're already at a low point. and honestly the isolation piece is underreported -- people assume if you're in a lab you have community, but that's not always the case at all. I'd like to think my experience is an outlier but I suspect it isn't

Q17.text: The research itself -- the freedom to work on something I genuinely care about and follow it wherever it leads. That's been sustaining, even on days when everything around it feels hard. And the few real connections I've made with other PhD students who get it, that matters more than I expected it to

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I believe there are several people in academy who try to do their best and be open and helpful to foreigners. However even in this country there is discrimination against non locals and many non locals receive lower or no pay in comparison to locals, and it is much harder for a foreigner to find a job too. We get selected less often for research stipend or funds and also we have a harder time adapting to what is locally expected because it is not clearly stated. There are cultural issues when doing research here and I would like that professors and academics in this country were more open to foreigners and to help us adapt to this country and I also think there is a need for sensitivity courses or something for all faculty members.

Q26.text: It's extremely focused on individual merit, even though it's very clear that many people's best performance is in groups. In academia there is an idea that "alternative careers are a great option if you cant make it in Academia". This is not what is happening. Academia is nowadays the "alternative career", so we should stop talking about alternative careers like failures , it's academia that creates this idea. Also, there is so little attention to well being and raising awareness towards mental health issues and harassment, that I don't feel like participating in a system like this. Plus, the academic system is extremely old school and just boring, when so many companies (and public organisations) have super interesting ways of working together and fostering creativity and inovation - which science is all about- that this old school system is just not attractive anymore for me. Q16.text: The thing that concerned me most early on was experimental failure — I went through a stretch where almost nothing worked and I genuinely questioned whether I had the ability to carry on. That's mostly resolved now, but the worry about transitioning into industry or policy-adjacent roles hasn't fully gone away. I sometimes wonder if skills I've built translate clearly to those environments, or if I'll need to rebuild my professional identity from scratch.

Q55.text: That failure is a normal and almost universal part of experimental research, not a signal that you're in the wrong field. I spent so much energy in my first year interpreting negative results as evidence of personal inadequacy, when really they were just... the process. knowing that earlier would have saved me a lot of unnecessary anxiety and probably sped up my learning too.

Q41.text: Translational research, most likely in industry or a government-linked research body where the work has a clearer path to real-world application. I'm drawn to roles that sit at the interface of science and policy or product development -- something with a leadership dimension eventually. Honestly I'm still figuring out what that looks like in practice, but the direction feels right.

Q60.text: Just that I hope research like this actually reaches the people making decisions about how PhD programs are structured, especially in contexts where students don't have the safety nets that well-resourced institutions provide. The experience of doing a PhD is shaped so much by factors outside the science itself -- access, mentorship quality, whether failure is normalized or treated as shameful -- and I think surveys like this are one of the few ways those structural realities get documented. So thank you for doing it. I tried to be as honest as I could.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly — there's something genuinely energizing about spending your days on a problem that no one has solved yet, even when the day-to-day is frustrating. I also find a lot of meaning in the collaborative side of it, talking through ideas with labmates and realizing that good science is rarely solitary. and I think being embedded in a research community, even an imperfect one, has shaped how I think in ways I couldn't have anticipated when I started.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Currently, the system where I do research is pretty good. The program is 5 years long, which gives us enough time to match with a lab and develop the project proposal. The department have a very organised and well-maintained core facility system, which makes daily lab work much more efficient. The lab space and consumables are adequate. The funding for my project and student stipend is sufficient for my personal need. However, I would have liked more teaching assistantship opportunities to develop my skills.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Failures and not knowing are a part of the learning process. I wish I wouldn't have been too dejected by this such things in the beginning and been braver in discussing my failed experiments with my supervisor, instead of trying to make things work on my own. It would have saved me months of going nowhere and doubting myself.

Q41.label: What type of career are you interested in pursuing after your graduate degree?
Q41.text: I would like to be involved in research after my graduate degree, preferably somewhere in an industry or government lab where I can do translational research. Another factor to consider would be a place that offers growth in terms of position, and where I'll be able to transition to decision making and administrative posts.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: I honestly hope that through this survey, there is more awareness in general about the problems and needs in graduate programs, especially in developing countries where a majority of the student force comes from or belongs too. This awareness needs to exist through all hierarchies in academia as well as among policy-makers in the governments. Another personal comment would be my wish to have grants for application processes to graduate programs at internationally well-known universities for students from low income countries, as the cost of going through multiple applications (including appearing for competitive exams to be eligible for such programs) is relatively higher for such students as compared to their counterparts in developed countries.

Q26.text: The academic system is, in my experience, pretty competitive and sometimes feels like it rewards perseverence more than actual talent or good ideas. there are genuine opportunities for collaboration and intellectual growth (which I do value), but the structures around funding and career progression can be quite frustrating -- it feels like you have to prove yourself repeatedly without much real security. I still think a postdoc path leading to a permanent position is achiveable, but its honestly not as straightforward as I expected when I started.

Q16.text: Mental health is something that I dont think gets talked about enough in academia -- the pressure to always be productive and publishing, combined with the uncertainity of whether your research area will even be viable long-term, can be pretty exhausting. I've had periods where I questioned whether I was cut out for this, which I think is probably common but feels very isolating when you're in the middle of it. The lack of stable funding in our group also adds a layer of anxiety that makes it hard to fully focus on the actual researc (which is what I came here to do in the first place).

Q55.text: How precarious the funding situation actually is -- I think I came in with this assumption that if your research was good enough the support would follow, but that's not really how it works. Understanding earlier that you need to be proactive about grants, networking, and positioning yourself for funding opportunities (rather than just focusing on the science) would have saved me a lot of anxiety and probably made me a more strategic researcher from the start. its not something supervisors always spell out clearly, and honestly I had to figure it out mostly through watching others struggle with the same thing.

Q41.text: Ideally I'd like to move into a postdoc position first -- there are a few research groups I've been looking at where my work might be a good fit -- and then eventually work toward a permanent academic position. I'm realistic that its a long road and the competetion is pretty intense, but I do think that's where I want to be. The alternative paths outside academia are there as a fallback I guess, but research and teaching in a university setting is still what I'm aiming for.

Q60.text: The main thing I'd add is just that the experience has been a real mix -- there are moments where the research itself feels genuinely exciting and meaningful, and then there are stretches where the structural stuff (funding gaps, career uncertainty, the general precariousness of it all) makes it hard to stay enthiuiastic. I hope surveys like this actually feed into some kind of change, because I think a lot of PhD students are navigating these pressures pretty much on their own. Thanks for running it.

Q17.text: Honestly the intellectual freedom is probably what I value most -- when the research is going well, there's something genuinely satisfying about working on problems that nobody has solved yet and feeling like you're actually contributing something. I also enjoy the collaborative side more than I expected, the conversations with other researchers (even outside my immediate group) have been some of the more stimulating parts of the whole experiance. Its not always like that, but when it is, that's what keeps me going.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system where i am pursuing my PhD at present is pretty good. Though, there is a stiff competetion to reach at the researcher level and then to opt for a permanent position along with a little bit burden to proove yourself as a self sufficient competitor in that enviroment. But overall being a PhD student, i found a number of collaborative opportunities inter and intra department which are very useful to carry out multi disciplinary research activities to establish a nice career ahead. Diplomacy in research is common everywhere and so is here but neglecting this part and accepting the positive one comes out to be very fruitful in term of facilities and faculities. Funding system is not so good as compared to other academic universities and research institutes which sometimes create an obstacle to carry out the researc with full zeal and enthiuiasm.

Q26.text: The academic system, as I've experienced it, rewards endurance over merit — you're expected to produce research with inadequate resources, navigate an opaque job market, and absorb career risks that faculty rarely acknowledge openly. There's genuine intellectual value here, but structural support is thin and the path forward is honestly pretty unclear.

Q16.text: The difficulty of seeking honest career guidance from within the department is something that honestly concerns me quite a bit. Faculty have a vested interest in perpetuating academic pipelines, so acknowledging that the job market is effectively broken carries social risk — you dont want to be seen as someone without conviction or commitment. The stigma around non-academic careers is real; I've watched colleagues be subtly discouraged from industry paths, as if that represents some kind of failure. it leaves you navigating these decisions largely alone, which is its own added burden.

Q55.text: That the academic job market is as constrained as it is — I came in genuinely believing that good work and perseverance would translate into viable career options, and it took a while to realize that structural scarcity, not individual merit, is the dominant factor. Knowing that earlier would have reshaped some decisions I made about where to invest my energy.

Q41.text: Ideally an academic or research position, but I'm increasingly skeptical that's realistic given the market. Q60.text: Just that the structural problems I've described aren't individual failures — they're systemic, and I think that distinction matters. The resource scarcity, the career opacity, the gatekeeping around what counts as a legitimate path after the PhD: these aren't edge cases, they're the norm for a lot of people in this position. I'd hope that whoever reads this takes it seriously rather than treating it as one frustrated respondent venting. The experience has been intellectually rewarding in genuine ways, but the institutional scaffolding around it is pretty broken.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Before beginning my PhD, I held a temporary academic position for two years in an institution that had a strong emphasis on group working dynamics, meeting facilitation, people management, and so on. I became used to working in a really well-structured, easy collaborative environment. Since starting my PhD research, which is extremely collaborative, I have found that collaborating with academics is very different. Most other PhD students and many faculty have not received, or likely even considered seeking, specific training on collaborative skills, which has seriously slowed down our progress. Collaboration is critical to modern scientific research, and it would be incredibly helpful if training in effective collaboration was more common. Q26.text: The academic system is fundamentally broken in ways it refuses to acknowledge -- it sells a mythology of intellectual meritocracy while systematically underpaying, overworking, and abandoning the people who actually do the work. My advisor left mid-program and the institution's response was essentially a shrug. that told me everything I needed to know about how dispensable researchers actually are

Q16.text: Financial anxiety has been a constant, low-grade hum throughout -- I'm in my final semester and I'm still doing the mental math on whether I can cover rent while finishing the thesis. The stipend stopped being livable years ago and the institution's answer to that is essentially "have you tried a scholarship you're already ineligible for." And honestly the isolation is something I wasn't prepared for. people outside academia don't understand how total it becomes, especially when your supervisor leaves and you lose the one relationship that was supposed to hold the whole thing together. I've watched friends build actual lives -- savings, stability, time off that doesn't feel like stolen time -- while I've been here trying to justify a pursuit that feels increasingly hollow the closer I get to the end of it.

Q55.text: That the institution has no loyalty to you, none, and that the sooner you stop extending it any in return the better off you'll be. I spent years operating as though good work and good faith would be reciprocated and they weren't -- not by my advisor, not by the department, not by the system. If I'd known to treat it transactionally from day one, I might have protected myself better.

Q41.text: Something outside academia, full stop. I've been watching people leave for industry for years and the only thing I regret is not doing it sooner -- I want work that pays a real wage, has actual boundaries between work and the rest of your life, and doesn't ask you to be grateful for conditions that would be unacceptable anywhere else. Tech or research-adjacent industry roles, probably. Something where the work is still intellectually honest but the institution isn't a monastery that expects you to take a vow of poverty.

Q60.text: Just that I hope someone actually reads these responses and doesn't file them into a drawer somewhere. The conversations I've had with other PhD students -- and there have been a lot of them -- all sound like variations on the same story, which suggests the problems aren't individual failures but structural ones. I'm nearly done and I feel more relieved than proud, which is probably the most damning thing I can say about the whole experience.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual work itself -- when it's going well, there's still something that feels like genuine discovery, like you're the first person to have thought something through in exactly this way. That part I can't pretend I don't value. But it's become increasingly hard to separate the enjoyment from everything it costs, and rn I'm not sure the ratio works in anyone's favor.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: This system is designed to break people slowly, so they don't realize what's happening until we can't sleep through the night and we feel guilt for watching tv on the weekends just to have a small break. The professors at my school expect everyone to be as dedicated as they are, but they have healthy salaries and good health insurance with families who can help them. Most of the grad students here are living in unhealthy situations. I am currently living in a house with termites and roaches 10 miles away from campus because it's all I can afford. My advisor quit her job as a professor and left me with no funding for my final semester of grad school, plus she has been a poor advisor overall because she is consistently underprepared, late, or distracted. I do not feel like a priority to her. Moreover, as an early career researcher herself, she doesn't have much experience or knowledge of opportunities even within academia, much less outside of it. I have been neglected for YEARS now, and no one can do anything about it because this kind of over-committed workload is considered "normal." Everyone is subjected to it, and it's expected of pre-tenured faculty. If this is all I have to look forward to, why would I want to stay in academia? I'm seriously rethinking my life goals. I don't want the rest of my life to be scrounging for money and working 60 hours a week with no chance of a break. The PhD has made me hate academia and question myself on every level, especially when it comes to the value of a PhD. I feel like I wasted my time earning one just to be thrown into a post-doc hell where the pay isn't much better and I'm still ignored. I want to do work that matters and has an impact. I don't think academia has that anymore, at least not from my perspective.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's kind of a paradox, I think -- personally I've been lucky (good supervisor, decent funding, a project I actually care about), but that doesn't change the fact that the system itself runs on people who are underpaid and overworked and, I guess, kept going mostly by their own love for the work. the precarity is real, and I don't think individual good fortune is a structural fix for that.

Q16.text: I think the thing that's crept up more than I expected is the anxiety about what comes after -- not just abstract job-market worry, but a kind of low-level, ongoing uncertainty about whether this path leads somewhere stable. And the work-life boundary has gotten blurrier than I anticipated, honestly. not in a crisis way, but in that quiet "is this sustainable long-term" way that I don't really have an answer for yet.

Q55.text: That boundaries don't set themselves. I kind of assumed that because I was passionate about the work, the balance would sort itself out naturally -- it didn't, and I wish someone had told me that explicitly rather than letting me figure it out two years in.

Q41.text: Ideally something that combines research and teaching -- I find both genuinely rewarding and I don't really want to give up either. Science communication is also something I'm increasingly drawn to, kind of as a way to stay connected to the broader public relevance of the work. But honestly, the traditional academic path feels pretty precarious rn, so I'm trying to keep options open without knowing exactly what that looks like in practice. I guess the honest answer is: something in or adjacent to academia, but I'm not sure I can afford to be too specific about it yet.

Q60.text: Just wanted to say that I think surveys like this are actually useful -- it's easy to feel like these experiences are just personal, so having them collected and studied feels kind of validating in a weird way. I guess I hope the data gets used to push for structural changes rather than just documenting the problem. and if there's ever a follow-up or results shared back with participants, I'd genuinely be curious to see them.

Q17.text: The intellectual autonomy, honestly -- the fact that, at least some days, I get to spend my time thinking deeply about something I actually chose and that feels genuinely worth doing. I also really value the conversations, with my supervisor, with other PhD students who are in the same kind of uncertain but engaged headspace. it's kind of a strange privilege, and I'm aware of that, but I don't want to understate how much it means to just... have work that feels like it matters.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: In my case, I can't complain as much given that apart from working long hours and some things not going as you expected, I have been lucky with my supervisors which have always looked for a way to pay me a salary and fund the projects for my PhD thesis. Regarding my University, I only have contact with it when I have to pay the enrollment fees each year and visit the evaluation board that follows what I have been doing during that year (a 5-minute meeting). I do not receive any specific training but they do offer some seminars that you can attend to if you have the time (which is never).   As I said, although my experience has been good, I do consider that overall doing a PhD is not well valued nor recognized as one of the highest degrees, if not the highest. We are well trained and educated people with careers, masters and lots of experience. Although we are overqualified, we are normally underpaid and work extra hours, not only at the lab/office but also at home. This includes weekends. Therefore, the "underpayment" increases while your life balance decreases. Moreover, none of this assures you a stable, successful or any kind of future which is very unsettling and makes you kind of want to be a PhD student the rest of your life. Not sure this is an academic system issue alone but it is clear that the number of PhD student keeps increasing, and the present and future working conditions do not increase with it.

Q26.text: The system rewards visibility and self-promotion more than genuine intellectual contribution, which I naively did not expect when I started. There is real richness here -- the ideas, the collegial exchange, the intellectual environment itself -- but the structural reality around permanent positions makes it difficult to sustain that initial idealism. alas, curiosity alone is not enough of a career strategy.

Q16.text: The financial dimension, honestly -- I underestimated how much of one's mental bandwidth goes to grant applications, contract renewals, and the general precarity of fixed-term positions. It creates a background anxiety that is difficult to separate from the work itself. And the competition among peers, which I think I naively assumed would be collegial, is often quite real and sometimes quietly corrosive to collaboration.

Q55.text: That following genuine curiosity into a research niche, without thinking strategically about where that niche sits in the job market, is a kind of career risk I simply didn't take seriously enough. I wish someone had told me that intellectual passion and professional viability are related but not the same thing -- and that the gap between them can be pretty wide.

Q41.text: A professorship, ideally -- though I'm increasingly realistic that this is more aspiration than likely outcome. My genuine interest is in an academic or research role where the intellectual work remains central. If that path closes, which statistically it probably will, something in government research or science policy is where I imagine landing. Not my first choice, but not without its own value I suppose.

Q60.text: Only that I hope the findings from research like this are actually read by people with the power to change something -- though I am, alas, not optimistic on that front. The structural problems in academia are well documented at this point; the gap between diagnosis and institutional will to act is where things tend to stall. Still, I appreciate the opportunity to reflect on it. Sometimes just being asked the question feels like a small acknowledgment that the experience is real.

Q16.text: The biggest thing that doesn't come up enough is how easy it is to lose months — genuinely months — to bench work without ever checking whether you're actually progressing toward the degree. Milestones exist on paper but nobody really holds you to them, and by the time you notice you're behind, you're really behind. Q55.text: That milestones aren't suggestions. Treat them like hard deadlines from day one, because nobody else will enforce them for you — and the cost of finding that out the hard way is genuinely really high.

Q60.text: Something I'd add -- and this is maybe more of a structural critique -- is that PhD programs in the life sciences are genuinely not designed for the career paths most students actually end up taking. I dont think programs are malicious about it, just slow to update. Would be good to see more honest conversations about that at the institutional level.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It's no longer an academic system. It is an imitation profit making business.  It used to be that the financial aspects were the means to an academic end. Now, the academic part is the "product" used to generate income from us "clients".  At the University where I study, OVER two thirds of employees are bureaucrats/administrators, and fewer than one third are academic staff. (And we're one of the better ones!) Decisions, on all matters, including teaching & scholarship ones are now made exclusively by the bureaucracy. Students, Staff and Alumni are actively discouraged, or, more often, administratively excluded from any role in the decision-making process. It's no longer and academic institution.  It's a business.

Q26.text: The system gives you real skills if you can manage the financial side of it. Funding inequality is pretty visible -- some students have comfortable scholarships, others, like me, had to work outside the program just to cover basic living costs. Q16.text: The funding gap honestly — I mentioned it briefly but it was more serious than it might sound. There were months where I wasn't sure how to cover rent while keeping up with lab work. It affects your focus in ways that are hard to describe to people who haven't been through it.
