Q60.text: Mostly just that the financial side of PhD programs deserves more attention from institutions. I think a lot of students struggle quietly and don't know what support exists -- I was one of them. The research training itself has been worthwhile, and I don't regret the path, but the system could do better at making it sustainable from the start.

Q17.text: Honestly the lab work itself — getting to work with real biological samples and actually see results from your own experiments. It's the part where you feel like the skills are paying off.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It got a lot better at the end of my PhD, but most of the time I had very low scholarship (310 USD), so I had to find a job. At the moment the scholarships in Czech Republic are higher and most people get extra funding, so it is much easier to focus on PhD. The conditions for students are unequal anyway. When they stay at faculty, they have to teach, often without getting paid. At other research institutions PhD. students usually do not have to teach and they can focus on their projects. On the other hand the PhD. students, especially in life science, are usually well prepaired for future jobs as they have to accomplish so many tasks. They have to write articles, present the results, attend lectures, seminars and conferences, pass final exam, teach younger students and of course work hard in lab. So it is quite valuable experience that hopefully pays off.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least from where I'm standing, is deeply hierarchical and honestly not designed with student wellbeing in mind. Power sits with supervisors and there's very little accountability for how it's used (or misused). I do find the university environment itself somewhat grounding -- the spaces, the sense of being around other researchers -- but the relational dynamics have been exhausting. and the expectation that you just endure it quietly is something I didn't fully anticipate going in.

Q16.text: Mental health is a big one, honestly -- I went through a period of depression that I didn't really see coming, and accessing support through the university was more complicated than it should have been. The fieldwork setbacks have also been a real concern; the drought affected my data collection significantly and that has consequences for my timeline I'm still trying to work out. And then there's the career question, which keeps me up at night. I'm not sure academia is where I want to end up, but the alternatives -- government work, conservation institutions -- feel uncertain too given the political climate here. It's a lot to hold all at once.

Q55.text: How much the supervisor relationship shapes everything -- not just your research, but your mental state, your timeline, your sense of whether you belong. I wish I'd known to ask harder questions about that before I committed. The project sounded right, the topic felt meaningful, but I didn't think carefully enough about who I'd be depending on and what it actually feels like when that relationship goes wrong. you can't separate the work from the person overseeing it, and I learned that too late.

Q41.text: Government or conservation sector work, ideally -- something applied, with real-world impact rather than staying in academia. I'm kinda drawn to environmental policy or protected areas management, but honestly I'm cautious about how stable those paths are given the political situation here. Academia feels less and less like somewhere I want to be, so I'm trying to think through alternatives, but it's not straightforward.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually leads to something -- it's easy to feel like surveys disappear into a void and nothing changes. The issues around supervisor power and student mental health are real and persistent, and I think the system protects itself more than it protects students. I dont have a neat conclusion, just that finishing this degree has come to feel like something I'm enduring rather than something I'm proud to be doing. and I hope whoever reads this takes that seriously.

Q17.text: The environment itself, honestly -- being on campus, around other researchers, having access to the library and the kind of focused atmosphere that's hard to find elsewhere. And the fieldwork, when it actually works, is something I genuinely love. Being out in the field, observing plant communities, that part still feels meaningful even when everything around it is difficult. I think the intellectual freedom is also something I'd miss if I left -- the ability to follow a question properly, not just tick boxes for someone else's agenda. It's just that those things have become harder to access because of everything else going on. the good parts are still there, they're just buried under a lot of weight rn.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I find the academic system flawed and the concept of the positions outdated. In my mind, you should not be catagorized on each degree or position you complete, but evaluated by seniority and experience like on the job market. After basic training, it would make more sense that people start working in research and can go from a junior scientist to a senior scientist depending on your abilities, not "suffer through" a phd and then"settle for" a postdoc and hopefully be able to publish enough papers to become a docent etc. The rule of publication is strange, comparing people who hold up their own projects for years alone and get a 1st author paper after years of work and publish in a nice journal, compared to a person who contributed to a research performed by 10 people. I don't think universities should have a rule of publication in a PhD. A person who gets a big dataset can get loads of results and publish easily while a person doing basic science has to work for years in calibrating and optimizing to get readable results.

Q26.text: Depends a lot on where you are, honestly. In Slovakia it's very hard -- limited resources, lot of administrative work that eats into actual research time, and feeling that you're always doing more with less. In UK and Switzerland I saw how different it can be when proper funding and infrastructure is there. The gap between Eastern and Western European academia is real and I think it holds back lot of talented people

Q16.text: Financial situation is honestly big concern -- PhD stipend in Slovakia is barely enough to live on, and when you see colleagues from Western Europe with proper salaries it's kind of demoralizing. Also the uncertainty about what comes after, whether staying in academia even makes sense given all the systemic issues I see.

Q55.text: That you have to be very proactive about seeking international opportunities early -- waiting for your institution to provide them is waste of time, especially in systems with limited resources. I wish I had applied for exchange programs and collaborations much sooner.

Q41.text: Independent research in industry or maybe my own venture -- academia in the traditional sense feels too constrained by the same systemic issues I've been dealing with. I want to work on problems that matter without constant fight for resources

Q60.text: The whole experience has been kind of eye-opening, and not always in good way. I came into PhD with lot of idealism about science and research, and the reality -- especially on the resource and bureaucracy side -- has been pretty sobering. But I dont regret it. The international experience showed me what's possible, and I think I'm more resilient and clear-eyed about where I want to go because of it. I just hope systems in countries like Slovakia improve, because there's real talent being wasted rn due to structural problems that have nothing to do with quality of research or researchers.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- working on problems that genuinely interest me and having space to think creatively. Even with all the systemic frustrations, that part is still real.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I would say, I was not really happy in Slovakian academic system. It is true I had  freedom in terms of proposing projects to my supervisor and pursuing them. However, we were short of money and we were forced to either prepare commercial chemicals or to supplement the work of technician. Third of my day-routine was doing stuff unrelated to my research. For this reason, I had to spend 12+ hours at work, to provide data and deal with my research. It was frustrating to witness how many collegues with no research ambitions/burnouts were stacked at academic posts. In terms of my international experience (UK, Switzerland), I did not observe such a thin. However I was not there for a long time.

Q26.text: The academic system rewards people who already know how to navigate it, and as a first-gen student I spent a lot of my early years just catching up on informal knowledge my peers seemed to absorb automatically. Intellectually it's been genuinely fulfilling — that part I wouldn't trade — but the structural reality is harder to sit with: the path to a faculty position runs almost entirely through postdocs, and postdoc salaries dont account for the fact that some of us have real financial obligations that can't be deferred for another five years. I think the system was designed with a particular kind of life in mind and it doesn't adapt well to people who fall outside that assumption.

Q16.text: Early on, the work-life balance issue was genuinely bad — I didn't have anyone in my family who could tell me that burning yourself out in year one wasn't actually a badge of honor, so I just did it, and it cost me more than I'd like to admit. I've gotten better at protecting my time, and honestly that's made me more productive, not less. But I do worry sometimes about the caretaker responsibilities I carry outside the PhD — it's not something I see acknowledged much in conversations about researcher wellbeing, and it can feel pretty isolating to be managing that alongside the work.

Q55.text: That rest is not the opposite of productivity — it took me an embarrassingly long time to figure that out, partly because I had no one around to model it. If I'd understood earlier that protecting my time and energy was actually a research strategy, not a concession, I think the first two years would have looked pretty different.

Q41.text: A faculty position, ideally — that's where my interests genuinely point. But I'm pretty clear-eyed about the fact that the standard route there runs through a postdoc, and I'm not in a position to do that rn given my caretaker responsibilities. So I'm holding that goal loosely while also trying to figure out if there are paths into research or teaching that don't require another five years of low pay.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research leads somewhere concrete — honestly, its easy to get cynical about whether surveys like this produce real change. The first-gen experience in particular feels like it gets oversimplified in policy conversations; the disorientation of navigating academia without anyone to ask isn't just a confidence issue, it's structural, and I'd love to see programs designed with that in mind

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly — being paid (modestly) to follow a question wherever it leads is something I don't take for granted, especially knowing it wasn't a given that I'd end up here. There's also a community aspect that surprised me; I assumed academia would feel more isolating than it has, and the relationships I've built with other grad students have been a real anchor, particularly on the harder days.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: overall, I have had a favorable (albeit stressful) PhD experience. I have realized that there is great benefit for those who have relative (e.g. parents) that also have their PhD, particularly in terms of networking for future opportunities.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: I wish I had built a better social support system (outside of my PhD program) from the beginning. In undergraduate training, you are largely on a semester-schedule. Any large projects have final due dates/completion dates. In PhD training, there is rarely a sense of "I've accomplished everything I need to", as there is always an experiment to plan, a paper to edit, or a new grant opportunity to pursue. At the beginning of my program, I put off self care/social networking opportunities in lieu of "I just need to finish _____, first". It is imperative to not put off taking breaks, lest burn out is inevitable. I have been much more productive in the last two years of my program since I started taking time for self-care/extra-curricular activities.

Q26.text: Structurally dysfunctional, though not without merit. The incentive system pushes quantity over quality — researchers are rewarded for output volume rather than rigor, and supervision of the supervisors is basically nonexistent. Funding is distributed in ways that entrench existing hierarchies rather than enabling genuinely good work. I still find the intellectual side meaningful, but institutional scaffolding around it is pretty broken.

Q16.text: The career pipeline concerns me honestly — more PhDs are produced than positions actually exist, and the system doesn't really acknowledge this. People are trained as though academia is a viable destination for all of them, when statistics suggest otherwise. The lack of support for, for instance, alternative career paths outside the academy is pretty glaring. and the social isolation compounds everything; I suspect that too is structural rather than personal failing.

Q55.text: That the career pipeline is far narrower than anyone admits at entry. I would have made different choices -- or at least more realistic ones -- had I understood from the start that academic positions are essentially a lottery for most PhD students. The system recruits people as if this is a reasonable destination for all of them, and it isn't, tbh.

Q41.text: Honestly, I'm not sure anymore. I came in assuming academia, but given everything I've said about the career pipeline, that feels like a naive position to hold. I'm looking at research-adjacent roles outside the university — policy, think tanks, maybe industry research -- but I haven't resolved it. The uncertainty is itself a product of not being given realistic information earlier.

Q60.text: Only that the publish-or-perish dynamic deserves more attention than it usually gets in these surveys. The pressure to produce output quickly -- often at the expense of doing the work properly -- is I think the single biggest driver of a lot of what I've described. Poor supervision, corner-cutting, the career anxiety -- a lot of it flows from that structural incentive. I don't think individual supervisors or students are primarily at fault. the system selects for speed over rigor and then everyone downstream adapts accordingly.

Q17.text: The intellectual autonomy, honestly — being able to work on problems that actually matter and dig into them properly. That part hasn't changed for me despite everything else. though it gets harder to protect that space when publication pressure is constant.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: To me, it seems that the academic system is often failing. The system of publishing is quite unfair; "catchy results" have more chance to get published. In addition, the reviewers should be experts in the field, but often, they are PhD students, because the research professors do not have time. In addition to publishing, acquiring funding seems to rely quite a lot on the prestige of the research institution and on having won funding before.  The academic system should give more importance to quality instead of focusing so much on quantity.  Last, regarding the PhD experience, there should be more supervision of the supervisors. Researchers often work independently a lot, and for some of them, when they become supervisors, they have difficulties to work together.

Q26.text: Structurally broken in ways that have nothing to do with the quality of the research happening inside it. The incentive architecture rewards prestige accumulation over actual knowledge production, and grad students absorb most of the cost. Q16.text: The opportunity cost, honestly. Every year I spend navigating committee politics and satisfying arbitrary milestone requirements is a year I'm not doing the kind of on-the-ground environmental work I actually care about. Academia moves slow by design -- and the climate doesn't have that kind of time.

Q55.text: That the damn dissertation is largely a credentialing exercise, not a contribution to anything urgent. Q41.text: Science communication and environmental advocacy, definitely not a tenure-track position. I want to do work that actually reaches people outside the academy -- policy, NGOs, maybe independent journalism. The skills transfer; the credential just opens certain doors.

Q60.text: The one thing I'd add is that surveys like this matter more than most researchers treat them — if the data actually informs how institutions support grad students, great, but too often it disappears into a report that administrators acknowledge and ignore. I hope that's not the case here. And honestly, the systemic stuff I flagged -- incentive structures, the credential treadmill -- those aren't fixable at the department level, so I don't want to overload the expectations of what a survey can do. But asking is better than not asking.

Q17.text: Genuinely, the intellectual autonomy -- being able to spend real time on a problem I actually chose. I don't want to oversell it, but those parts are real.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: My program is interdisciplinary and eclectic, so there's less intra-program competition than average (I've seen, heard, and read enough about other programs' experiences, at the same university and others). Nonetheless I know that the academic system overall remains needlessly hyper-competitive and deeply harmful to work-life balance for most. It encourages far too high a level of self-doubt and self-criticism among PhD candidates (witness the high-level of impostor syndrome, despite high competence), as well as social isolation, anxiety, burnout, and other constituents of abysmal mental health.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: The single most important -- i.e. necessary -- thing about getting a PhD is that you HAVE to want to write the damn dissertation. If you don't want to produce a book-length, professional piece of writing on X, Y, or whatever your topic is, then you'll never finish it. It doesn't matter how badly you may want the accreditation, the skill-development, the additional career prospects, whatever. You HAVE to want to write a dissertation. If you're not sure about this, don't do a PhD.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Filled with pettiness on the part of PIs. In my experience, if another lab is working on similar research, the comments range from saying the other lab is not as good as theirs or downright accusations that the other lab somehow stole their idea. There is paranoia that any sharing of information will directly result in proprietary theft, unwillingness to listen to other ideas or change their mind when evidence suggests they are wrong. This all trickles down to students, who are either forbidden from presenting research, asking for information from other labs that are experts in a certain area in order to get useful information or sent on a wild goose chase without any means of actually getting somewhere. The pettiness is also prevalent within the same department of the university, where a certain PI dislikes another and this gets placed on the students, creating an awkward and unfriendly atmosphere that is entirely counter-productive.

Q16.text: Honestly, the career preparation piece — specifically for non-faculty paths — has been a real gap. I've had to construct my own picture of what a staff scientist career actually looks like through informal networks, because the formal infrastructure just doesn't support that curiosity. It's not malicious neglect, but it is a structural problem.

Q55.text: That the career paths beyond the tenure track are genuinely viable and worth mapping out early. I absorbed, somewhat uncritically at first, an implicit hierarchy that treated staff scientist roles as consolation prizes — when they're actually well-suited to people who want to stay close to the bench and, honestly, have a life outside of it. Knowing that sooner would have saved me a fair amount of misplaced anxiety.

Q41.text: Research staff or senior scientist in an academic or research-institute setting — staying close to the bench without the administrative overhead of running a lab. I'm pretty deliberate about that choice at this point, not settling for it.

Q60.text: Just that I hope surveys like this one actually feed into something actionable — whether that's better career advising infrastructure, or at least a more honest institutional acknowledgment that "success" in a PhD program shouldn't be synonymous with landing a faculty position. The bench scientists, the research staff, the people who choose depth over administration -- we're not failed academics. and it would help to hear that earlier.

Q17.text: The actual bench work -- the experiments, the troubleshooting, the occasional moment when something works and you understand why. I also genuinely value being embedded in a community of people who care deeply about ideas, even when the structural stuff is frustrating. Q26.text: The academic system is interesting, but honestly it's deeply unequal depending on where you are. In Portugal the funding situation is a constant bottleneck -- you spend more energy chasing grants than actually doing research. And there's a cultural bias toward theoretical work that makes applied contributions feel undervalued, even when the real-world impact is clear

Q16.text: The supervision dynamic has been fine, but the isolation is real. When your work doesn't fit the dominant theoretical mold, you kind of stop expecting colleagues to engage with it seriously. And honestly the salary situation in Portuguese academia is pretty discouraging -- I'm doing cutting-edge applied AI work and the compensation reflects none of that. It makes the idea of building something of my own, or moving to industry, feel less like a plan B and more like the obvious path

Q55.text: That the research environment matters as much as the research itself. I came in focused on the technical problems -- medical imaging, model performance, all of that -- and didnt really account for how much the institutional context would shape what's actually possible. If I'd known how constrained the funding landscape in Portugal really was, I probably would have sought international collaborations or external grants from day one instead of assuming the system would support good applied work on its own merits

Q41.text: Building my own product in the AI/health space is the main goal, tbh. But I'm also seriously looking at top-tier tech companies -- the kind doing real applied research, not just shipping features. Academia in Portugal doesn't make much sense for me at this point.

Q60.text: It's been a useful exercise to reflect on all of this. I think the main thing I'd add is that the structural problems I mentioned -- funding, the applied vs theoretical divide -- these aren't unique to my experience, a lot of my peers feel the same way and just dont talk about it openly. Hopefully research like this actually reaches people who can influence policy, because the talent drain from countries like Portugal to industry or abroad is real and its accelerating

Q17.text: The freedom to define my own research direction is honestly what keeps me going. working on medical imaging problems that have real clinical relevance -- that's the part that feels meaningful. The autonomy is something I dont think I'd find easily in regular job.

For instance, the amount of money spent by my Government on research is much less per Researcher than in other European countries. This is a complete bottleneck over what is happening to R&D in Portugal.

Q26.text: El sistema académico tiene muchas fallas estructurales que afectan profundamente a los doctorandos, sobre todo a quienes venimos de otros países. Funding policies are honestly inadequate for researchers with families -- it's not just a personal struggle, it's a systemic failure. Hay mucho que mejorar si se quiere atraer y retener talento diverso

Q16.text: La xenofobia dentro del propio departamento ha sido algo que no esperaba encontrar. Compañeros y mi supervisor han tenido comportamientos que solo puedo calificar como acoso, y eso ha afectado mi salud mental más de lo que pensaba. It's been honestly the hardest part -- harder even than the funding situation. No se habla suficientemente de esto en los programas de doctorado, y creo que debería.

Q55.text: Que las políticas de apoyo a familias en los programas doctorales son casi inexistentes -- y que eso iba a condicionar tantas decisiones, desde dónde vivir hasta si mi marido podía acompañarme o no. I wish someone had been upfront about this from the start, because I could have planned differently. Nadie te dice estas cosas en la entrevista.

Q41.text: Investigación académica, y también me interesa la administración pública relacionada con políticas educativas. Honestly both feel like paths where I can make something change -- not just publish and move on. But I know how difficult the permanent academic post is to get, especially as a foreigner.

Q60.text: Agradezco que haya espacio para comentarios adicionales. Lo que más quiero destacar es que las universidades deben crear políticas concretas de apoyo a las familias de los doctorandos -- no documentos bonitos, sino medidas reales que permitan a las parejas trabajar legalmente y a los investigadores no tener que elegir entre su carrera y su familia. And honestly, the issue of harassment and xenophobia in departments needs to be addressed more seriously, not left to individuals to manage alone. Espero que estas respuestas sean útiles.

Q17.text: Lo que más disfruto es la investigación en sí -- la sensación de que estás contribuyendo algo que importa, aunque el camino sea muy duro. Honestly, on the good days, that sense of purpose is what keeps me going. También valoro la libertad intelectual, aunque a veces el precio que se paga por ella es demasiado alto.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Hay deficiencia en cuanto a orientación profesional, académica y porqué no, personal. He sentido xenofobia, por lo que los tutores son muy subjetivos a la hora de trabajar. Sentí acoso laboral de parte de mis compañeros y de uno de mis tutores. Todo esto afecta el rendimiento académico y por tanto el sistema académico.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: Falta de dinero suficiente para vivir con mi familia (esposo e hijo) en otro país, ya que en este país no le permiten trabajar.  Esto ha sido un gran problema durante todo mi doctorado, pues me ha llevado a alejarme de ellos.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The system is slightly broken and congested. There are good, smart, hardworking people who deserve more recognition than they get. There is an unhealthy focus on pushing papers out into the world which causes scientists to push rushed or bad science out the door. There is also a major lack of focus on education at major universities. These large R1 universities hire faculty based on their ability to pull funding and push out papers (which is important) but their job is to also teach students at that university and mentor graduate students. These qualities are not being promoted and therefore I have seen many horrible educators and mentors that hold high positions in academia. There are good people, but too often they are not recognized because they chose to focus on being better mentors or teachers than push that one extra paper out the door.

Q26.text: Honestly, the academic system has real strengths -- the freedom to explore ideas without immediate commercial pressure is something I genuinely value -- but it can be pretty insular, especially in how it defines success. Publishing metrics and citation counts feel disconnected from real-world impact, which has been a recurring tension for me given my industry sponsorship. The mental health side is something I think about a lot too; the isolation that comes with a PhD isn't really talked about enough, even in programs that are otherwise well-resourced

Q16.text: One thing that's been sitting in the background is the question of research independence -- my industry sponsor has been broadly supportive, but there are moments where I wonder whether my research agenda is genuinely mine or whether it's been quietly shaped by commercial interests I haven't fully acknowledged. That kind of ambiguity wasn't something I expected going in, and honestly I'm not sure supervision structure is really equipped to help you work through it

Q55.text: How much the emotional labour compounds over time. I knew it would be intellectually demanding, but I genuinely underestimated the cumulative weight of sustained ambiguity -- not knowing if your work is good enough, or relevant enough, or even really yours in the way you imagined. Building deliberate support structures early, rather than assuming you'd work it out as you went, would have made real difference.

Q41.text: Industry R&D primarily, though I'd want a role that blends technical work with project management and client-facing responsibilities -- I think a purely lab-based position would feel too removed from the kind of applied impact I actually care about. The PhD has clarified that for me more than I expected it to, tbh.

Q60.text: Just that I think surveys like this are genuinely useful, and I hope the findings feed into something concrete rather than sitting in a report somewhere. The mental health dimension in particular feels underaddressed in most PhD programs I'm aware of -- and industry-sponsored candidates are a bit of a gap case, because we don't fit neatly into the standard pastoral support structures. It'd be good to see that acknowledged more explicitly in how universities design their policies.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom is probably the thing I'd miss most if I left -- being paid to go genuinely deep on a problem, without a quarterly deadline forcing a premature answer, is something I don't take for granted. There's also something I wasn't expecting, which is the quality of the people you meet; other PhD students are, by and large, thoughtful and curious in ways that make even the frustrating days kind of worthwhile.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I would say the academic system is aimed at publishing relevant research work which will make an impact. My PhD is sponsored by an industrial company and so they put many of my results in an industrial context with less of an emphasis in publishing in high impact journals, we aim for lower impact journals where the expert industrialists in my field are likely to interact with the paper (this is true of conference attendance as well). However, my case seems to be the minority amongst my peers. I would say the general practice is to publish work at the highest impact journal and attend the biggest conferences to ensure your work gets read by the largest proportion of the academic community, with less emphasis on who should read the paper in your field to the research to the next level.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least as I have experienced it here, is one that operates on a kind of invisible hierarchy -- not always formal, but felt in very concrete ways, especially if you are someone who does not fit the default image of a researcher in your department. There is much that is genuinely stimulating about it, the intellectual freedom, the possibility of contributing something original, and I dont want to dismiss that entirely. But there is also, I think, a structural tendency to reward those who already belong, in ways that are difficult to name precisely but very easy to feel -- whether in how feedback is distributed, whose ideas are taken seriously during meetings, or simply in who gets invited to certain conversations at all. My own experience has been shaped considerably by working under a supervisor who, while well-meaning I suppose, does not have deep expertise in my specific research area, which means I have had to find other routes to mentorship and guidance on my own initiative, something that not every PhD student should be expected to do. And honestly the system kind of assumes a particular support structure that not everyone actually has access to, and it does not always account for the additional labour that some of us carry that others simply... don't.

Q16.text: One thing I have not fully articulated, though it sits with me more than I expected it would, is the question of belonging -- or rather, the particular absence of it in certain contexts. There have been moments, more than a few, where I felt that my presence was not quite... expected, I suppose, in certain rooms or conversations, and I say this carefully because these are not experience that are easy to document or prove in any formal sense, but they are real and cumulative in their effect. A comment here, an assumption there, the way certain colleagues look past you when distributing credit or deciding whose input actually merits a response -- these things accumulate, and honestly I find myself spending a considerable amount of energy managing the emotional residue of those interactions in a way that I don't think my European colleagues have to do with the same regularity. It is not the academic work itself that concerns me most, I feel capable enough in that domain, but the social and institutional texture around it, the sense that one must work considerably harder simply to be considered present before one can even begin to do the actual research. That is a fatigue I did not fully anticipate when I started, and it is one that is difficult to raise with anyone in the department without feeling that you are making yourself into a problem.

Q55.text: That finding mentorship outside your immediate supervisory relationship is not a failure or a workaround -- it is actually just how things work in practice, especially when your supervisor's expertise does not fully map onto your research area, which I did not understand when I began. I think I spent a long time, maybe the first year and a half, assuming that the formal structure would provide what I needed and that to go looking elsewhere was somehow to admit a deficiency either in myself or in the arrangement, when in fact the people who seemed to navigate the system most smoothly were almost always those who had built lateral networks quietly and without making much fuss about it. I wish someone had told me that plainly at the start rather than letting me discover it through the slow accumulation of unmet expectations.

Q41.text: Postdoctoral research, most likely, though I say this with some qualification -- I am genuinely interested in continuing in an academic trajectory, contributing to an area where I feel I can make a real difference, and the postdoc route seems the most natural next step given where my work is heading. I am cautiously optimistic about it, though I will admit that some of what I have experienced during this PhD has made me think more carefully about which environments I would want to enter into, and whether a given institution or research group has the kind of culture where someone like me would actually be supported rather than just... tolerated. So the interest is real, but I think I am more deliberate now about what I am looking for than I might have been when I started.

Q60.text: Only that I hope the responses I have given are actually useful in some concrete way, because I have found myself being more candid here than I might have anticipated, and I suppose that reflects how rarely there is a space to say these things plainly, without the concern that saying them will somehow reflect badly on you in your immediate environment. The experience of doing a PhD is genuinely complex, and I think surveys like this one risk flattening that complexity if the analysis stays at the level of aggregate satisfaction scores -- what I would hope is that the particular texture of certain experiences, the ones that are harder to quantify, receives some attention. For those of us who are navigating not just the intellectual demands but also the social dynamics of departments where we are, for various reasons, not quite the expected type of researcher, the challenges are not always the ones that appear most prominently in the standard literature on PhD wellbeing. I dont want to overstate my difficulties, I am still here, still working, and I believe in what I am doing -- but I think the system would benefit from a more honest reckoning with who it is actually built for, and I say that not out of bitterness but out of a genuine hope that the people who come after me might have a slightly easier time of it than I have had.

Q17.text: The intellectual substance of it, honestly -- the feeling, when it is going well, of being genuinely at the edge of what is known and contributing something that did not exist before. That is not something I take for granted, and even on the more difficult days it remains a real source of meaning. I also find, perhaps unexpectedly, that some of the most sustaining part of the experience has come from collaborations that crossed departmental or even disciplinary lines -- working with people outside my immediate group who brought different frameworks and who engaged with my ideas in a way that felt, I don't know, genuinely collegial in a manner that was not always present closer to home. There is something particular about those exchanges that has kept me going through periods where the local environment felt less than welcoming. And I suppose there is also the freedom, the basic freedom to pursue a question because it is worth pursuing, which I think I undervalued before I had it and which I would find very difficult to give up. It is imperfect, and the freedom is not evenly distributed in the way that it is sometimes presented to be, but it is real, and I would not want to be entirely ungrateful for it.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: I am a non-European student pursuing a PhD in a university in the Netherlands. Q26.text: Honestly, it's a system that does some things really well -- the training in scientific thinking, the depth you develop in your specific area -- but kind of fails at preparing people for the actual careers they'll end up in. Most of us aren't gonna land R1 positions, and the whole structure is built like we are. The ethical dimensions of the work also rarely get addressed in any systematic way, which bothers me more and more the further along I get. Not a bad system, but a weirdly narrow one.

Q16.text: The thing that's crept up on me more than I expected is how isolating the process can be -- not just socially, but intellectually. By year three you're so specialized that conversations outside your subfield feel weirdly performative, like you're constantly translating yourself. And the mental health piece is real; I wasn't prepared for how much of the PhD is just sitting with uncertainty for long stretches. I also worry that the specific research skills I'm building don't map neatly onto the roles I actually want -- a teaching-focused position doesn't really need someone who can run a western blot at 2am, and its a strange thing to be developing expertise in something you're not sure you'll use.

Q55.text: That the PhD is fundamentally a research training program, not a career preparation program -- and that those two things are much more distinct than anyone told me. I came in thinking the skills would transfer more naturally, that doing good science would more or less set me up for whatever came next, and it took me probably two years to realize that the institution is not actually tracking whether you end up employed or satisfied, just whether you produce a thesis. Knowing that earlier would have pushed me to be much more intentional about building the other stuff alongside the research -- the teaching experience, the mentorship relationships outside my lab, the clarity about what I actually wanted -- instead of treating all of that as secondary to the "real" work.

Q41.text: Teaching-focused academic positions, ideally at a mid-sized university where the balance tilts toward instruction rather than a relentless research output model. I'm genuinely interested in the kind of place where you can know your students and build a coherent course sequence over time -- not somewhere that treats teaching as the thing you do when you're not getting grants. I'd still want to do some research, honestly, but on a scale that's actually sustainable and that I can meaningfully involve undergrads in, rather than the pressure-cooker pace I see modeled around me rn.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of data actually gets used to push for structural changes rather than sitting in a report somewhere -- I've filled out enough surveys at this point to be a little cynical about whether any of it lands. But I do think the questions here touched on things that don't get surfaced enough: the gap between what PhD training does and what it's implicitly promising, the way ethical dimensions of research get treated as optional add-ons rather than core curriculum. If I'm being honest, I found the process of answering kind of clarifying for myself, which I wasn't expecting. I guess I'd just say: the students who are most aware of these gaps are probably the ones most likely to leave academia, and that's a loss worth taking seriously.

Q17.text: The depth of engagement, honestly -- the way you can spend months with a single problem and develop a relationship with it that nobody else in the world has quite the same view of. There's something genuinely rare about that, and I don't think I'd get it anywhere else. I also really enjoy the teaching and mentoring I've gotten to do on the side; its the part that most clearly maps onto what I actually want to be doing, and there's a particular satisfaction in watching someone understand something for the first time that I wasn't fully prepared for.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It's a weird apprenticeship that's not actually an apprenticeship for most people. That is to say, you really only learn how to be a better scientist (designing project, learning techniques, etc.), but few labs/progams seem to provide training in mentorship, grantsmanship, money allocation, etc. Blacksmiths learn blacksmithing, but also which items sell best, and I feel like that should be more of the formal training. It's obviously harder for an academic mentor to provide that for students interested in non-academic careers, but perhaps the programs could do better. I'm fortunate that my PI talks about that stuff and tries to involve us, but I don't hear that mentioned by most students.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The ethics of things I'm working on that may be used how I wouldn't choose (e.g. a better understanding of the genes that cause neurodevelopmental disease being used to alter future humans) makes me less excited to pursue things I'd otherwise be really interested in studying;  Finding a project that will work well in a teaching-intensive environment (my planned academic track) when my PhD is at a major research center

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: How to choose a lab to rotate in. I had a plan going in, but many of the PIs I was interested in rotating with decided not to take students my year so I didn't have as much forethought in the labs I ended up rotating in. I'm fortunate I ended up with a great mentor and an awesome lab group, but I would have preferred to have thought more about how my PhD research could translate into research I could do at a university that doesn't have as much funding down the like (i.e. picking a non-human, non-mouse model system).

Q26.text: Structurally inefficient but intellectually rich, I think — the system rewards persistence in ways that can feel pretty arbitrary, and the quality of one's experience varies greatly depending on factors (advisor communication, departmental culture) that remain largely opaque to incoming students.

Q16.text: The opacity of advisor-student expectations, honestly — there's very little structural scaffolding for what "good" advising looks like, so when communication breaks down you have almost no institutional recourse, and that ambiguity can be pretty corrosive over time.

Q55.text: How variable the advisor relationship is as a determinant of your overall experience — I came in thinking the work itself would be the main factor, and it turns out the communication dynamic with your supervisor shapes almost everything else, in ways that are genuinely hard to anticipate or correct for once you're in it.

Q41.text: Teaching-focused academic position, ideally — I'm drawn to institutions where teaching is genuinely valued rather than treated as a service obligation attached to research output.

Q60.text: The advisor-student dynamic really does deserve more systemic attention than it gets — idk if it's a solvable problem given how decentralized graduate education is, but the current arrangement puts an enormous amount of load on a single relationship that students have almost no power to renegotiate once they're in it. and the fact that this is so widely understood among PhD students and so rarely addressed institutionally is kind of telling in itself.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom to pursue genuinely difficult questions without having to justify every step to a market logic -- that's rare, and I'm aware enough of the broader system to appreciate it even when other parts of the experience are frustrating.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: PhD students match with an advisor based on the topic the student wants to study and then the advisor helps and/or assigns them a project in that space. The student works to achieve the goals of that project (as set by the advisor or the student, based on the student-advisor relationship and the advisor's confidence in the student's intellectual abilities). Pace of work is motivated by the advisor and their need to get research grants based on current experimental findings and thus the pressure to collect data can be variable. While the student is researching, they are given teaching responsibilities to make up for the time in which the professor/advisor cannot be in the classroom in a student facing role, but the value of the PhD student's teaching hours for their own academic career pursuits varies greatly. All of this is occurring in a space not at all visible to the majority of the undergraduate university population so segregation of the academic levels is high.

Q26.text: The academic system, as I've experienced it, is structurally inequitable -- evaluation criteria privilege certain research styles and established networks over genuine intellectual contribution, and supervision quality varies so dramatically that two students in the same program can have entirely different outcomes. There's something valuable about the university environment itself, the intellectual community and access to ideas, but the institutional scaffolding around it is, honestly, poorly designed and rarely prioritized by those with the power to change it.

Q16.text: Mental health is the obvious one -- the anxiety around adequacy and failure is something I didn't fully anticipate, and the institution offers very little structured support for it. There's also a concern about whether the skills I'm developing are actually legible outside academia, given how specialized training is. I guess I worry that the investment -- in time, in cost, in opportunity -- may not translate into the kind of career flexibility I'm hoping for

Q55.text: That supervision quality is not guaranteed by institutional affiliation -- I assumed enrolling in a reputable program meant access to adequate mentorship, but the reality is you can spend years in a poorly matched or actively unsupportive supervisor relationship with very limited recourse. Honestly, if I'd known that, I would have treated supervisor selection as the most critical decision of the entire PhD, not an administrative formality.

Q41.text: Policy-adjacent roles are where I'm most drawn -- applied research or advisory positions where analytical work has some tangible impact, whether that's in government, a research institute, or an industry context that takes evidence seriously. I'm genuinely open to non-academic paths; tbh the idea of a traditional academic career feels less certain than it once did, partly because of what I've seen of how institutions actually function.

Q60.text: The main thing I'd add is that surveys like this feel valuable but only if the findings actually reach decision-makers -- I've participated in similar exercises before and there's a real question about whether the data translates into institutional change or just academic output. Structurally, I think PhD programs need mandatory, transparent supervision agreements with genuine accountability mechanisms; right now the power asymmetry is so significant that students have very little formal recourse when things go wrong. And honestly, the equity dimension is underexamined -- not everyone comes in with the same social capital to navigate informal systems, and that gap compounds over time in ways that are pretty significant.

Q17.text: The intellectual environment, honestly -- being surrounded by people who care deeply about ideas, having access to resources and conversations that don't exist outside academia. There's something I find genuinely sustaining about that, even on the harder days. The autonomy to pursue questions I actually find meaningful is also real, even if the structural conditions around it are less ideal than I'd hoped.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Unstructured and stochastic with some labs/research groups that provide a lot of guidance for PhD students and others that leave PhD students completely alone and unsupervised. Inequality of resources and support (intellectual and financial), huge administrative load and impossible bureaucracy that strongly affect the quality of research. Doing a good PhD seems to be a lottery determined more on many external factors than on the students’ skills. Wrong evaluation criteria that do not take into account the student’s personal abilities and history but are just “performance-based” (publications number vs actual learning). A PhD seems more like a job for already advanced researchers to show what they can produce rather than a scientific training period for students to consolidate knowledge and learn new skills.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: Failing the PhD because of lack of help/support in the lab and of thesis supervision. Dropping the PhD for not being able to carry on the thesis alone. Feeling inadequate for the standards of the lab/the scientific community. Feeling judged by peers.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: That research experience counts more than good GPA during bachelor/masters and it’s better to wait before applying for a PhD program (maybe doing a RA position) in order to know if you get along with the supervisor and the lab environment. This, because once you have started a PhD there is no way back (if you drop it’s unlikely to find another PhD and it’s very hard to change supervisor if you are directly funded by him). Also to write a *clear project plan for the whole PhD* and have it validated by senior supervisors instead of starting designing experiments during our PhD.

Q26.text: Teaching-driven and severely underfunded, at least where I am. Research is possible but not really supported -- you have to find your own way without much infrastructure or community. Honestly, it demands a lot more from individual than it probably should.

Q16.text: Balancing full-time work with the PhD has been harder than I expected -- I underestimated how much it would cost in terms of time and honestly social life. The financial compensation from the university alone wouldnt be enough to live on, so the industry job is necessary, but it leaves very little room for deep research engagement. I guess that's the structural trap: the system doesn't fund you enough to be a full-time researcher, so you find yourself doing both and neither properly.

Q55.text: How demanding the time trade-off would actually be. Q26.text: In my country, the academic system is not based almost at all on research. The main concern of everybody is teaching many students, on a level, which is not too high, just enough to teach the student to get a job in the industry. The funding or pay for research work is almost non-existent, people in the academic system earn their money from teaching, thus the priority for them is not research. However, in spite of this, there are many people at the universities doing research. But it is very low paid. For example, the PhD scholarship, which can come only from the government, is not enough for a normal life. It is around the minimal wage, slightly higher, but still not enough to live in a city full of universities.

Q26.text: The system is very hierarchical and I think it doesn't really serve the research itself. Junior people carry a lot -- teaching, admin, actual lab work -- but the credit and the pay flow mostly upward, and honestly that's been one of my bigger frustrations here. I still love the intellectual side of it, genuinely, the ideas and the problems are real. But the structural issues are hard to ignore, like it was built for a different era and nobody bother to update it.

Q16.text: The financial side of it, honestly. I knew it wouldn't be lucrative but the actual precarity -- short contracts, not knowing if there's funding beyond this year -- it gets in your head more than I expected. And I think it affects the work too, its hard to think long-term about your research when you're not sure you'll have a position to continue it in. That uncertainty is something I didn't fully anticipate before starting

Q55.text: Honestly, how much the whole experience depends on your supervisor and not just your own ability or the quality of the project. I came in thinking it was mostly about the research itself, and yes that matters, but the relationship -- whether your supervisor is actually present, whether they genuinely care about your development -- that shapes literally everything. I would have asked much harder questions at the interview stage.

Q41.text: Academic research, ideally running my own lab at some point. I know that sounds ambitious given everything I just said about the system, but I still want it -- I just want to do it differently, build a group where people are actually supported and the mentorship is real. That's the version of academia I'd like to contribute to. whether I get there is another question, and the funding reality makes it genuinely uncertain, but that's the goal.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually leads somewhere, like that someone reads these responses and thinks seriously about what early-career researchers are dealing with. It's not just individual bad luck or bad supervisors -- its structural, and I think the people who design these systems mostly don't see it from where we are. So. thank you for asking, genuinely, it's not nothing to be asked.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly. The fact that I get to spend my days actually thinking about a problem that matters, following it wherever it leads -- that part is still exciting even when everything else is frustrating. And the conversations with other researchers, when they happen, that feeling of being around people who genuinely care about ideas. I dont take that for granted

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I think we have a lot of Master Students, and PhD students are the people who teach and supervise them. So PhD student have to conciliate their project and master students' supervision. And since master student are always appearing and then leave, PhD student are always teaching the same thing again and again without taking profits of what they teach them. And some times as a PhD student, I feel a lack of inspiration of people that should me guide and give me inputs.  So I think it is like an inverted pyramid, where young people teach young people.

Once we have it, the PI's will want us to stay longer than we should, to get their money's worth. It's a fundamentally flawed system.

Q26.text: The academic system has some genuinely wonderful things about it -- the intellectual community, the freedom to chase ideas, colleagues who actually care about their work. But it's built on power structure that can be pretty brutal when it goes wrong, and honestly there's almost no accountability for it. The precarity of academic careers is real and I think people pretend it's more manageable than it is.

Q16.text: The family planning piece is something I dont think gets talked about enough. I'm at the age where that's a real consideration and the structure of academia -- the postdoc grind, the geographic uncertainty, the "you'll get a permanent job eventually maybe" -- makes it genuinely hard to plan a life around. And then if you say you're thinking about leaving for policy or something outside the lab, there's this subtle but real message that you've somehow failed or given up. It's exhausting to navigate that stigma on top of everything else.

Q55.text: That advisor relationships can make or break your entire experience, and you have almost no way to assess them from the outside before you commit. I wish I'd talked to more current and former students in the lab before I signed on -- not the ones the advisor introduces you to, but the ones who quietly left.

Q41.text: Science policy and science communication, honestly. I spent a long time feeling like that was somehow admitting defeat, but I've made peace with it -- I'm genuinely more interested in how research shapes public decisions than in running my own lab. the precarity of the academic track just isn't something I'm willing to build a life around, especially with everything else I'm weighing right now.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually leads somewhere useful. The issues I've described -- the advisor power dynamics, the career stigma for people who leave, the way academia makes family planning feel like a personal failure -- these aren't new complaints, and I've heard a lot of surveys and reports that document them without anything changing. So I guess I'm cautiously hopeful but a little skeptical. If someone is reading this and has the ability to actually move policy on any of it, I'd genuinely love to know what comes out of this data.

Q17.text: The intellectual community, genuinely. The conversations you have with other grad students -- at conferences, in the hallway, over bad coffee -- are unlike anything I've found elsewhere. People who are deeply curious and actually want to argue about ideas for fun. that part I'll miss, whatever comes next.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Tenure means that upward mobility in the field stalls at the PostDoc and tightens an already competitive field. I didn’t want to gamble on a post doc and then risk having to move again in 2-3 years for another and another.  I want to start planning for a family and pursuing a string of post docs was not conducive to what I want my family life to be like.  I didn’t see a way to continue to be successful in academia with a family

I think that’s even more important than the research fit unless you’re in incredibly independent person and can receive professional and personal mentoring from other sources.

Q26.text: Honestly, the academic system has a lot to offer intellectually — the depth of inquiry, the freedom to pursue questions that genuinely matter. But the structural side of it is pretty brutal. The pressure to publish, to meet supervisor expectations, to build career in a field where permanent positions are increasingly scarce... it takes a real toll on mental health, mine included. I think reform is possible, but it would require institutions to actually take that seriously rather than treating it as an individual problem.

Q16.text: The financial side is something I dont always talk about openly. Stipends barely cover living expenses, and watching peers go into industry earning two or three times as much... it's hard not to question whether the sacrifice is worth it, even when you believe in the work.

Q55.text: That the relationship with your supervisor shapes almost everything — not just your research, but your mental state, your confidence, your whole experience of the degree. I spent a long time thinking the anxiety I felt was my own failing, when really a lot of it came from that dynamic. Knowing that earlier might have helped me seek support sooner, or at least not internalize so much of it.

Q41.text: A career in academia, ideally. I know the odds aren't great and I'm not naive about the precarity, but research is genuinely what I want to do. I guess the honest answer is that I'm committed to trying, even if I might need to reassess that at some point.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually reaches people who can make decisions. It's easy to feel like surveys disappear into a void, but the issues here — the mental health pressures, the precarity, the way supervisory relationships can make or break someone's experience — these aren't fringe concerns. They're pretty widespread, and I think a lot of students suffer quietly because the system doesn't give them language or space to name it. So thank you for asking.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual side of it is what keeps me going. There's something genuinely rewarding about sitting with a problem that doesn't have an answer yet and slowly working toward one — I dont think I could give that up easily. And the people around me, colleagues who are equally obsessed with their work, that sense of being in a community of people who care deeply... it matters a lot, even when everything else feels hard.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I overall have a positive view of the academic system but I see that it has many problems that can make it loose quality. One main problem is the absence of positions after postdoc apart from PI positions. I see as a big problem how many good scientists could not want to become leaders of their own group and are forced to leave academy at some point for this reason. Another big problem is the high level of stress, especially for the need of having results of high impact, both for career or for getting founds. Academic research loses many good scientists also for this reason. I've met already several people who left because they couldn't cope with stress, and I'm afraid it could be the same for me one day.

Q26.text: The academic system is fundamentally extractive -- graduate students generate real intellectual and institutional value while being compensated at poverty wages with minimal job security. Having split time between a public R1 and an Ivy has made that disparity impossible to ignore; the difference in how institutions actually invest in their students is staggering, honestly. I still want academic career, but it's hard not to feel like the system isn't designed to make that sustainable for most people.

Q16.text: The two-body problem has been a constant undercurrent -- my partner is also finishing a PhD, and the prospect of two academic job searches overlapping in a field that's already brutal is something nobody in the department wants to engage with directly. My advisor, while genuinely enthusiastic, is early-career in ways that have had real professional consequences; I've had to seek out mentorship elsewhere and piece together kind of guidance that should realistically come from one person. it's seeded genuine doubt about whether my training will actually be competitive when it matters.

Q55.text: How much advisor selection actually determines your professional trajectory, not just your research direction. I spent a lot of time evaluating research fit when I was applying and almost no time thinking about whether my advisor had the professional capital and experience to actually advocate for me -- in the room at conferences, with hiring committees, with collaborators who matter. Enthusiasm and intellectual alignment aren't the same thing as mentorship capacity, and I learned that the hard way. I think if I'd asked different questions during visits, or honestly just talked to more advanced students in the lab, I would have gone in with clearer eyes about what I was signing up for.

Q41.text: Academic research, ideally a tenure-track position, though I'm increasingly uncertain whether that's realistic given the market and everything else. I'd probably consider research positions at elite institutions or well-funded labs if faculty lines aren't there, but industry research feels like a concession I'm not ready to make rn.

Q60.text: The thing I'd add is that surveys like this feel both necessary and insufficient -- it's good that someone's asking, but graduate student experience at underfunded public institutions is genuinely a structural problem that doesn't get fixed by data collection alone. I hope the responses here actually reach people with decision-making power, because the gap between how elite and public programs treat their students isn't closing on its own. And honestly, the two-body problem deserves its own dedicated study; it's one of the primary reasons people like me end up leaving academia despite wanting to stay.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom is genuinely irreplaceable -- there's something about being paid (poorly, but still) to spend your days thinking hard about questions that actually matter to you that I don't take for granted. My split appointment has given me access to collaborators and conversations I couldn't have gotten otherwise, and honestly those interactions are what keep me going on the days when the institutional frustrations feel heaviest. I still find the work itself exciting, which I think is the only reason high-strain environment like this stays tolerable at all.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The public university system in the US has become a mechanism for providing the university with slave labor in both the lab and classroom setting while providing minimal support to the student. As someone who does lab work at an Ivy League institution but spends the majority of my year at a Public R1 school, i feel that my creativity and independence are extremely stifled and degraded at my home institution compared to my peers at my research lab institution. Public universities have become a cost center for state governments but have decreased the quality of their services for those they are supposed to be serving. I grew up in an academic household and have been around R1 institutions my whole life, there has definitely been a shift in the focus of how graduate students are treated in the last 20 years.

Q26.text: The academic system has genuine strengths -- collaborative networks, intellectual freedom, the satisfaction of contributing to something real. But it's structurally distorted by publication metrics in ways that I think genuinely undermine the science itself. Good work gets sidelined if it doesn't yield high-impact outputs, and honest incremental progress rarely gets the recognition it deserves

Q16.text: The lack of consistent feedback has been harder to deal with than I expected. I came in assuming mentorship would be more structured, but a lot of it is pretty ad hoc -- you're left to gauge your own progress mostly through comparison with peers, which doesn't exactly help with self-doubt. I'm never quite sure if my work is actually good or just good enough to avoid comment

Q55.text: How much the publication culture would shape everything -- not just your output, but your sense of your own worth. If I'd understood earlier that "good work" and "publishable work" aren't always the same thing, I think I'd have been less thrown by the gap between what feels meaningful and what actually gets recognised.

Q41.text: Industry, specifically pharma or biotech -- I'd like to work in a setting where the science is evaluated by whether it actually works, not just whether it publishes well. I've also thought about scientific publishing itself as a way to influence how research gets communicated and valued.

Q60.text: The thing I'd add is that surveys like this one feel meaningful precisely because the structural problems aren't widely acknowledged -- at least not officially. Informally everyone knows that the metrics game warps incentives, that mentorship quality is a lottery, and that imposter syndrome is basically endemic. But there's a kind of institutional silence around it. So I appreciate the opportunity to put it on record, even if just as data.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual autonomy is what I value most -- being able to pursue a question because it genuinely matters, not because it fits someone else's agenda. And the people. Colleagues at this level tend to care deeply about what they're doing, and those conversations are often the best part of the week, tbh.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Too much emphasis on publications, particularly the over-valuing of journal impact factor. Because publication is the only metric that seems to matter to most professors, they are not incentivized to work very hard on their teaching or on their career mentoring of students. I found the quality of courses in my PhD program to be very sub-par, mostly because none of the professors care very much about teaching. This emphasis on publication also allows professors to ignore problems in their labs, as long as papers are still being churned out. I really like the collaboration aspect of academia, and this is only hurt by the emphasis on publication, because people worry about being scooped. I think if more academics took metrics other than journal impact factor and number of publications seriously, we would all be able to work better.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The constant feeling of not working hard enough. During a PhD, in contrast to undergraduate work, you have to go long periods of time without much feedback or validation (since there are not constant assignments for which you receive grades). Adjusting to "playing the long game" has been difficult.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Don't try to do too much at once. I know it can be frustrating when you feel like you aren't making fast enough progress, but if you try to do too much at once, you'll make mistakes. Think carefully about experiments and plan your time well.

Q26.text: The academic system is more contingent than it presents itself, honestly — 'successful' PhDs often reflect supervisor quality and experimental luck as much as any intrinsic ability or work ethic. There's something structurally uncomfortable about a training model that packages those external variables as personal achievement. that said, the depth of learning you can get (when circumstances align) is genuinely hard to replicate elsewhere

Q16.text: The lack of any real 'standardized' feedback on progress is something that bothers me more than I expected — you can work hard for months and have genuinely no sense of whether you're on track or not, because the benchmarks are so supervisor-dependent. And I think that opacity hits harder when you're already questioning whether your timeline is reasonable, or whether a slower period reflects something about you versus just the inherent unpredictability of biological systems. it's a concern I didn't anticipate going in

Q55.text: How much the quality of your supervisor relationship determines — not just shapes, but genuinely determines — your experience and timeline. I came in thinking the science was the main variable, and it is, but only downstream of whether your mentor actually has time for you, whether they give useful direction versus just 'feedback,' and whether they're incentivized to see you finish or to keep you producing. I wish I'd treated the supervisor selection as the single most consequential decision of the PhD, because tbh everything else is kind of noise by comparison.

Q41.text: Research leadership in industry — specifically aiming for a group leader or equivalent role in a biotech company where the science can actually move at a pace that isn't contingent on grant cycles.

Q60.text: It would be useful if whoever is reading these responses actually loops them back into how PhD programs are structured — this kind of survey tends to feel like data extraction that doesn't close the loop. I'm genuinely uncertain whether anything systemic changes as a result, which isn't a criticism of the survey itself so much as the broader culture around 'listening' to PhD students without fundamentally revisiting the incentive structures that create these problems. That said, I think the questions were well-chosen and got at things I haven't been asked to articulate before, which I appreciate.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, genuinely — being paid (however modestly) to go deep on a specific problem without someone pulling you toward something more commercially immediate is rare, and I'm aware enough of that to not take it for granted. And honestly the people: the other students especially, who are mostly thoughtful and kind of obsessively curious in ways that make the day-to-day environment pretty stimulating, whatever the structural frustrations.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: It concerns me now how much luck goes into how "successful" your PhD feels and how quickly you can earn your PhD, i.e. how much luck goes into whether or not you decided to do the "right experiments" at the right time to move your project forward (which you only realize afterwards, once you have the results of those experiments). I realize more now that PhD students studying different topics or even different projects within the same topic will complete their PhDs in very different lengths of time, and this concerns me. I wish there were a better way (it is difficult, I know) of "standardizing" the PhD experience so it doesn't take 4 years for some students and 8 years for other students.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: I wish I had known that the best mentor for me is not just one who is nice and acts supportive but one who actually helps you by giving you useful advice and who can help you distinguish properly between the important experiments and the not-so-important experiments.
