Q26.text: The academic system has genuine intellectual appeal, but in practice it depends very much on which lab and supervisor you end up with. I think the structural incentives are not always aligned to the development of early career researchers -- contributions, including authorship, tend to be distributed more by power dynamics than merit. Honestly I'm more cautious about it now than when I started.

Q16.text: The main thing that concerns me is the slow progress on my own project -- I spent considerable time contributing to work that wasnt really mine, and this has delayed my own research timeline. I'm also somewhat worried about mental load of navigating the lab dynamics on a daily basis. Honestly I dont always know how to raise concerns without damaging relations I still need in order to graduate

Q55.text: That the supervisor relationship matters far more than the research topic itself. I chose my lab mostly based on the project description, but the day-to-day reality is shaped almost entirely by who you are working with and what kind of lab culture they have built. If I had spent more time talking to current PhD students in the group before accepting, I think I would have had a more realistic picture of what to expect in terms of autonomy and how credit for work is attributed.

Q41.text: Ideally I would stay in research -- I still find the intellectual side genuinely rewarding -- but whether that means academia or industry research depends a lot on how the next year or two goes. If my current projects produce something I can actually put my name on, I would consider postdoc positions. But honestly, if things continue as they have been, I'm not sure I want to stay in an environment where your career progress depends so much on who likes you rather than what you produce.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research is useful for people considering a PhD -- I think there is a gap between how PhD programs are advertised and what the day-to-day reality can look like, especially in terms of how much depends on lab culture rather than the formal structures. I dont think my situation is unique, and its something that probably deserves more attention at the institutional level. Good luck with the study.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom is still something I value -- being able to read widely, follow ideas across disciplines, and work on problems that feel genuinely open. I also enjoy the conversations with other PhD students, tbh that peer community has been more sustaining than anything coming from above. I think if the structural side of things were better managed, the day-to-day intellectual life would be quite good. It's just hard sometimes to separate what I enjoy about the work from the frustrations around how the work is recognised and attributed.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: On my experience, it really depends on 1) the team (what includes the size of the team (i.e. big groups need to be well-structured so that a PhD will be correctly supervised), the financing (grants, materials, etc.) and the opportunities to collaborate with other researchers and attend to conferences) and on 2) the project (if not only the objectives but the experimental design is well planned since the beginning of the PhD, and the lab politics do not interfere with, the PhD student can be more independent since the beginning of his/her PhD).

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: My biggest concern it was indeed the lab politics, in the sense of not having a clear project to focus in and follow since the beginning of my PhD and having being rather helping to finish the unfinished work of a postdoc without receiving the recognition that should accompanied it (first authorship).

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: 1) Choose your lab for their ressources (economical and for publication) but most importantly for their teaching capacity. A PhD is the moment of maximum learning of a researcher, the moment in which you will really face a project, and this will always turn better if you have the constant guidance of someone that has been through it. Full freedom at this point can be counter-productive.  2) Lab politics are complicated. Before collaborating in any project, make sure your contribution will be recognised, what means, do not be afraid of openly discussing the position that you will get in an article.

Q41.text: At the beginning of my PhD I would have said academia. But right now, I have no idea and I am afraid my decision will depend on how the projects I have just started will go on (which I am conscious is not the best choice).

Q26.text: The academic system, at least in biomedical research, is under enormous pressure to produce -- and that pressure really does distort what gets studied and how. There's a tendency to chase publishable outcomes over genuinely interesting questions, and I think we loose a lot of creativity in that process. My PI is untenured, so I see the stakes up close, which is both motivating and kind of exhausting honestly. The gender dynamics are also something you can't ignore, especially in how certain kinds of work get valued or attributed

Q16.text: The isolation of being the first student in a new lab is something I didn't really anticipate -- there's no one ahead of you to normalize the experience or tell you what's reasonable to expect. And honestly the question of whether I'd even be good mentor someday weighs on me more than I expected it to.

Q55.text: That the relationship with your supervisor shapes almost everything -- the science, the timeline, the culture of your lab -- and you should ask very pointed questions about that before you commit, not after.

Q60.text: Just that I hope surveys like this actually feed into something -- it's easy to feel like these kinds of reflections disappear into a database somewhere and nothing changes. The systemic issues I mentioned, the publish-or-perish culture, the gender stuff, the precarity of early-career PIs, they're not individual problems and I dont think individual resilience is the right answer to them. I'm genuinely hopeful that the field can change but I think it requires people with institutional power to actually act on what they hear.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom to follow a genuinely interesting question, even when the system makes that hard. and honestly being at the edge of what's known in your field is still pretty exciting, even on the frustrating days.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system that we follow was set up with the right ethos. But in the execution we have all collectively faltered. It was one field of work which accommodated heterogeneity and diversity in all forms especially ideas and way of life but increasingly the system is trying to homogenize people making them loose their individuality. In older studies, journals reviewed and argued the science behind what the authors did, but now they review and make authors add more experiments which they want to see not necessarily needed for proving what the authors did. If big data is the current trend every research group is expected to have omics in their paper.  There is also this wave of applied research which as a standalone field is very good but inadvertently penetrates into basic research. All research cannot be applied immediately. Lots of drugs that are there in the market exist because their mechanism of action was a phenomenon some graduate student/post doc uncovered which could eventually get targeted. The original study may not even have proposed it. This also encourages researchers to portray hypothetical forced biomedical applications of their research findings and mislead people  when actually there may be none.  I also feel the system inherently assumes that people in academia don't have a life beyond work. They reinforce this assumption in their expectations from students and PIs. In fact its almost considered unusual if you are single and want to leave for home at decent hours after work. Family is the qualifier you need to enjoy time after work. This notion is largely in India. There are other inherent assumptions too like people doing science should look shabby and unkempt. This portrayal of scientists has become like a norm and if you don't fit into their mold you are not considered a serious scientist. People who are well dressed, especially women therefore have a hard time being taken seriously.

Academia should be more than just faculty positions.

Q26.text: The academic system is structurally well-designed in theory -- the mentorship model, the freedom to pursue questions that actually matter -- but in practice it depends almost entirely on individual supervisors who operate with minimal accountability. When that relationship works, it's genuinely wonderful. When it doesn't, there are almost no mechanisms to protect students, and the institution tends to protect its reputation over its people.

Q16.text: The mental health piece, honestly -- I've watched colleagues spiral in ways that felt entirely preventable, and the support systems, while improving, still feel reactive rather than structural. You shouldn't have to hit a crisis point before anyone intervenes. And the normalization of overwork as a badge of commitment is something the institution hasn't really grappled with yet.

Q55.text: How much the supervisor relationship determines everything -- not just your research outcomes but your mental health, your timeline, your sense of self. I came in focused on the science and treated the PI selection almost as an afterthought. I wish I'd known to treat it like the most consequential decision of the whole degree, and to ask former students directly, not faculty references, about what working with that person is actually like day to day.

Q41.text: Industry, specifically biotech -- I came into the PhD thinking academia was the path, but I've become pretty disillusioned with how the system treats people, and I'd rather be somewhere where the work culture is at least nominally more accountable.

Q60.text: The university's efforts around graduate mental health are genuinely appreciated -- I don't want this to read as purely critical. But the structural issues are real and they predate any individual PI or program. If anything, I hope this data gets used to push for actual accountability mechanisms, not just more wellness resources that ask students to cope better with conditions that shouldn't exist in the first place.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual environment -- being surrounded by people who genuinely care about ideas, who will argue about methodology over lunch because they actually find it interesting. That part is real and I'd miss it. The freedom to follow a question wherever it leads, when the conditions support that, is something industry probably won't replicate.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Improperly incentivized. The lack of vetting and/or mandatory training for PIs on both financial and interpersonal matters is just asking for catastrophe, but even when those catastrophes occur, they are ignored if enough grant money is being brought in. Emphasizing good stewardship, both of the students whose training and career prospects are entrusted to PIs and of the vast sums of public money awarded in grants, would reclaim the academy for what it should be at its core - education - and also give actual teeth to the efforts to improve graduate student mental health.

Watch out for troubling patterns and bounce them off your network early and often.

Q26.text: The intellectual environment is genuinely rewarding, but the structural incentives are pretty broken. Pay doesn't reflect the training and output expected of PhD students, tenure-track odds are grim enough that you'd be irrational not to account for them, and visibility within a lab often depends more on personality than quality of work. I still want an academic career, but I can't pretend the system is well-designed for the people inside it.

Q16.text: The financial strain is more acute when you have a family depending on your income. A stipend that might be manageable for a single person in their mid-twenties doesn't stretch the same way, and that pressure doesn't just sit in the background -- it shapes how you think about timelines, about whether to push through a difficult year or cut your losses.

Q55.text: That the informal dynamics of a lab — who your supervisor actually pays attention to, who gets the opportunities — matter as much as your research quality. I wish I'd been more deliberate about making myself visible early on, rather than assuming good work would speak for itself.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: My time as a PhD has been great so far. However, there are structural problems with the academic system in terms of both advancement and in most countries financial support. The number of positions in academia outside of a tenured faculty slot is limited and the path to get such a tenure track position unclear. Exacerbating this problem is the dismal salary paid to individuals who have done in many cases 10 years of formal training which in any other skilled profession would be unacceptable. While passion, creativity, and love of knowledge should drive a scientific career, this should not come at the expense of financial hardship, especially when one has a family.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's a bit of a mixed bag. There's genuine intellectual freedom and the teaching side I really enjoy, but the bureaucratic overhead -- the admin, the box-ticking, committees that seem to exist just to generate more committees -- is no where near proportionate to what it actually produces. I've grown a lot more than I expected through this process, developed real confidence in my own abilities, but the system itself could be so much more efficient if it just got out of its own way.

Q16.text: The job market, honestly. Q26.text: The academic system, based on what I've lived through so far, has become something closer to an industry than a vocation -- science has been hollowed out by a relentless pressure to produce papers rather than ideas, and the supervisory structure that's supposed to nurture early researchers is too often just a mechanism for extracting labor while protecting established reputations. Everyone knows this. Curiosity isnt rewarded, output is, and that distinction matters more than most people in comfortable positions are willing to acknowledge.

Q16.text: The mental health dimension is something nobody talks about honestly -- the isolation, the chronic uncertainty, the way you're expected to perform confidence and productivity while privately wondering if any of it means anything. And the financial precarity that underlies all of it, the way a stipend that doesn't keep pace with rent is treated as a privilege rather than an injustice. I came into this wanting to contribute to human knowledge and instead I spend a lot of energy just trying to survive the conditions that are supposed to make that contribution possible. its exhausting in a way that accumulates quietly.

Q55.text: That supervisor relationships are fundamentally power relationships, and no amount of shared intellectual interest changes that basic dynamic. I wish someone had told me that the person who shapes your entire career trajectory also has almost no accountability for how they treat you, and that the institutional systems supposedly in place to protect students are mostly there to protect the institution. I spent the first year genuinely believing the warmth was genuine and the mentorship would be mutual, and by the time I understood what I'd actually signed up for I was already too embedded to easily exit. knowing that going in wouldn't have made it perfect but it might have made me less naive about where the power actually sits.

Q41.text: Tenure-track academic position is still what I'm working toward, honestly -- the idea of having real autonomy over a research agenda, building something that lasts. Though I'm not naive about the odds anymore and I've thought a lot about editorial work, journal editing, as a fallback that at least keeps me adjacent to the ideas even if the system itself has made the professorship feel more like a lottery than a meritocracy.

Q60.text: Just that I hope someone actually reads these responses and doesn't aggregate them into a statistic that gets cited once in a policy document and then quietly shelved. The people designing these surveys often seem more interested in producing data than in understanding what the data is pointing at -- which is ironic, given that that's exactly the critique I'd make of the broader system we're all operating inside. There are real structural problems here that aren't going to be fixed by wellness workshops or better supervisor training modules, and I think researchers and institutions both know this but find incremental gestures easier than genuine accountability. I dont have a tidy solution to offer. But I do think the gap between what academia promises and what it actually delivers to most PhD students is wide enough now that pretending otherwise is its own kind of dishonesty, and surveys like this at least create a small space where that gap can be named.

Q17.text: The intellectual work itself, when I actually get to do it -- those moments when a question opens up into something genuinely unexpected and you realize you're thinking about a problem in a way nobody has quite framed it before. That still happens, and it still matters to me. Honestly it's the only thing that makes the rest of it bearable. The conversations too, with other students who are equally obsessed and equally frustrated, where you remember that the ideas were supposed to be the point all along. The system does a remarkable job of surrounding that core with everything designed to diminish it, but the core is still there, and I guess I still care about it more than I probably should given everything.

Q26.text: I came in with a high level of reverence to this system, but I believe academia is not like 80s or 90s anymore, It is getting worse because of unreasonable and unrealistic expectations set by authorities in journals and publishing houses and supervisors that are also embracing this idea and madly running behind this culture. It seems to be a cultural issue in academia lately where the thought process has deteriorated. There is a lot of productivity but no creativity. It is a very dangerous concept due to which Science is losing lot of able and bright minds

Q55.text: That I will not be acknowledged for who I am, my merits and demerits, strengths and weaknesses. Basically if my expectations were set appropriately, then I will know what I am signing up for and will not waste time thinking if such a pattern would repeat itself in future by other PIs as well and not have generalized fear and frustrations about the working environment being so negative and dreading. I wish I had known that science has been commoditized these days.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: A lot of freedom with not much oversight. Given the lack of hard and fast rules, it is easy for toxic environments and people to poison the well of a lab. The lack of diversity at the faculty level makes it challenging for students from underrepresented backgrounds to find role models to emulate. In the same vein, unless PhD programs put in a LOT of effort toward promoting diversity and nurturing an inclusive environments, we will miss out on unique perspectives in the scientific enterprise.

Q26.text: Honestly, it is a system that rewards individual prestige more than genuine collaboration — labs operate like islands and there is very little incentive to build bridges across groups. I find this kind of exhausting, because the research itself is what I love, but the culture around it can be insular and ego-driven in ways that dont really serve the science. I still believe academia could be something better, more open, but rn it feels like that potential gets wasted on territorial behavior and competition over credit.

Q16.text: The personal side of it, honestly. I have missed important family moments — my parents' health declining, siblings having children — and I carry real guilt about that. There is also the pressure from people back home who dont fully understand what a PhD involves, they expect results, a clear timeline, and explaining delays is its own kind of burden I didn't really anticipate when I started.

Q55.text: That you can love the work and still feel completely alone doing it — I wish someone had told me the culture of a lab matters as much as the research itself. I chose my program based on the project, but the isolation that comes from working in a group that doesn't collaborate with others is something I was not prepared for at all.

Q41.text: Independent research, outside of a traditional academic lab structure if possible. I want the freedom to set my own agenda and actually work across disciplinary lines -- something that feels almost impossible in a lab environment rn. Maybe a research institute or independent fellowship, something like that.

Q60.text: It has been useful to reflect on all of this, tbh. I think what I keep coming back to is that the structural problems I described -- the insularity, the competition over credit -- are not personal failures, they are features of how academic culture is organized right now. That doesn't make it easier to live with, but it helps to name it. I hope this kind of research contributes to something, even in a small way.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- the moments when a problem opens up in an unexpected direction and you follow it wherever it leads. That feeling doesnt exist in most jobs. I also value the time to think deeply about something that actually matters, even when the surrounding culture makes it harder than it should be. Those moments of genuine discovery are what I keep coming back to, what makes the rest of it worth tolerating.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Academic system works more efficiently when there is an open environment. In my experience, I have seen a complete gap here. Many labs working on multiple aspects have different expertise which can be used within the different groups. We struggle on our own, confined in our lab, but cannot seek help from the other lab. PIs have some insecurity or ego issues that lead to a total lack of openness. Ultimately, Ph.D. student struggle on their own at the cost of their time. Many academicians are also very rigid about there research they do not welcome new ideas. The academic system should be more open and acceptable.

Q26.text: The academic system has real strengths -- the depth of inquiry it enables, the collaborative networks -- but it's structurally poorly designed for people who wont end up in the professoriate, which is most of us. Staffing is chronically under-resourced, which creates a kind of pressure that trickles down through every lab, and the training pipeline still defaults to a tenure-track assumption that doesn't reflect where the PhD workforce actually goes.

Q16.text: One thing that hasn't come up is the mental health dimension -- not just individual stress, but the way culture actively discourages acknowledging it. And honestly, there's almost no formal pathway for engaging with policy work during the PhD, so if you want that experience you're essentially building it yourself, on top of everything else.

Q55.text: That institutional structures move slowly and individual advocacy matters less than I expected — building external networks early, outside your department, is probably the single most useful thing you can do for both your career and your sanity.

Q41.text: Science policy or science communication, most likely outside academia. I've kind of come to terms with the fact that the tenure-track path isn't what I'm building toward, and honestly that clarity has been useful -- it's helped me think more intentionally about what skills and networks I actually need to develop.

Q60.text: It would be good to see future iterations of this survey ask more explicitly about non-academic career preparation -- I think a lot of respondents in this position have things to say about that gap but the questions don't quite open it up. Also, the mental health piece feels underexplored in how these surveys are typically framed. Structurally these are systemic issues, not individual ones, and it'd be worth the research reflecting that.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual freedom is hard to match -- being able to dig deep into something that actually matters, on your own terms, is pretty rare. I also find the collaborative side genuinely energising when it works well, the conversations you have with people across disciplines that you just wouldn't have in most jobs.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: There's not enough people to do the amount of work needed, but no funding to supply additional people even though there are plenty available.  What would be useful would be to have another person in the lab to help on multiple projects without increasing the overall productivity of the lab. This would enable everyone in the lab to to maintain a work-life balance.  However, if another person joins a lab, it's expected that they will do another project or that productivity in a project will double.  There needs to be a collective push by the field to bring working hours down back to 40 hours/week/person - with a few exceptional weeks of extra time.

Q26.text:
Honestly, I think it's a system that was designed for a very different era and hasn't updated itself to reflect the reality of what it's asking people to give up. The mentorship model in particular is structurally broken — you have a single person with enormous power over your career, your income, your daily wellbeing, and basically no institutional accountability if they abuse that. I know this from experience, not abstraction. I spent three years in a lab where the environment was genuinely harmful and the department's response was, essentially, nothing. The idea that you just "find a good supervisor" puts all the responsibility on the student to somehow identify a toxic dynamic before they're already inside it, and that's not a reasonable ask of a 22-year-old applying to grad school.

And then there's the financial reality, which I feel like gets talked about in the abstract but never actually addressed -- stipends haven't kept pace with cost of living in most cities, and the assumption that you'll just defer everything else in your life (housing stability, relationships, having kids if you want them) for however many years the degree takes is starting to feel like it asks too much from too many people. I'm 30 and I feel like I've been treading water for years waiting for my "real life" to start.

The thing that gets me is that there are people doing genuinely important work in these programs, and the system manages to grind a lot of them down anyway. It doesn't have to be this way, and the fact that it is feels less like an accident and more like a structural choice no one powerful enough has bothered to revisit

Q16.text:
The career piece is something I think about constantly, and I'm not sure it came through fully in what I said before. I'm actively trying to leave academia — government policy, maybe something adjacent to animal welfare research — and the PhD is supposed to be the credential that opens those doors, but honestly at this point I'm not sure it reads that way to non-academic employers. There's this assumption baked into the degree that you're training for a faculty job, and if that's not what you want (or if, like me, you've watched the system closely enough that you genuinely don't want it), there isn't much infrastructure for figuring out what comes next. Career services at my institution are pretty much useless for anyone going off the standard academic track.

The mental health stuff is also real and I feel like it gets a lot of lip service but not much structural change. I went through a genuinely bad period after I switched labs -- lost a lot of confidence, wasn't sure I could finish, and the support available was basically "here's a counselling waitlist." I got through it but I don't think I should have had to manage that largely on my own.

And honestly, the thing that concerns me most on a personal level is just the time. I'm 30, I want to have kids at some point, and every year this drags on is a year I'm making decisions about my life around a degree that has already taken so much more than I thought it would when I started. that's not a complaint exactly, more like -- I wish someone had been honest with me about the odds before I signed up
</s>

Q55.text:
How to actually vet a supervisor before saying yes. Not the official stuff — the lab website, the publication record, the glossy pitch you get at the campus visit — but the real picture of what it's like to work for that person day to day. I didn't know to ask past students who had left, or to look at whether anyone had finished in a reasonable time, or to notice that the advisor who seemed so intellectually generous in a one-hour meeting was a completely different person once you were dependent on them. I thought "do good work and find a good supervisor" was a reasonable plan. it isn't, not when the information asymmetry is that extreme and a 22-year-old is supposed to make a decision that shapes the next five to eight years of their life.

I lost three years to a situation I probably could have avoided with better information and I don't think that's entirely on me — but I do wish someone had given me a concrete framework for what to look for, and more importantly, what to look out for. The red flags were there. I just didn't know they were red flags yet

Q41.text: Government policy, most likely, with a focus on something related to animal welfare or science policy more broadly. I've spent enough time watching how research funding decisions get made and how little evidence actually shapes policy to feel like that's where I could do more good than grinding out another postdoc. Industry is also on the table -- there are a few organisations working on alternative proteins and animal welfare advocacy that do real research, and that feels like meaningful work in a way that another academic position honestly doesn't anymore. I'm not attached to a specific title or sector at this point, I just want to do something that feels like it has a legible impact and doesn't require me to keep betting my entire life on an academic job market that was already brutal before I started and has only gotten worse since.

Q60.text:
Just that I hope this data actually gets used for something. I've filled out surveys like this before and had the sense they were going in a drawer somewhere, and given how much I've written here I'd like to think it's useful to someone trying to understand what's going wrong structurally and not just anecdotally.

The thing I keep coming back to is that none of what I've described is unusual — that's the part that should alarm people. I'm not an outlier. Every single PhD student I know has some version of this story: the advisor who was great until they weren't, the funding that didn't quite cover the reality of living in a city, the dawning realisation that the career they were training for was a mirage. What's unusual about my situation is maybe the degree of it, but the underlying shape is completely typical, and I think that's worth sitting with.

If I had one ask for whoever reads this, it's to not treat the mental health and mentorship issues as separate from the structural ones. They're not. The reason students end up in crisis isn't bad luck, it's that the system creates conditions where a single relationship has disproportionate power and there are basically no checks on it. Fix the structure and a lot of the individual suffering follows. I don't know if a survey can do that but I hope it's at least part of the argument

Q17.text:
Genuinely, the intellectual freedom — when it's there. There are days where I'm deep in a problem that I actually care about and the work feels meaningful in a way that's hard to replicate anywhere else, and I think that's the thing that kept me going through the harder stretches. The specific questions I'm working on now, around mechanisms I won't bore anyone with here, are ones I chose because they matter to me, not because a grant required them. That kind of autonomy is real and I don't want to pretend it isn't.

I also think the people, surprisingly. Not the institution, not the departmental machinery -- but the other grad students, the ones who are also in the thick of it and understand what it actually costs. Some of my closest friendships have come out of this experience and I think that's partly because shared difficulty creates a particular kind of intimacy. you trust people who've seen you struggle.

But honestly, even answering this question I notice I'm qualifying everything, and I think that's telling. The things I enjoy are real, but they exist inside a structure that makes them harder to access than they should be, and that tension is pretty much constant. I enjoy the work. I wish the conditions for doing it were better

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system is quite flawed in my opinion. Most of the classes I had to take in my first year were useless and interfered with time I could have better spent in the lab. Important skills that would have benefited most students in my graduate studies (e.g. statistical knowledge) were never even touched on.  I had a very bad relationship with my first PI and my department had no way of knowing until I brought it to their attention. As I had never been a graduate student, I thought the situation was normal until I started discussing it with other students. By the time I realized what a toxic situation it was, I had already spent 3 years on the project. Furthermore, after running into some former students by chance, I learned that I wasn't the first student to be treated this way. This suggests that there are PIs out there who have a history of treating students unfairly but basically it is either swept under the rug by the department or never even brought to the attention of the department. I was definitely scared to speak out as my PI hinted that her recommendation would be the most important thing in my future. As far as I know, she is still a PI in the department and still accepting students. Even though I did interview with the lab and spoke to the grad students alone, they did not tell me any of the problems in the lab. But looking back I probably wouldn't either because it might get back to the PI.  As well, almost all PIs are academic. This means that many have no advice or connections to help students who would like to pursue non-academic career paths. I definitely feel like I am on my own once I graduate.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: I started my PhD in a different lab then the one I am in now. I had a very bad relationship with my previous PI and moved lab after 3 years. I had to completely change projects and as a result I am in the 6th year of my PhD and won't finish till at least my 7th or 8th year. With the low pay and high cost of living, I have many things 'on hold' until I graduate and can get a better paying job. The low pay and high stress and workload of an academic job is one reason I am not even considering continuing in academia. One large concern I have going into my future career is that I want to have children fairly soon after I graduate as I am already 30. It's hard to think about finishing a PhD, finding a job, and also having children before I am too old.  At present I can't even say for certain that I will find a good job or one I am interested in...all I know is lab-based research.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: I wish I'd known that I could change departments when going from undergrad to grad studies. I thought since I did an undergraduate in biochemistry and I couldn't pursue a different graduate program. This limited the pool of PIs and projects I was looking into. I think this is probably common knowledge for many students but as my parents did no attend university, they had weren't able to guide me and prospective universities don't really advertise this.  I also wish I had known to look at the number of publications per year that my prospective PI was publishing. If there are very few, it could point to problems in the lab unless they are pursing lengthy studies (e.g. animal aging). Also are their postdocs in the lab? I now work in a lab with postdocs and having that extra mentoring is amazingly useful. I would now look for labs where the project I am placed on is ongoing and one-on-one mentoring/teaching is available - either from a postdoc or ideally, another graduate student who is passing the project on as they are about to graduate. My first project was leftover (and unpublished) from about 6 years before and hadn't been investigated since. This is a big problem because not only do you have no one to talk to but other labs could be close to publishing results that may make the previous work obsolete.

Q41.text: I am really hoping to get into a government policy job or something in industry. I really like working with animals and would love to improve conditions of research animals. However I'm not sure if there is any job where I could do that. Currently I find the federal animal care organization to be more concerned about paperwork then the actual housing conditions and well-being of the animals. There is definitely a big divide now between the vets and the compliance officers that I would like to see solved.

Q26.text: The academic system has genuine intellectual merit — I wouldn't still be here if it didn't — but it's burdened by bureaucratic inertia and, increasingly, a kind of ideological conformity that I find somewhat troubling. The pressure to frame research through particular theoretical lenses rather than following evidence wherever it leads does disservice to the broader goal of knowledge production. and the system's indifference to mental health is, I think, a related problem — sustained creativity requires something other than anxiety and overwork. Reform is possible, but it requires people willing to say uncomfortable things.

Q16.text: The reproducibility crisis in social sciences is something I think about more than I should — it raises genuine questions about whether the work I'm doing will hold up, and whether the field has the institutional honesty to correct itself when it doesn't. That uncertainty is, honestly, pretty draining on top of everything else.

Q55.text: That your mental health isn't a side issue to manage around the real work — it IS the work, in the sense that sustained output over years is only possible if you treat it seriously from day one. I spent a long time thinking the emotional difficulty was a personal failing rather than a structural feature of the environment, and that cost me more than I care to admit.

Q41.text: Data science or statistical consulting — probably outside academia, though I wouldn't rule out a research-adjacent role if the environment were less politically constrained than what I've experienced. The skills transfer well, and honestly the idea of working somewhere where results matter more than ideological alignment is pretty appealing rn.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this data is actually used to push for structural changes rather than filed away. The mental health piece especially — it's systemic, not individual, and institutions keep treating it like the latter. anyway, thanks for asking questions that felt worth answering.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom to pursue genuinely interesting problems is, at least in principle, what keeps me engaged — and on good days, it actually delivers on that promise. There's something that doesn't exist in most jobs, this sense that you're the world's leading expert on your specific narrow question, and I find that legitimately exciting even when everything else is difficult.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I am frustrated about the bureaucracy associated with academic systems, as sometimes I spent hours on dealing with "red tape" matters. As a very non-conformist person, this annoys me very much. I also find that academia is full of people who condone everyone critiquing politically correct opinions (e.g. feminism and left vs. right politics). The latter point is also somewhat disappointing, as I would expect that academics would be the people who are able to entertain thoughts without accepting them.

Q26.text: There is not enough support in case 1) the goals are not met (requirement to publish one paper per PhD) and 2) if there is conflict between the student and the supervisor.   1) Due to the poor finantial support nation-wide, not many labs are well-funded. So I was invited to either remain working without a stipend in order to  publish and try to finish my PhD or leave and drop 5 years of work. My programme's committee did not intervene, yet they were aware of this situation.  2) My programme's committee simply does not know how to protect the student if the supervisor invites them to leave. I was wrongly accused of not working enough by my supervisor and forced to have my progress evaluated not once (which is normal after the first PhD year), but four times. I proved my supervisor and my evaluators wrong at every turn, but I was just told by my programme's committee to "keep on going" and if they talked to my bullying supervisor, "maybe it would make things worse".  There is a lot of work to do to make things better for PhD students world-wide.

I've seen smart people make questionable choices under publication pressure, and its hard not to internalize that. There's genuine intellectual richness here -- the caliber of people I work with is exceptional -- but the incentive structures often reward output over integrity, and that tension doesn't go away.

Q16.text: The MD/PhD identity tension is something I don't think gets talked about enough. You're not quite a regular PhD student, and during the research years you're not really a clinician either -- it's this weird liminal space where you sometimes feel like you don't fully belong in either world. And honestly the timeline is just long. Watching friends from med school enter residency while I'm still in the lab is fine intellectually, I made this choice, but emotionally its a strange thing to sit with sometimes.

Q55.text: How much the advisor relationship shapes everything. I knew intellectually it mattered, but I didn't understand that it would define the entire texture of my PhD -- what projects I work on, how I publish, my mental health, all of it. Choosing a lab is less like picking a research topic and more like picking a boss for five years. I'd have been a lot more deliberate about that conversation if I'd internalized it early.

Q41.text: Physician-scientist at an academic medical center -- 80% research, 20% clinical. I want to keep a foot in patient care but honestly the lab is where I see myself spending most of my time. The clinical side keeps the work grounded, reminds you why any of this matters.

Q60.text: The system is worth improving, and I do think the people trying to do that work matter. But its set up in ways that make honest science harder than it should be -- not impossible, just harder. And for MD/PhDs specifically, there's very little structural support for the identity piece, which I think leads to unnecessary attrition. Someone should study that more seriously, if the incentives ever allow for it.

Q17.text: Honestly, the people. The intellectual caliber of the folks around me -- faculty, postdocs, other grad students -- is something I don't take for granted. And there's a kind of freedom in research that clinical training doesn't have; you're genuinely building something new, which still feels meaningful even on the hard days.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It’s an interesting, unique environment. Friends and family in ‘normal’ jobs will probably never really understand exactly the daily work that I do and will do. I am fortunate to surround myself with very bright people who have innate intellectual curiosity, and our goals and how we view work itself is fundamentally different than say, my mom’s view of her job. Also, being in an MD/PhD program, I also view my role and training slightly differently that other PhD peers. We all have intellectual curiosity, but the drive to pursue particular research questions might be slightly different. I know I have a lot of medical training still ahead of me, on top of my research training, so that is always in the back of my mind, and affects how I mentally prepare myself for the future or decide to or not to pursue certain projects

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: Some PIs who game the system and publish for the sake of publishing rather than actually contributing to science (one PI I have in mind published a lot in Nature type journals, but that is because of their connections and hype around their career). Also, the currency of academia is papers. Publish or perish. That is the first commandment of our field.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: How to read and write more efficiently. The quicker I can read, the quicker I can get a sense of the gaps I can fill with my research. The quicker I can write, the better off I’ll be with publishing my findings, and not get scooped

Q26.text: It's a system that rewards access as much as talent -- knowing the unwritten rules about publications, networking, finding the right supervisor matters more than it should, honestly. There's real intellectual community here that I genuinely value, but the academy loses lot of capable people because of structural failures that nobody officially acknowledges or takes responsibility for.

Q16.text: The mental health piece is something I didn't expect to navigate so heavily. There's a kind of ambient anxiety that comes with funding uncertainty and unclear timelines -- the program doesn't really prepare you for it or acknowledge it exists, honestly. and the isolation of the later PhD years can be pretty significant too, especially when your cohort disperses and you're left grinding on a project that only you and maybe your supervisor actually care about.

Q55.text: The publication pipeline looks completely different depending on whether you're an RA or TA -- I wish someone had told me that upfront rather than leaving me to figure out why some students seemed to have so much more momentum. It's not just about working harder; it's about structural access to research output, and that shapes your CV in ways that compound over time.

Q41.text: Academic research, ideally. I'd like to stay in the academy if the system makes space for it -- though I'm clear-eyed about the odds, and I know a lot comes down to supervisor connections and whether you land in the right network at the right time.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually feeds back into how programs are structured -- there's no shortage of data about what's going wrong, but the gap between knowing and institutional change is where things tend to stall. The supervisor relationship in particular feels underexamined as lever for systemic improvement, not just individual luck.

Q17.text: The intellectual depth of the conversations -- when you find the right people, the quality of thinking you get to engage with daily is genuinely hard to replicate outside academia. I also find real satisfaction in being the person who knows a problem more thoroughly than almost anyone else, even if that depth sometimes feels like it comes at the cost of breadth.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I think many people with drive and talent are being left behind because they don't know the hidden curriculum of a PhD. The hidden curriculum includes all the norms, protocols, expectations, etc. that go along with PhD life - and these things are not in handbooks. I also think that the process of publication is emphasized too much for graduate students - they have their whole lives to publish. On the positive side, I've come out of my PhD work with critical thinking stills that I never would have developed elsewhere as well as opportunities to meet and work with many talented individuals.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: I am in a program where some students are supported as research assistants (RA) and others as teaching assistants (TA). The PIs do not seem to place as high a value on the TA research as the RA research and thus TAs are at a publication disadvantage despite being equally talented.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: I wish I had been assigned to work with a PI who was willing to help me through the hidden curriculum earlier.

Q26.text: Intellectually rewarding but structurally pretty poor, honestly. the research itself is genuinely satisfying, but the system around it -- supervision quality, career development, what counts as a good PhD -- is kind of left to chance. There's no real accountability for whether your supervisor is actually equipped to mentor you, and it sort of assumes you'll figure out the career side on your own, which doesn't work well for most people

Q16.text: The lack of any structured training — like actual research methods courses or even just workshops on how to write grants or navigate the job market — is something that bothered me more as I got further in. it's just assumed you'll absorb it all through osmosis, which works fine if your supervisor happens to be engaged and well-connected, but that's a pretty big if.

Q55.text: That supervisor fit matters way more than project topic or prestige of the institution. I picked my lab largely based on the research area, which in hindsight was kind of naive -- the day-to-day reality of a PhD is mostly shaped by whether your supervisor actually has time for you and knows how to develop people, not just do science.

Q41.text: Academic research -- ideally a postdoc first, then aiming for a fellowship or lectureship and eventually a senior scientist or independent researcher role. I'm pretty clear on the direction, even if the path is obviously uncertain.

Q60.text: Just that I hope surveys like this actually feed into something -- it's easy to feel like this kind of feedback disappears into a void. the issues aren't unsolvable, they just require institutions to actually take PhD training seriously as a structured process rather than an apprenticeship model that depends entirely on supervisor lottery.

Q26.text: Meritocratic in theory, tribal in practice. The best science doesn't always get funded -- it gets funded when it sounds like what reviewers already believe in. Q55.text: That the informal hierarchy matters as much as the formal one. Q60.text: The NSF thing still stings a little, if I'm being honest. I've made my peace with it, but I think about how many other people don't say the quiet part out loud on their applications and just... perform the expected ambitions. Q26.text: The academic system is genuinely impressive in certain ways -- the depth of knowledge people develop, the real commitment to the work -- but structurally it's pretty broken once you've seen it up close. There's a culture of protecting institutions over people, and the power imbalance between PIs and students means abuse can go unchecked for a long time. I've experienced that directly. And the insurance situation for grad students handling carcinogens and mutagens is, tbh, kind of absurd. That said, I've landed somewhere with a mentor who actually cares, and that changes everything -- which honestly just highlights how arbitrary it all is, that your entire PhD experience hinges on one person's character rather than any real systemic protection

Q16.text: The nepotism thing -- honestly it bothers me more than I expected. There's a pattern where certain students get opportunities, authorship, visibility, based on proximity to the right people rather than merit, and it's hard to raise without sounding bitter, so most people just don't. And the blame culture when something goes wrong in a lab is real -- it almost always lands on the student, even when the failure is systemic or the PI set up conditions that made it inevitable. I also think about how little mental health infrastructure there actually is versus how much it gets advertised. Like, we have a counseling center that's booked out six weeks. That's not a resource, that's a liability shield.

Q55.text: How to actually vet a PI before committing. I knew to look at publications and funding, but I had no idea how to assess someone's mentorship style, how they handle conflict, whether they're the kind of person who throws students under the bus when something goes wrong. You can't get that from a lab website. You have to talk to current students -- and even then, people are scared to be honest because word gets around. I wish someone had told me to treat choosing a lab like a job interview where you're also the one doing the hiring, and that it's okay to walk away from an offer if something feels off. The cost of getting it wrong is enormous and it took me longer than it should have to understand that the institution wasn't going to protect me if it did go wrong

Q41.text: Government science or policy, or science communication -- honestly I've become pretty skeptical of staying in academia long-term after everything I've seen. I'm open to research roles at government agencies or maybe science journalism and outreach, something where the work still matters but the power dynamics aren't so completely stacked against you. Medical institutions are on the table too, but only if the environment is right. I'm not ruling anything out, I just dont want to spend my career in a system that protects itself over the people doing the work.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this data actually gets used for something -- I've filled out enough surveys that went nowhere to be a little cynical about it, but I do think the issues I've described are real and pretty widespread, not just my bad luck. The PI selection problem, the insurance gaps for students working with hazardous materials, the mental health theater -- these aren't edge cases. And I think the field loses a lot of good people because the structural problems feel too entrenched to fight. I'm still here and still genuinely love the science, which I guess says something. but I wouldn't want someone else to go through what I went through just to get to that point.

Q17.text: Honestly, the science itself -- just the actual work of figuring something out, running an experiment and getting a result that surprises you, that part is still genuinely exciting to me. And I've really found a home in outreach and science communication -- getting to explain what we do to people outside the field, watching someone go from confused to curious, that feels meaningful in a way that another paper sometimes doesn't. I also love the conversations you have with other grad students, the kind of late-night "what does any of this mean" talk that you cant really have anywhere else. Those things are real and I don't want to lose them in all the frustration with how the system works. it's part of why I'm still here.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It is awful. In the states, there are not enough offers, incredible nepotism, and overall the people leading our program are combative and self-minded. The lower people (such as my current PI) are outstanding and offer the greatest ability to their students. So overall, personal laboratories are fantastic in their support but the program offer little to no assistance and drives down the whole. It is the issue with the tiered academic system I believe.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: That list was quite comprehensive. My issue, personally, any problem is always attributed to the student without investigating the cause. This causes students to lose faith in their programs and doubt their propsects. We also have graduate students with injuries that we cannot fix due to lack of insurance, yet, we (graduate students) work with carcinogens, mutagens, radioactivity etc on a daily basis but have no protection for accidents unless severe and these will come with penalties later in the form of repercussions. We have a graduate student who broke her arm and cannot get the necessary care she needs because lack of affordable health insurance.

Therefore, picking PI is quite important and if the PI has never had students -- there is a reason why.

Q26.text: The academic system assumes that proximity to a supervisor translates into mentorship, and that assumption fails often enough to be a structural problem, not just an individual one. In practice, you can complete a PhD having received almost no genuine intellectual guidance, and the system records that as a success. What's absent is any accountability mechanism that distinguishes real mentorship from administrative oversight dressed up as supervision -- and honestly, that gap is not small.

Q16.text: The peripheral nature of my project within the group is something I didn't anticipate being a problem. Work that sits outside the group's main interests receives no organic feedback -- you can go months without anyone engaging critically with what you're doing, and honestly that kind of isolation is slow-acting. It compounds in ways that are hard to attribute to any single failure.

Q55.text: The gap between a supervisor's administrative role and their actual capacity for mentorship. I knew supervision varied in quality, but I didn't understand that you could be assigned to someone who had effectively stopped doing science -- someone whose engagement with your work is procedural rather than intellectual. Knowing that earlier would have changed the questions I asked at the selection stage, honestly.

Q41.text: Research-focused roles primarily, though I'm also drawn to consultancy and technical leadership where the work remains substantively analytical. Academia as a path feels less straightforward than it did at the start -- the institutional side of it is not what I'd hoped to be embedded in long-term.

Q60.text: The experience has clarified something I didn't expect to come away with: a fairly precise understanding of what doctoral training requires and how often it falls short. That's not nothing, but it's a harder-won insight than it should have been. The supervision question is structural -- it won't resolve by hoping for better individual fit. I think surveys like this are a reasonable place to surface that, though I'm skeptical anything systematic changes as a result.

Q17.text: The intellectual autonomy is real, even when the support around it isn't. Working through a problem on your own terms -- following the logic wherever it leads without someone redirecting you for administrative reasons -- has a clarity that's genuinely hard to find elsewhere. That part of it, the actual physics, is not the problem.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Uneven. Some research groups in my department seem to be well balanced, with a good supervisor-student ratio and sufficient post-docs to support. The students learn from and work with the academics and post-docs. My group has a large number of students, only two full time academics, and a varying number of post-docs who change every year or two. Supervision is inadequate. Students mostly train each other. Supervisor interaction with individual students projects is very shallow.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: I hoped my supervisor would become my scientific mentor. My supervisor actually turned out to be a manager who is good at securing funding, but taught me no science and was completely uninspirational. My project was different from the main work of the group, and so I mostly worked alone. It was very disappointing, slowed my work, and is not at all how things should be, or could be.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: A supervisor with many PhD students is a bad thing. A very well respected physicist I met told me he only ever took on one PhD student at a time - any more and he would not be able to give them the time they need. I would look for a keen supervisor with at most one or two other students, who has a passionate interest in the science who would actually be interested in the project, not just its funding stream.

Q26.text: The academic system is honestly pretty competitive in ways that aren't always productive. There's genuine collegiality in some pockets — good collaborators, people who share ideas freely — but the incentive structures push everyone toward self-preservation. you end up in this environment where citations and output matter more than actual scientific progress, and work-life balance gets treated like a personal failing if you prioritize it. I'm glad I'll be moving into industry, where at least the dysfunction is more openly acknowledged.

Q16.text: The mental load of it, honestly — not just the research itself but the constant background hum of anxiety about whether you're moving fast enough, whether your experiments will pan out. I've gotten better at not tying my self-worth to my results but it took longer than it should have

Q55.text: That your emotional wellbeing and your experimental outcomes are completely separate things. I spent way too long treating every failed run as a referendum on whether I was cut out for this, and it's exhausting in a way that compounds over time. Separating the two doesn't come naturally -- you have to actively choose it.

Q41.text: Industry research, ideally at a well-resourced lab where I can do meaningful science without the publish-or-perish grind.

Q60.text: Just that I think these kinds of surveys are worth doing -- the PhD experience gets romanticized a lot and it's useful to have actual data on what people are going through. Hopefully it's useful to someone.

Q17.text: The flexibility, honestly. You set your own hours, you can go deep on a problem without someone pulling you into a meeting, and when the work clicks it's genuinely satisfying in a way that's hard to replicate. I also appreciate the people -- when you find colleagues who are actually collaborative rather than competitive, those relationships are pretty great.

Q26.text: I think some people are very helpful but others are very selfish and do not want to help if it does not directly influence them. That said some people are very approachable and will help. We have to do a progress report after a year and a half and I found that the feedback I got from other PIs in the department was great. It was a good opportunity to sit down with my PI and discuss their thoughts about where my project is going

Q26.text: The academic system is, in many respects, shaped as much by circumstance as by raw ability. There are genuine structural problems -- the precarity of early-career positions, the pressure to publish rather than think -- but I find these frustrations matter considerably less when one's motivation is primarily intellectual rather than instrumental. In short, it tends to reward those who treat research as path to status, which is perhaps why so many find it demoralizing; those drawn chiefly by curiosity navigate it rather better.

Q16.text: The concern that surfaces most readily is perhaps not about my own experience but about the broader culture I'm entering. I've noticed how quickly ambition can curdle into careerism -- people chasing metrics rather than questions, which I find genuinely dispiriting to witness. That said, it hasn't threatened my own sense of purpose rn, more a kind of ambient unease about the environment rather than any specific obstacle I face personally.

Q55.text: That the pace of genuine intellectual progress is far slower than you expect — and that this is completely normal. I came in imagining breakthroughs arriving at regular intervals; what I found instead is that most of the real work is a kind of patient, unglamorous accumulation. I wish someone had told me early on that uncertainty isnt a sign you're doing it wrong, its actually the medium you work in.

Q41.text: Academic research and teaching -- those are the two things the PhD has clarified for me more than anything else. I came in with a vague sense that I wanted to stay in academia, and the experience has, if anything, deepened that commitment rather than shaken it.

Q60.text: Mostly I'd just say that the survey asked the right kinds of questions -- the ones about motivation and culture felt more probing than I expected, which I appreciated. The experience of doing a PhD is genuinely difficult to capture in a questionnaire, but I think this came closer than most. My only observation would be that the framing occasionally assumed a degree of dissatisfaction I don't fully share; not every PhD student is struggling, and some of us are here because this is exactly where we want to be.

Q17.text: Honestly, the thing I enjoy most is the sustained freedom to follow a question wherever it leads -- without having to justify its immediate utility to anyone. There's something I find pretty irreplaceable about that. And the teaching, when it happens, reinforces rather than interrupts the research; explaining ideas carefully is its own form of thinking. I guess what I'm describing is just intellectual autonomy, which sounds abstract until you've had it and know you'd struggle to give it up.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The problem with the academic system is I think that a lot of people don't have the right reasons for doing a PhD. You have to be really engaged with the research and understand why it is important and why you are doing it. I think it is important to interact beyond academia if one is to have a sense of what the rest of the world does. If this is the case, then it becomes clear that fundamental research is a very special vocation to follow. Additionally, the opportunity to educate the next generation is a very serious and humbling task. I feel that people pick the wrong reasons to enter the academic system beyond undergraduate, such as prestige, university life and academic "independence". In short, I don't think that people understand that it can be really hard to do research and end up blaming the system instead. Of course, there are many aspects that can be fixed - like mental health awareness, work-life balance, integration for under represented communities - but they don't address the fundamental issue that research is hard, primarily solitary, and probably not for everyone - and this is okay.

Q55.text: Research is hard and that having an open mind and asking the obvious questions to people who know what they are doing is very beneficial.
