Q26.text: The academic system, at least as I have experienced it, functions primarily as a labor extraction mechanism sustained by the myth of meritocracy and the increasingly threadbare promise of tenure-track positions that fewer than 15% of graduates will ever hold. Graduate students are simultaneously students, cheap instructors, and research assistants, with no meaningful union protections at right-to-work institutions and no real recourse when the workload becomes genuinely unsustainable. In my second year I was assigned four lab sections — 120 students — while being expected to maintain research productivity; the math simply doesn't work unless you accept that sleep and mental health are optional inputs. The structural incentives reward faculty who extract the most from graduate students and punish those who resist, which is why individual mentorship quality varies so wildly -- it's not a personality lottery, it's a design feature. I've been fortunate to have an adviser who treats me like a colleague, but she is housed in a different department, and the department I nominally belong to has made clear in ways both explicit and implicit that my presence is tolerated rather than valued. Mental health crises among graduate students aren't individual failures; they're the predictable output of a system that combines financial precarity, hierarchical vulnerability, and profound isolation, and then tells you to visit the counseling center. Honestly, the most clarifying thing my PhD has given me is a granular understanding of exactly what I want to work to change at the policy level.

Q16.text: The near-exit I had in year two deserves its own mention. My primary research question was scooped by a lab with five times the resources and institutional support, and the department's response was essentially administrative silence — no bridge funding, no formal guidance on how to pivot, just an implicit suggestion that perhaps this wasn't the right fit. My adviser, again from outside the department, is the reason I'm still here; she spent weeks helping me reframe the project and, critically, located a small grant that bought me eight months of runway. That experience clarified something important: the material conditions for completing a PhD at a right-to-work institution are genuinely fragile in ways that have nothing to do with intellectual capability, and the support infrastructure collapses exactly when you need it most. and honestly the administrative dysfunction isn't incidental — it functions as a filter that disproportionately removes students who lack external social capital or financial cushion, which is worth noting when departments celebrate their "diverse" entering cohorts without tracking who actually finishes.

Q55.text: The distinction between your adviser and your department is not a technicality — it is a structural reality with material consequences, and I wish someone had spelled that out before I signed anything. I evaluated my program almost entirely on my adviser's reputation and our early conversations, which were genuinely excellent, and I paid almost no attention to the department's culture, its completion record, or whether it had any meaningful mechanisms for addressing labor disputes. At a right-to-work institution, none of those mechanisms exist in any enforceable form anyway, and the department's culture is the only check on exploitative conditions -- which is to say, at many institutions, there is no real check at all. Knowing to ask "what does the department do when a student's project gets scooped mid-degree?" or "what is the median time to degree, and why?" would have given me information I could actually have used. My adviser has been the reason I'm still here, honestly, but an excellent adviser embedded in a hostile department is at best a partial solution to a structural problem

Q41.text: Work in international public health policy, specifically with an organization like WHO, MSF, or a mid-size NGO focused on research ethics or health equity governance. I'm not interested in academia -- the system I've described doesn't produce institutions I want to reproduce, and I think the policy level is where the structural changes I care about actually happen. My PhD has been clarifying in that sense, if not in others.

Q60.text: I'd just add that surveys like this one are valuable precisely because they generate the kind of disaggregated, self-reported data that departments and universities prefer not to collect themselves -- there's an obvious institutional interest in not having completion rates, time-to-degree, or teaching load distributions documented in any systematic way. So I appreciate that this work is being done. But I'd encourage whoever analyzes these responses to resist the temptation to treat the patterns as primarily attitudinal -- i.e., that students who struggle have the wrong expectations or insufficient resilience. The material conditions I've described aren't perceptions. Four lab sections is four lab sections. Eight months of bridge funding located by my adviser through her personal network is not a support system; its the absence of one. The difference matters for what kinds of interventions actually help. I hope the data is used accordingly.

Q17.text: The intellectual content itself, genuinely. When I'm deep in a methodological problem or reading across fields that don't usually talk to each other, that part still feels meaningful -- it's the reason I came, and it hasn't entirely been ground out of me yet. My relationship with my adviser is also something I don't want to minimize; she treats my ideas seriously and has gone well beyond any reasonable professional obligation to keep my project viable. Those two things -- the work itself and one good professional relationship -- have been enough to keep me functional, which is maybe not the strongest endorsement of the overall experience but is an honest account of what the enjoyment actually looks like from inside it.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Garbage. While I've been lucky to have an excellent mentor and dedicated committee, the department and school I'm in offer at best little support for graduate students, and at worst, active attempts to sabotage those students. The default assumption is that a funded graduate student will teach all five years of their funding package, and the burden of responsibility of those teaching assignments has steadily increased over the five years of my PhD. For example, introductory lab teaching responsibilities have increased from 2 courses/week per TA to 3 courses/week per TA. This adds another 30 students' worth of grading to grading responsibilities, and another 5 hours per week between actual lab run time (3 hours), setup and cleanup (1 hour) and office hours (1 hour per lab session). This makes it impossible to confine teaching responsibilities to the 20 hours/week we're paid for (if you're spending 15 hours a week teaching, that leaves 5 hours a week to grade 90 lab reports. You try grading 90 lab reports in 5 hours. It doesn't happen--and that's not counting troubleshooting via email or addressing student concerns over email). Additionally, the number of trainings for teaching responsibilities we are expected to complete rises steadily every year, creating an unpredictable time commitment that varies from semester to semester. The end result is a burdensome, difficult to navigate system that means for most of the time you're working, you're doing teaching-related activities. Late in the programme, as I am, this can be deadly--you're faced with a choice of whether to assume debt for your last year or years or quit the programme due to simply not having time for research due to teaching responsibilities.  This wouldn't be so bad if those assignments were predictable and reliable, but they aren't. Colleagues haven't received their contract or their funding until well after the semester's actually started; I've been badgered for weeks by the financial services offices on campus because my tuition remission hasn't gone through in a timely manner. The actual wages do not reflect the cost of living. I am lucky because I receive a degree of financial support from my family, but medical and other kinds of debt among graduate students at my institution is common. I've been cycled through five separate teaching assignments before the semester started, with the administrators responsible indicating that I might not have one, even if my funding package guarantees it. Overall, it means there's a great deal of insecurity in funding even well into the programme and with a funding package.   There is no ability to unionize or organize for better working conditions. This university is in a right-to-work state, and the graduate student government, while claiming to be lobbying for better wages, is in effect toothless and has had no success in improving working conditions. With the expected ruling that graduate student workers are students first and workers second, there is little likelihood that this will change.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The way in which graduate students are entirely at the mercy of the faculty they teach for, and the faculty and administration of the university, even with a good relationship with an adviser. The total lack of protection for graduate student workers, and the lack of pressure on universities to provide a living wage and fair employment conditions for graduate student workers.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: That in the department I chose, setbacks in research were not an accepted part of the process. I was urged to leave the programme in my second year because the project I'd been working on got scooped. I wish I had changed departments at that point because even though I rescued my project and degree, I have felt unwelcome and unsupported in my programme ever since; my adviser is actually from another department, and only two of my committee are from my 'home' department. But the administrative burden in switching departments was prohibitive. If I'd known about this I would have started in my current adviser's department.

Q41.label: What type of career are you interested in pursuing after your graduate degree?
Q41.text: I want to pursue a career in either an international organization or an NGO in public health policy and ethics.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: Please do something to change the culture around graduate school. We are used as disposable workers, with little support or assistance available, and power imbalances mean that if a faculty member wants you out, you're out. Mental health initiatives are laughable; seeing a therapist once a week treats symptoms, but the underlying cause is an unhealthy, exploitative environment in which students are entirely at the mercy of faculty and paid extremely poorly. It would be better to allocate that money to paying students better and improving working conditions, thus alleviating the prevalent economic anxiety  and mental illness from stress and overwork. Mental health support is a band-aid. It's better to have it than nothing at all, but it doesn't actually prevent the injury in the first place.
